title: Nanowire networks' interconnection graphs from their photomicrographs
summary: Self-assemblies of tunable units are being intensively studied as physical systems with signal-processing capabilities. Specifically, silver nanowire networks (AgNWNs) have demonstrated accumulation, non-linearity, and memory retention with multiple timescales, features that enable a wide variety of neuromorphic implementations. In this study, we aim to extract the interconnection scheme to analyze the experimentally obtained network architecture and, eventually, use it as input to a previously developed simulation platform. By post-processing photomicrographs of AgNWN, we present a pipeline optimized to extract the interconnection diagram, recognizing the intersections formed among the nanowires, to determine the associated graph for each physical sample. A graph is a collection of nodes and edges whose properties can be associated with different electrical responses. It is thus possible to study graphs' metrics, such as the degree distribution, community size, clustering coefficient, and path-length, to compare the experimental assemblies' attributes to those of topological models of reference. Small-world, modular, and scale-free are well-known structures in the field of mathematical graphs. By analyzing the degree distribution, the adjacency matrices, among other useful representation means, the experimental assemblies reveal similarities to both small-world and modular topologies. All the mentioned analyses were conducted considering the interconnection scheme obtained from zenithal-view optical images, which overestimates the number of NWs' interconnections (due to the impossibility of distinguishing real junctions from spurious cross-points between vertically displaced NWs). For that reason, this communication also studies the impact of artificially removing junctions from the resulting graphs on the previously calculated clustering coefficient and path length.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a pipeline to extract interconnection graphs from photomicrographs of silver nanowire networks (AgNWNs) for neuromorphic computing. The extracted graphs are analyzed using metrics like degree distribution, clustering coefficient, and path length, revealing similarities to small-world and modular topologies. The study also addresses overestimation of junctions due to zenithal-view imaging by artificially removing spurious cross-points and analyzing the impact on graph metrics.
AI.motivation: To extract the interconnection scheme from experimentally obtained silver nanowire networks and use it as input for a simulation platform, enabling better understanding and modeling of their neuromorphic signal-processing capabilities.
AI.method: A pipeline optimized to post-process photomicrographs of AgNWNs, recognizing intersections among nanowires to extract the interconnection diagram. Graph metrics (degree distribution, community size, clustering coefficient, path length) were computed and compared to topological models (small-world, modular, scale-free). Artificial junction removal was performed to address overestimation from zenithal-view images.
AI.result: Experimental AgNWN assemblies show similarities to both small-world and modular topologies based on degree distribution and adjacency matrix analysis. The study quantified the impact of spurious junction overestimation by artificially removing junctions and measuring changes in clustering coefficient and path length.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline effectively extracts network graphs from physical AgNWN samples, and the experimental networks exhibit structural properties resembling small-world and modular graphs, relevant for neuromorphic computing applications. Accounting for overestimated junctions is critical for accurate network characterization.

title: Point Group Equivariant Graph Neural Networks for Materials
summary: Equivariant graph neural networks have proven effective tools for inference of material's properties directly from their structure. Traditionally, these have been applied such that they respect full $O(3)$ equivariance, so that any rotation or reflection of the input structure is respected in the model's output. While this works for general arrangements of atoms, additional symmetries of atomistic systems are left unleveraged. Furthermore, any symmetries of the filter functions are implicitly learned from the full dataset and not strictly enforced. In this work, we introduce point-group symmetry aware equivariant graph neural networks (PGEqNN) for materials science, with filter functions aligned with symmetry-aware indices for greater granularity in predictive tasks. With this architecture, we show that most of the predictive power of equivariant networks for tensorial elastic and dielectric datasets lies in the trivial subspaces of the point-group adapted bases. Exploiting this, an $A_1$-restricted variant matches or improves on its full point-group and $SO(3)$-partitioned counterparts while training fewer active parameters, yielding leaner models of equal accuracy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces point-group symmetry aware equivariant graph neural networks (PGEqNN) for materials science, showing that most predictive power for tensorial properties lies in trivial subspaces, enabling leaner models with fewer active parameters while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Traditional O(3)-equivariant graph neural networks for materials property prediction do not leverage additional symmetries of atomistic systems, and filter function symmetries are only implicitly learned rather than strictly enforced.
AI.method: The authors propose PGEqNN with filter functions aligned to symmetry-aware indices. They also introduce an A1-restricted variant that uses only trivial subspaces of point-group adapted bases.
AI.result: Most predictive power for tensorial elastic and dielectric datasets lies in the trivial subspaces of point-group adapted bases. The A1-restricted variant matches or improves upon full point-group and SO(3)-partitioned counterparts with fewer active parameters.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting point-group symmetry enables leaner and equally accurate models by using symmetry-aware indices and restricting to trivial subspaces, reducing parameter count without sacrificing performance.

title: Transport-Weighted Coercivity in Granular CrO2: Why Magnetoresistance and Magnetization Can Disagree
summary: Magnetoresistance hysteresis is often used to estimate the coercive field of a magnetic material. We reanalyse our published magnetotransport and magnetometry data on compacted powders of the half-metallic ferromagnet CrO2 and show that this identification can fail in a granular conductor. The field Hp at the resistance maximum may be close to, above, or below the bulk coercive field Hc, depending on temperature and measuring current. For three samples with different particle shapes and insulating-shell thicknesses, the digitized ratio Hp/Hc follows the same qualitative sequence and suggests a common crossover near 15 K. We interpret this behaviour as a change in which interparticle junctions control the electrical response. Bulk magnetometry averages over the entire magnetic volume, whereas tunnelling resistance gives the largest weight to the small set of links that carries the current. Cohn's exact network-sensitivity theorem provides a rigorous linear-response definition of these transport weights. In simple terms, Cohn showed that the influence of a given contact on the total resistance is proportional to the square of the current flowing through that contact. Combined with known magnetic pair-correlation effects, this leads to the concept of transport-weighted coercivity. In granular sensors and spin-dependent composites, the resistance peak cannot automatically be treated as the bulk coercive field. Conversely, the difference Hp - Hc may serve as a diagnostic of current-path localization, barrier evolution, and device-to-device variability.

AI.tldr: The coercive field estimated from magnetoresistance hysteresis (Hp) can deviate from the true bulk coercive field (Hc) in granular conductors like CrO₂ compacts, due to transport-weighting effects where current-carrying junctions dominate the resistance response rather than the entire magnetic volume.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that using magnetoresistance hysteresis to estimate coercive fields can be misleading in granular conductors, and to explain the physical origin of deviations between Hp and Hc.
AI.method: Reanalysis of published magnetotransport and magnetometry data on compacted CrO₂ powders with different particle shapes and insulating-shell thicknesses; application of Cohn's network-sensitivity theorem to interpret transport-weighted coercivity.
AI.result: Hp/Hc varies with temperature and current, showing a qualitative crossover near 15 K across three samples. Hp can be close to, above, or below Hc depending on conditions.
AI.conclusion: The resistance peak in granular systems should not be automatically equated to bulk coercive field; the difference Hp - Hc can serve as a diagnostic for current-path localization, barrier evolution, and device variability.

title: Distinct reentrant transitions in a quasi-periodic Raman lattice
summary: We investigate a one-dimensional lattice with spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and a Zeeman potential containing uniform and quasiperiodic components. By tuning SOC, anomalous mobility edges emerge that separate critical from non-critical states, yielding a reentrant transition between two mixed phases, M$_1$$\to$M$_2$$\to$M$_1$, where M$_1$ (M$_2$) lacks (hosts) anomalous mobility edges. A new \emph{reentrant criticality transition}, defined as multiple entries into the critical phase, is identified. As a counterpart to reentrant delocalization/localization transitions, it completes the basic framework of reentrant phenomena across extended, localized, and critical states. The uniform Zeeman potential drives a reentrant delocalization transition, arising from the splitting of the localized region induced by the shift of mobility edges. This reveals a distinct pathway for reentrant phenomena beyond hybridization mechanisms.

AI.tldr: This paper studies a 1D lattice with spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman potential with uniform and quasiperiodic components, discovering reentrant transitions between mixed phases and a new reentrant criticality transition involving multiple entries into the critical phase.
AI.motivation: To understand how spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman potentials with quasiperiodic components give rise to anomalous mobility edges and reentrant transitions between critical, extended, and localized states.
AI.method: Investigates a one-dimensional lattice model with spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman potential containing both uniform and quasiperiodic components, analyzing the resulting mobility edges and phase transitions.
AI.result: Identifies anomalous mobility edges separating critical from non-critical states, a reentrant transition M1→M2→M1 between mixed phases, and a new reentrant criticality transition. The uniform Zeeman potential drives a reentrant delocalization transition via splitting of the localized region due to mobility edge shifts.
AI.conclusion: The findings complete the basic framework of reentrant phenomena across extended, localized, and critical states, revealing a distinct pathway for reentrant phenomena beyond hybridization mechanisms.

title: Relativistic bound-state solutions for a non-central Schi{ö}berg-type hyperbolic potential with double ring-shaped angular terms
summary: Singular interactions can reshape quantum spectra by changing admissible wavefunction domains. In this study, we investigate this mechanism in the Klein--Gordon equation for a non-central Schiöberg-type hyperbolic potential with double ring-shaped angular barriers. Equal scalar and vector couplings separate the radial and angular dynamics. We solve the angular equation exactly and treat the radial equation with the Greene--Aldrich approximation, obtaining Jacobi-polynomial wavefunctions and an implicit relativistic quantization condition. The equatorial inverse-square singularity splits configuration space into reflection-related sectors with identical angular spectra. Reducing the barrier to zero within one sector retains only odd-parity states, unlike the regular full-domain problem, which restores both parities. The nonrelativistic limit recovers the Schr{ö}dinger spectrum. For NaH and Na$_2$, low-lying vibrational energies agree reasonably with experiment, whereas near-dissociation deviations reveal asymptotic limitations.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how singular interactions, via a Klein-Gordon equation with a Schiöberg-type potential and double ring-shaped angular barriers, reshape quantum spectra by altering admissible wavefunction domains, leading to parity selection effects and reasonable agreement with experimental vibrational energies for NaH and Na₂.
AI.motivation: To understand how singular interactions, particularly through domain modifications from angular barriers, reshape quantum spectra in relativistic settings, and to test the model against experimental data for diatomic molecules.
AI.method: The Klein-Gordon equation with a non-central Schiöberg-type hyperbolic potential and double ring-shaped angular barriers is studied. Equal scalar and vector couplings separate radial/angular dynamics. The angular equation is solved exactly, and the radial equation uses the Greene–Aldrich approximation. Jacobi-polynomial wavefunctions and an implicit relativistic quantization condition are derived.
AI.result: The equatorial inverse-square singularity splits configuration space into reflection-related sectors with identical angular spectra. Reducing the barrier to zero within one sector retains only odd-parity states, unlike the regular full-domain problem. The nonrelativistic limit recovers the Schrödinger spectrum. For NaH and Na₂, low-lying vibrational energies agree reasonably with experiment; near-dissociation deviations reveal asymptotic limitations.
AI.conclusion: Singular interactions via angular barriers cause parity selection effects in relativistic quantum spectra. The model works well for low-lying states but has asymptotic limitations near dissociation for diatomic molecules.

title: The Geometry of Semantic Space: A Continuous Geometric Framework for the Transformer Architecture
summary: We present a continuous geometric framework that models the discrete algebraic operations of the Transformer architecture as an integro-differential equation (IDE) on a semantic fiber bundle $\calE = \calM \times \R^d$. Beginning from a single geometric axiom -- that the token sequence forms a discrete $1$-manifold equipped with a canonical measure lattice -- we translate every core component of the modern Transformer (RMSNorm, RoPE, Softmax Attention, FFN, Residual Stream, SGD, Weight Decay) into a cohesive vocabulary of differential geometry, measure theory, and stochastic calculus. The resulting framework yields quantitative predictions spanning entropic optimal transport (Attention as a Schrödinger bridge) and non-equilibrium thermodynamics (SGD as Itô diffusion violating detailed balance). We conduct a six-part experimental campaign across five architectures (Qwen3, LLaMA\nobreakdash-3.1, Gemma\nobreakdash-3, GPT-2, Mistral) spanning $124$M to $8$B parameters. The empirical observables are quantitatively consistent with the geometric predictions: the $ε^{-1/2}$ Lipschitz scaling calibration at machine precision ($R^2 = 1.000$), the Lie--Trotter operator-splitting torsion, the symmetric ablation instability confirming the Dual-Law of Topological Stability, the $\calO(1/\sqrt{k})$ thermodynamic suppression of Poincaré recurrence on the RoPE torus, the thermodynamic context-limit phase transition, and the Non-Equilibrium Steady State parameter vortex -- verified across two optimizers (AdamW and Pure SGD) to exclude momentum artifacts. The results demonstrate that analyzing Transformers through the lens of continuous stochastic differential geometry provides a predictive descriptive vocabulary for the stability limits, context bounds, and optimization dynamics of Large Language Models.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a continuous geometric framework modeling Transformer operations as an integro-differential equation on a semantic fiber bundle, deriving quantitative predictions (optimal transport, non-equilibrium thermodynamics) and empirically validating them across five architectures (124M–8B parameters) with high precision consistency.
AI.motivation: To unify the discrete algebraic operations of Transformers (RMSNorm, RoPE, Softmax Attention, FFN, SGD, etc.) under a single continuous geometric formalism using differential geometry, measure theory, and stochastic calculus, enabling predictive understanding of stability limits, context bounds, and optimization dynamics in large language models.
AI.method: Constructs a semantic fiber bundle ℰ = ℳ × ℝ^d where token sequences form a discrete 1-manifold with a canonical measure lattice. Each Transformer component is translated into differential-geometric, measure-theoretic, and stochastic calculus terms. The framework yields predictions including: Attention as a Schrödinger bridge (entropic optimal transport), SGD as Itô diffusion violating detailed balance (non-equilibrium thermodynamics), ε^{-1/2} Lipschitz scaling, Lie–Trotter operator-splitting torsion, Dual-Law of Topological Stability, O(1/√k) thermodynamic suppression of Poincaré recurrence on the RoPE torus, a thermodynamic context-limit phase transition, and a Non-Equilibrium Steady State parameter vortex. Validation across five architectures (Qwen3, LLaMA-3.1, Gemma-3, GPT-2, Mistral) from 124M to 8B parameters using two optimizers (AdamW, Pure SGD).
AI.result: Empirical observables are quantitatively consistent with geometric predictions: ε^{-1/2} Lipschitz scaling calibration at machine precision (R² = 1.000), confirmed Lie–Trotter torsion, symmetric ablation instability confirming the Dual-Law of Topological Stability, O(1/√k) thermodynamic suppression of Poincaré recurrence, verified context-limit phase transition, and confirmed Non-Equilibrium Steady State parameter vortex across AdamW and Pure SGD optimizers.
AI.conclusion: Analyzing Transformers through continuous stochastic differential geometry provides a predictive and descriptive vocabulary for the stability limits, context bounds, and optimization dynamics of large language models, unifying disparate empirical phenomena under a single mathematical framework.

title: EPIC-CIM: Training Convolutional Neural Networks on a Coherent Ising Machine via Equilibrium Propagation
summary: Quantum convolutional neural networks, due to the involvement of quantum measurements and discrete quantum state evolution, face inherent training challenges associated with non-differentiable operations and discrete optimization dynamics, which make conventional gradient-based learning difficult to apply effectively. In this context, energy-based learning provides a promising alternative by reformulating network training as an energy minimization process without explicit gradient backpropagation.In this framework, input data are processed through convolutional operations, followed by quantum sampling to generate intermediate binary representations, while the output layer also relies on quantum sampling to produce final predictions. The overall network energy is composed of convolutional feature matching terms, linear coupling terms at the output layer, and global output constraint terms, enabling both parameter updates and feature evolution to be described through physically interpretable energy dynamics. Furthermore, under the equilibrium propagation mechanism, the energy difference between the free phase and the weakly clamped phase is exploited to drive parameter updates without explicit gradient computation, thereby enabling stable and consistent learning in non-differentiable and discrete spaces. While remaining consistent with classical convolutional learning theory, the proposed framework enhances interpretability and observability through quantum energy modeling, offering a unified physical perspective for efficient QCNN training and the integration of quantum computing with artificial intelligence.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an energy-based learning framework for quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) that addresses training challenges caused by non-differentiable operations and discrete quantum state evolution. By reformulating training as energy minimization with equilibrium propagation, parameter updates are driven by energy differences between free and weakly clamped phases, eliminating the need for explicit gradient computation.
AI.motivation: Quantum convolutional neural networks face inherent training difficulties due to quantum measurements and discrete quantum state evolution, which make conventional gradient-based learning methods ineffective because of non-differentiable operations and discrete optimization dynamics.
AI.method: The network is trained via energy-based learning: input data undergoes convolutional operations, then quantum sampling generates intermediate binary representations and final predictions. Network energy comprises convolutional feature matching terms, linear coupling terms at the output layer, and global output constraint terms. Parameter updates are driven by equilibrium propagation, exploiting energy differences between the free phase and the weakly clamped phase without explicit gradient computation.
AI.result: The framework enables stable and consistent learning in non-differentiable and discrete spaces, providing a physically interpretable energy dynamics for both parameter updates and feature evolution, while remaining consistent with classical convolutional learning theory.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enhances interpretability and observability through quantum energy modeling, offering a unified physical perspective for efficient QCNN training and bridging quantum computing with artificial intelligence.

title: Statistical-mechanics of a three-body Hopfield model with finite connectivity
summary: A three-body Hopfield model defined on sparse random graphs with finite mean connectivity is studied using a replica-symmetric (RS) analysis. By extending the functional replica framework for conventional two-body finite-connectivity Hopfield models, self-consistent equations for the local-field distribution are derived and solved numerically by population dynamics. In contrast to two-body sparse Hopfield models, three-body interactions induce a discontinuous retrieval transition, coexistence of paramagnetic and retrieval solutions, and a distinct spinodal structure. Starting the RS population dynamics from an uninformative finite-amplitude field distribution leads to a spin-glass-like fixed point at low temperatures rather than to the retrieval state. This trapping already occurs for a single embedded pattern, where conventional cross-talk noise among stored patterns is absent, indicating that it originates from the combination of sparse connectivity and three-body interactions. Within the RS description, increasing the number of embedded patterns drives a crossing between the retrieval and glassy free-energy branches, making the glassy branch thermodynamically stable at high load. Finite-size Monte Carlo simulations using population annealing support the RS description of the retrieval branch and reproduce the trapping behavior under cooling, while deviations from the RS spin-glass branch point to replica-symmetry breaking in the low-temperature glassy regime. The characteristic storage load scales linearly with the mean connectivity, reflecting the sparse number of couplings. These results clarify how many-body discontinuity and sparse graph disorder simultaneously influence the accessibility and capacity of associative memory.

AI.tldr: This paper extends replica analysis to a three-body Hopfield model on sparse random graphs, revealing discontinuous retrieval transitions, spin-glass trapping even with a single pattern, and linear storage capacity with mean connectivity, supported by Monte Carlo simulations.
AI.motivation: To understand how many-body interactions and sparse connectivity jointly affect associative memory, particularly the retrieval transition, spin-glass trapping, and storage capacity in neural networks.
AI.method: Replica-symmetric analysis using a functional replica framework extended to three-body interactions on sparse random graphs, solved via population dynamics; validated by finite-size Monte Carlo simulations with population annealing.
AI.result: Three-body interactions cause discontinuous retrieval transitions, coexistence of paramagnetic and retrieval phases, and spin-glass trapping even with a single pattern. RS theory captures retrieval behavior but deviates in the glassy regime due to replica-symmetry breaking. Storage capacity scales linearly with mean connectivity.
AI.conclusion: The combination of sparse connectivity and many-body interactions fundamentally alters associative memory dynamics, introducing glassy trapping and discontinuous transitions, with RS analysis valid only on the retrieval branch.

title: QR-SPPS: Quantum-Native Retail Supply Chain Risk Simulation via VQE, ADAPT-VQE Counterfactual Policy Ranking, and DOS-QPE Boltzmann Tail Risk Quantification
comment: 38 pages, 12 figures, 9 tables. Developed for the Fujitsu Quantum Simulator Challenge 2025-26. Source code and supplementary materials available upon request
summary: Classical supply chain risk models treat node failures as statistically independent events, systematically underestimating correlated cascade failures across multi-tier supplier networks. We present QR-SPPS (Quantum-Native Retail Shock Propagation and Policy Stress Simulator), a quantum-native framework for retail supply chain risk analysis implemented on the Qiskit ecosystem using OpenFermion-based Ising Hamiltonian encoding. A 40-node, four-tier supply network is mapped to a 40-qubit Hamiltonian with ZZ coupling terms representing correlated supplier dependencies. A hardware-efficient Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) computes the stress ground state, revealing entangled cascade failures that differ substantially from classical Monte Carlo predictions. We further introduce the application of ADAPT-VQE gradient screening for counterfactual policy evaluation, enabling real-time ranking of six crisis interventions without repeated variational optimization. Finally, Density-of-States Quantum Phase Estimation (DOS-QPE) reconstructs the eigenspectrum through Trotter evolution and estimates Boltzmann-weighted catastrophe probabilities as a function of market-volatility temperature, providing a quantum-native tail-risk metric compatible with Value-at-Risk analysis. The framework demonstrates scalable quantum algorithms for correlated supply chain stress propagation, policy optimization, and systemic risk quantification while highlighting the exponential computational barriers faced by classical simulation at industrial-scale problem sizes.

AI.tldr: QR-SPPS is a quantum-native framework using VQE, ADAPT-VQE, and DOS-QPE on a 40-qubit Ising Hamiltonian to model correlated cascade failures in multi-tier retail supply chains, demonstrating advantages over classical Monte Carlo in stress propagation and policy evaluation.
AI.motivation: Classical supply chain risk models assume independent node failures, which systematically underestimates correlated cascade failures across multi-tier supplier networks.
AI.method: Maps a 40-node, four-tier supply network to a 40-qubit Ising Hamiltonian with ZZ couplings; uses VQE to compute stress ground states, ADAPT-VQE for counterfactual policy ranking, and DOS-QPE with Trotter evolution for Boltzmann-weighted catastrophe probabilities and tail-risk metrics.
AI.result: The VQE ground state reveals entangled cascade failures diverging from classical Monte Carlo; ADAPT-VQE enables real-time ranking of six crisis interventions; DOS-QPE provides quantum-native Value-at-Risk metrics.
AI.conclusion: The framework shows scalable quantum algorithms for supply chain risk analysis and highlights exponential classical barriers at industrial scale.

title: Semi-fractality and localization on a chiral Cayley tree
summary: We study a quantum particle hopping on an infinite Cayley tree with nearest-neighbor hopping amplitudes drawn from a distribution singular as $|t|^{-a}$ near weak links and no on-site disorder. Because the graph is bipartite, the model has chiral symmetry, which strongly affects the statistics of eigenstates at the center of the spectrum. Using population dynamics to solve the cavity equations for the propagator, we analyze the distribution of the local density of states and show that it develops broad power-law tails. These tails imply an unusual form of wave-function statistics, which we call semi-fractality: the eigenstates occupy an extensive fraction of the system, but their higher moments behave as in a multifractal state. We find that the symmetry properties of the local-density-of-states distribution are not fixed only by the symmetry class, but vary continuously with the exponent controlling the power-law hopping distribution. As this exponent is changed, the system crosses from a semi-fractal regime to a localized one. At the transition, the wave functions realize an extreme intermediate form that we call semi-localized, simultaneously extended in their support but localized according to higher moments.

AI.tldr: A quantum particle on a Cayley tree with singular hopping distribution and chiral symmetry exhibits "semi-fractality"—eigenstates are extensively supported but have multifractal higher moments—with a continuous symmetry-class variation and a transition to localized or semi-localized states.
AI.motivation: To understand how chiral symmetry and singular hopping on a bipartite tree affect eigenstate statistics, beyond conventional Anderson localization and multifractality.
AI.method: Population dynamics solving cavity equations for the propagator on an infinite Cayley tree with power-law-distributed hopping amplitudes (~ |t|^{-a}) and no on-site disorder.
AI.result: The local density of states develops broad power-law tails; eigenstate moments show semi-fractality (extensive support but multifractal higher moments); symmetry properties vary continuously with the hopping exponent a; a transition from semi-fractal to localized occurs, with "semi-localized" states at the critical point.
AI.conclusion: Chiral symmetry in a singular-hopping model yields novel intermediate wave-function phases (semi-fractal and semi-localized) not captured by standard symmetry classification alone.

title: Intelligence-Guided Adaptive Purification for DDoS-Resilient Quantum Networks: A CUDA-Q based Study
summary: Quantum-repeater networks require adaptive control policies that balance entanglement generation rate, end-to-end fidelity, purification overhead, and memory-induced latency. This tradeoff becomes more complex when the classical control plane is degraded by cyber anomalies or denial-of-service traffic. We develop a CUDA-Q/SeQUeNCe co-simulation workflow for studying adaptive entanglement purification in heterogeneous linear repeater chains. CUDA-Q noisy quantum kernels are used to estimate primitive entanglement purification and swapping behavior, while SeQUeNCe provides an event-layer model for stochastic link generation, waiting-time-dependent memory decay, purification failure, and end-to-end swapping. Under stationary conditions, we compare no purification, local threshold purification, mean-field predictive purification, fixed purification, and a resource-penalized risk-aware predictive policy. In an 8-node chain, the resource-penalized risk-aware controller increases above-target delivery probability relative to fixed purification while reducing latency and purification overhead. We then couple the quantum-network controller to anomaly scores derived from the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 benign-to-SSDP intrusion-detection trace. During the attack period, the attack-unaware controller maintains high raw delivery, but its above-target entanglement delivery falls to 0.098+/-0.007; the IDS-aware resource-adaptive controller switches to more purification-heavy masks and increases above-target delivery to 0.344+/-0.011, closely matching the oracle-aware value of approximately 0.335. These results demonstrate that cyber-state awareness can improve useful quantum-network outcomes by trading raw throughput for fidelity-qualified entanglement delivery.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a CUDA-Q/SeQUeNCe co-simulation framework to study adaptive entanglement purification in quantum-repeater networks under cyber anomalies. A resource-penalized risk-aware predictive policy outperforms fixed purification in above-target delivery, latency, and overhead. When coupled with IDS anomaly scores from CSE-CIC-IDS2018, the IDS-aware controller maintains above-target entanglement delivery (0.344) during SSDP attacks, closely matching the oracle-aware baseline (0.335) and significantly outperforming the attack-unaware controller (0.098).
AI.motivation: Quantum-repeater networks require adaptive control policies that balance entanglement generation rate, end-to-end fidelity, purification overhead, and memory-induced latency, especially when the classical control plane is degraded by cyber anomalies or denial-of-service traffic.
AI.method: The authors develop a CUDA-Q/SeQUeNCe co-simulation workflow: CUDA-Q noisy quantum kernels estimate primitive entanglement purification and swapping behavior, while SeQUeNCe provides an event-layer model for stochastic link generation, memory decay, purification failure, and end-to-end swapping. They compare no purification, local threshold, mean-field predictive, fixed purification, and a resource-penalized risk-aware predictive policy in an 8-node chain, then couple the controller to anomaly scores from the CSE-CIC-IDS2018 intrusion-detection trace.
AI.result: In an 8-node chain, the resource-penalized risk-aware controller increases above-target delivery probability relative to fixed purification while reducing latency and purification overhead. During SSDP attack periods, the IDS-aware resource-adaptive controller achieves above-target delivery of 0.344+/-0.011, closely matching the oracle-aware value (~0.335), versus the attack-unaware controller's 0.098+/-0.007.
AI.conclusion: Cyber-state awareness can improve useful quantum-network outcomes by trading raw throughput for fidelity-qualified entanglement delivery.

title: A Hybrid Classical-Quantum Approach for Multi-Constrained Location Optimization Problem
summary: The Maximal Covering Location Problem (MCLP) is an NP-hard Combinatorial Optimization Problem (COP) that aims to determine the optimal facility placements that maximize total coverage. It is characterized by both equality and inequality constraints, which ensure correct coverage but significantly increase the complexity of exploring the solution space as instance size grows. Hybrid quantum-classical approaches might offer a promising alternative to classical optimization methods by enabling the exploration of complex energy landscapes through quantum superposition and probabilistic sampling. In this work, the MCLP is formulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model, where constraint embedding plays a critical role in solution quality. In particular, Unbalanced Penalization (UP) is employed as an alternative to the Slack Variables (SV) for handling inequality constraints without increasing the number of variables. This study focuses on QAOA and one of its variants, the WS-QAOA, which leverages a biased initial state derived from a continuous relaxation of the problem. Additionally, a linear ramp (LR) parameter schedule is incorporated to reduce optimization complexity. The performance of these techniques is evaluated both individually and in combination, as a function of circuit depth $p$ and problem size. Results show that the combined approach of UP, LR, and WS-QAOA consistently improves solution quality and feasibility metrics, while maintaining robust performance as the problem size increases, highlighting its potential within hybrid quantum-classical optimization frameworks.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates hybrid quantum-classical approaches (QAOA and WS-QAOA with linear ramp schedules) for solving the Maximal Covering Location Problem (MCLP) formulated as a QUBO, using Unbalanced Penalization (UP) to handle inequality constraints without increasing variable count. The combined UP + LR + WS-QAOA method consistently improves solution quality and feasibility as problem size grows.
AI.motivation: MCLP is NP-hard with complex constraints that make classical exploration of the solution space difficult as instance size scales. Hybrid quantum-classical methods (QAOA, WS-QAOA) are explored as promising alternatives due to their ability to leverage quantum superposition and probabilistic sampling.
AI.method: MCLP is formulated as a QUBO model. Inequality constraints are handled via Unbalanced Penalization (UP) instead of Slack Variables (SV) to avoid increasing variable count. The study applies QAOA and WS-QAOA (using a biased initial state from continuous relaxation) with a linear ramp (LR) parameter schedule. Performance is evaluated at varying circuit depths $p$ and problem sizes.
AI.result: The combined approach (UP + LR + WS-QAOA) consistently yields better solution quality and feasibility metrics, with robust performance as problem size scales.
AI.conclusion: The UP + LR + WS-QAOA combination shows strong potential within hybrid quantum-classical optimization frameworks for solving constrained COPs like MCLP.

title: Number Fluctuations and Entanglement-Spectrum Participation in Monitored Free Fermions
summary: Monitored free-fermion chains show a crossover in entanglement scaling as the measurement rate is increased, from a subextensive weak-monitoring regime to an area law at strong monitoring. I test, using trajectory-resolved correlation-matrix simulations of chains up to $L=96$, whether two diagnostics built from the single-particle entanglement spectrum add practical value: the bipartite particle-number fluctuation $F_A=\sum_kν_k(1-ν_k)$ and a participation-style effective number of entangling modes $\mathcal{M}_A=\exp[-\sum_k w_k\ln w_k]$, with $w_k\proptoν_k(1-ν_k)$. Both quantities track the crossover, decreasing monotonically with measurement probability and losing system-size dependence in the strongly monitored regime. However, at the level of trajectory- and time-averaged steady-state values, $\mathcal{M}$ is almost a deterministic function of $F$: a pooled curve captures 99.7\% of its variance across all measurement rates, so $\mathcal{M}$ carries little independent information in this model. Its main advantage is statistical: the trajectory-to-trajectory coefficient of variation of $\mathcal{M}$ is up to a factor of about 2 smaller than that of the entropy or $F$ at strong monitoring. A model comparison of subsystem scaling at $L=48$--$96$ further shows that, at weak monitoring, a pure logarithmic law is not statistically preferred at these sizes; a small residual quasi-extensive component and a drifting effective logarithmic coefficient remain. I conclude that $F$ is the natural experimentally motivated companion to the entropy, while $\mathcal{M}$ is best viewed as a variance-reduced numerical summary of largely the same information, not an independent diagnostic.

AI.tldr: This paper studies entanglement diagnostics in monitored free-fermion chains, finding that the effective number of entangling modes $\mathcal{M}$ carries nearly the same information as the particle-number fluctuation $F$, with 99.7% variance explained by a pooled curve, though $\mathcal{M}$ offers reduced trajectory-to-trajectory variance at strong monitoring. The author concludes $F$ is the natural experimentally motivated diagnostic, while $\mathcal{M}$ is best viewed as a variance-reduced numerical summary.
AI.motivation: To test whether two single-particle entanglement spectrum diagnostics — bipartite particle-number fluctuation $F_A$ and effective number of entangling modes $\mathcal{M}_A$ — add practical value beyond entanglement entropy in monitored free-fermion chains, especially given the experimental relevance of number-resolved measurements.
AI.method: Trajectory-resolved correlation-matrix simulations of free-fermion chains up to L=96 under continuous monitoring, computing the entanglement entropy, $F_A$, and $\mathcal{M}_A$ across varying measurement rates, and analyzing their statistical relationships and scaling behavior.
AI.result: Both $F$ and $\mathcal{M}$ monotonically decrease with measurement rate and lose system-size dependence at strong monitoring. $\mathcal{M}$ is almost a deterministic function of $F$ (99.7% variance explained). $\mathcal{M}$ has up to ~2× lower trajectory-to-trajectory coefficient of variation than entropy or $F$ at strong monitoring. At weak monitoring, subsystem scaling is not purely logarithmic at L=48–96; residual quasi-extensive component and drifting log coefficient remain.
AI.conclusion: $F$ is the natural experimentally motivated companion to entropy, while $\mathcal{M}$ is best viewed as a variance-reduced numerical summary of largely the same information, not an independent diagnostic.

title: A Novel Hybrid Quantum Reservoir Computing (nHQRC) for Phase Transition Detection in Non-Equilibrium Dynamical Systems
summary: The analysis of highly non-linear stochastic data within non-equilibrium dynamical systems requires computational frameworks capable of detecting latent phase transitions before systemic structural breakdowns occur. Traditional Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are frequently bottlenecked by vanishing gradients, the barren plateau problem, and prohibitive training overheads. In this paper, we propose a novel Hybrid Quantum Reservoir Computing (nHQRC) framework, which bypasses these limitations by employing a frozen, disordered Transverse-Field Ising Model (TFIM) to project time-dependent stochastic driving forces into an exponentially large Hilbert space. To resolve the physical phase multi-wrapping vulnerabilities present in baseline quantum reservoir models, we introduce a lookahead-free, pre-amplification manifold scaling technique. Multi-qubit configurations are genetically optimized to the "edge of chaos," while quantum state tracking is performed by extracting von Neumann entropy ($S$) and exact mixed-state Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) to act as leading entanglement witnesses. Utilizing these quantum triggers as boundary constraints, trajectory predictions are constructed via a generative Stochastic Schrödinger Bridge (SSB) readout. By subjecting the quantum reservoir to an 8-dimensional non-stationary stochastic driving field, the framework significantly improves systemic drift-to-diffusion efficiency ($η$) and actively arrests maximum trajectory decay (MTD) by over 13% compared to standard classical benchmarks. This establishes a robust, $\mathcal{O}(1)$ temporal overhead blueprint for near-term quantum regime detection and macroscopic subsystem stabilization.

AI.tldr: A novel hybrid quantum reservoir computing framework (nHQRC) uses a frozen disordered Transverse-Field Ising Model with pre-amplification manifold scaling and quantum Fisher information tracking to detect latent phase transitions in non-equilibrium stochastic systems, achieving over 13% improvement in arresting trajectory decay compared to classical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) suffer from vanishing gradients, barren plateaus, and high training overhead, making them impractical for analyzing highly non-linear stochastic data in non-equilibrium dynamical systems where detecting latent phase transitions before systemic breakdown is critical.
AI.method: Proposes nHQRC framework using: (1) a frozen disordered Transverse-Field Ising Model (TFIM) as a quantum reservoir to project stochastic driving forces into an exponentially large Hilbert space; (2) a lookahead-free pre-amplification manifold scaling technique to resolve phase multi-wrapping; (3) genetically optimized multi-qubit configurations to the edge of chaos; (4) von Neumann entropy and exact mixed-state Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) as entanglement witnesses; (5) a generative Stochastic Schrödinger Bridge (SSB) readout for trajectory predictions.
AI.result: Under 8-dimensional non-stationary stochastic driving, nHQRC improves systemic drift-to-diffusion efficiency (η) and actively arrests maximum trajectory decay (MTD) by over 13% compared to standard classical benchmarks, with O(1) temporal overhead.
AI.conclusion: The nHQRC framework provides a robust, low-overhead blueprint for near-term quantum regime detection and macroscopic subsystem stabilization in non-equilibrium stochastic systems, effectively bypassing VQA limitations.

title: The Quantum Correction to Gaussian Information Geometry is the Killing Form of the Symplectic Algebra
summary: On the admissible cone $\mathcal C_Ω=\{Σ\in\mathrm{Sym}^+(2n):Σ+iΩ\ge0\}$ of Gaussian covariance matrices, the classical Bures--Wasserstein transport metric, the Fisher--Rao information metric, and the quantum Bures metric are individually well understood, but their mutual relationship is obscured by the operator equations defining them. Working with the contravariant (dual) metrics, we show that the exact difference between the dual quantum Bures metric and the dual Fisher--Rao metric is independent of the covariance matrix: it is identically the trace form, proportional to the Killing form, of the symplectic algebra $\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb R)$, pulled back through the isomorphism $X\mapstoΩX$. The signature of this form on the Cartan decomposition reproduces the anisotropic stiffening of the quantum metric at the pure-state boundary: it is negative on the compact subalgebra $\mathfrak u(n)$, which carries the divergence, and positive on the noncompact complement. Because the correction is quadratic in the momenta, a no-go lemma shows it cannot arise from minimal coupling to a principal connection. We realize it instead through a Schur complement of a pseudo-Riemannian metric on a phase bundle, whose base reduction is the quantum Bures metric and whose horizontal metric is the classical-limit Fisher--Rao metric. All identities are verified numerically to working precision.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals an exact, covariance-independent relationship between the dual quantum Bures metric and dual Fisher-Rao metric on the Gaussian covariance matrix cone, identified as the Killing form of $\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb R)$. This correction explains the anisotropic stiffening at the pure-state boundary via Cartan decomposition signatures, cannot arise from minimal coupling, and is instead realized via a Schur complement on a phase bundle.
AI.motivation: The individual metrics (Bures-Wasserstein, Fisher-Rao, quantum Bures) on the Gaussian covariance matrix cone are well understood, but their mutual relationship is obscured by operator equations. The authors aim to clarify this relationship exactly.
AI.method: Working with contravariant (dual) metrics, the authors prove that the difference between the dual quantum Bures metric and dual Fisher-Rao metric is identically the trace form (proportional to Killing form) of $\mathfrak{sp}(2n,\mathbb R)$, pulled back via $X\mapsto\Omega X$. They analyze its signature on the Cartan decomposition and realize the correction via a Schur complement on a phase bundle.
AI.result: The exact difference is independent of the covariance matrix, being a constant quadratic form. Its signature reproduces anisotropic stiffening: negative on $\mathfrak u(n)$ (compact, carrying divergence) and positive on the noncompact complement. A no-go lemma shows minimal coupling cannot produce this correction.
AI.conclusion: The quantum Bures metric arises from a pseudo-Riemannian metric on a phase bundle via Schur complement, with the classical-limit Fisher-Rao metric as the horizontal metric. All identities are numerically verified.

title: Hamiltonian Lift of Bures--Wasserstein Covariance Dynamics with a Spectral Floor
summary: Covariance dynamics on the positive-definite cone are commonly described by gradient flows, which encode dissipative relaxation but obscure the underlying phase-space structure. We construct a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian lift of covariance dynamics on Sym$^+_n$ equipped with the Bures--Wasserstein metric. The natural mechanical Lagrangian yields canonical momentum $Π=\tfrac12 L_Σ[\dotΣ]$, where $L_Σ$ is the Lyapunov operator, and explicit Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}(Σ,Π) = 2{\rm tr}(ΠΣΠ)+V(Σ)$. Adding Rayleigh dissipation recovers the Bures--Wasserstein gradient flow in the overdamped limit. For a spectral-floor and trace-control potential, the quadratic fluctuation Hamiltonian around the isotropic equilibrium separates trace and traceless modes; the baseline stiffness diverges as $(s-ν)^{-2}$ as the equilibrium covariance approaches the floor. The construction identifies a conservative parent system for constrained Bures--Wasserstein covariance relaxation and fixes the local stiffness scale induced by the spectral floor.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a Hamiltonian lift of covariance dynamics on the positive-definite cone with the Bures-Wasserstein metric, revealing an underlying phase-space structure that gradient flows obscure. It derives explicit Hamiltonian mechanics, recovers overdamped gradient flow via dissipation, and analyzes fluctuation spectra near equilibrium with a spectral-floor potential, identifying diverging stiffness as the covariance approaches the floor.
AI.motivation: Gradient flows on the positive-definite cone describe covariance relaxation but lack phase-space structure. The authors aim to uncover the underlying Hamiltonian (conservative) parent system to better understand the dynamics, particularly near constraints like spectral floors.
AI.method: The authors construct a finite-dimensional Hamiltonian lift on Sym$^+_n$ with the Bures-Wasserstein metric, deriving the mechanical Lagrangian and canonical momentum via the Lyapunov operator. Rayleigh dissipation is added to recover gradient flow in the overdamped limit. A spectral-floor and trace-control potential is analyzed via quadratic fluctuation expansion around equilibrium.
AI.result: The Hamiltonian is $\mathcal{H}(Σ,Π) = 2{\rm tr}(ΠΣΠ)+V(Σ)$. For the spectral-floor potential, the quadratic fluctuation Hamiltonian separates trace and traceless modes. The baseline stiffness diverges as $(s-ν)^{-2}$ when the equilibrium covariance approaches the spectral floor.
AI.conclusion: The construction identifies a conservative parent system for constrained Bures-Wasserstein covariance relaxation and fixes the local stiffness scale induced by the spectral floor, bridging dissipative and Hamiltonian perspectives on covariance dynamics.

title: The Norton Theorem for Quantum Circuits and Systems
summary: It is well known that classical analog circuits and systems benefit from the powerful Thevenin and Norton theorems. These theorems enable rigorous and exact mathematical simplification and representation of the effect of the rest of a system on the part we want to focus on. We show that there are corresponding versions of a "Quantum Norton Theorem" that enable exact simplification and reduction for quantum circuits and systems, not just for one port, but also for multiport and even open quantum systems. We demonstrate the method on two level systems, chains, system environment partitions, Lindblad examples, and Grover search. The Grover examples show how the reduced network isolates the bright pole governing ideal search and exposes how diagonal disorder transfers spectral weight into dark poles that degrade performance. By partitioning finite dimensional Schrodinger dynamics into retained and eliminated sectors, we show that Gaussian elimination gives an exact reduced equation in which the eliminated subsystem appears as a dynamical self energy and a source term. In the circuit representation, these terms become the Norton admittance and Norton current source seen by the retained quantum port. The same Schur complement construction extends to multiport reductions, composite system environment partitions, density matrix dynamics, and Lindblad evolution in Liouville space.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a Quantum Norton Theorem—a generalization of classical circuit theorems—that allows exact simplification and reduction of quantum circuits and systems, including multiport and open quantum systems, demonstrated on two-level systems, chains, Lindblad examples, and Grover search.
AI.motivation: Classical analog circuits benefit from Thevenin and Norton theorems for rigorous simplification; the authors aim to extend this powerful reduction framework to quantum circuits and systems, enabling exact mathematical simplification for quantum engineering.
AI.method: The authors show that Gaussian elimination on finite-dimensional Schrödinger dynamics, partitioning the system into retained and eliminated sectors, yields an exact reduced equation where the eliminated subsystem appears as a dynamical self-energy and source term. This Schur complement construction extends to multiport reductions, composite system-environment partitions, density matrix dynamics, and Lindblad evolution in Liouville space.
AI.result: The Quantum Norton Theorem isolates the bright pole governing ideal Grover search and reveals how diagonal disorder transfers spectral weight into dark poles that degrade performance. The method works for two-level systems, chains, system-environment partitions, Lindblad examples, and Grover search.
AI.conclusion: A quantum analog of the classical Norton theorem exists and provides exact simplification for quantum circuits, multiport systems, and open quantum systems, with the eliminated subsystem represented as a Norton admittance and Norton current source.

title: Sample-based quantum diagonalization approach for open-shell transition-metal complexes in gas and implicit-solvent
summary:
Open-shell $3d$ transition-metal complexes challenge electronic-structure methods because competing spin states, charge transfer, and solvation jointly determine their energetics. Here, we combine sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with the integral-equation-formalism polarizable continuum model (IEF-PCM), extending SQD to correlated open-shell transition-metal systems in a dielectric environment.
  We investigate the octahedrally coordinated $\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)_5CO_2]^{2+/3+}}$ complex across two oxidation states, four spin multiplicities, and a metal-ligand dissociation coordinate. We study the Co(III) singlet and quintet states and the Co(II) doublet and quartet states, incorporating open-shell references into SQD-IEF-PCM through an outer self-consistent reaction-field loop. Using samples collected on an IBM Heron quantum processor and active spaces of up to 50 qubits, SQD reproduces coupled-cluster and heat-bath configuration-interaction benchmarks within the same active space in the gas phase and implicit solvent, with a largest observed deviation below 9 $mE_h$. Along the dissociation coordinate of high-spin quintet $\mathrm{[Co(H_2O)_5CO_2]^{3+}}$, SQD resolves an avoided crossing caused by internal charge transfer; this feature is absent in the singlet and the lower oxidation state of the complex. Relative to the gas phase, implicit solvation stabilizes for the quintet state the neutral CO$_2$ dissociation and suppresses the avoided-crossing feature.
  To our knowledge, this is the first hardware demonstration of SQD for an open-shell $3d$ transition-metal complex in gas phase and implict solvent. These results establish SQD as a robust quantum-centric approach for transition-metal chemistry where spin state ordering, charge transfer, and environmental effects are strongly intertwined.

AI.tldr: The paper extends sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) with implicit solvent (IEF-PCM) to study open-shell Co complexes, demonstrating accurate reproduction of benchmarks (deviation <9 mEh) on an IBM Heron quantum processor, resolving charge-transfer avoided crossings in high-spin states, and establishing SQD as a robust quantum-centric method for correlated transition-metal chemistry.
AI.motivation: Open-shell 3d transition-metal complexes are challenging for electronic-structure methods because spin states, charge transfer, and solvation jointly determine energetics, and existing quantum computing approaches have not addressed these systems in dielectric environments.
AI.method: SQD combined with IEF-PCM via an outer self-consistent reaction-field loop; samples collected on an IBM Heron quantum processor with active spaces up to 50 qubits; open-shell references incorporated for Co(III) singlet/quintet and Co(II) doublet/quartet states.
AI.result: SQD reproduces coupled-cluster and heat-bath CI benchmarks within the same active space (largest deviation <9 mEh). High-spin quintet [Co(H₂O)₅CO₂]³⁺ along dissociation shows an avoided crossing from internal charge transfer, absent in singlet and lower oxidation state. Implicit solvation stabilizes neutral CO₂ dissociation for the quintet and suppresses the avoided crossing.
AI.conclusion: First hardware demonstration of SQD for an open-shell 3d transition-metal complex in gas phase and implicit solvent. SQD is established as a robust quantum-centric approach for transition-metal chemistry where spin state ordering, charge transfer, and environmental effects are strongly intertwined.

title: Dissipative Stabilization of Floquet-Engineered Many-Body Order
summary: Floquet driving underlies Hamiltonian and gate engineering, and produces dynamical orders with no equilibrium counterpart. These phenomena are, however, transient in well-isolated systems. We show that statically coupled dissipative auxiliaries cool the system toward low-energy states of the Floquet-engineered Hamiltonian, stabilizing orders in the steady state. The excess energy density is controllably small at high drive frequency and weak coupling and is captured by rate theory based on Fermi's Golden Rule. We numerically confirm robust cooling in a Floquet-engineered transverse-field Ising chain in both phases, and demonstrate discrete time-crystalline order, with a period-doubled magnetization response, in the steady state of a long-range Ising chain. Our results provide a rare analytical handle on the steady states of driven dissipative systems.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that coupling a Floquet-driven system to dissipative auxiliaries can cool it to low-energy states of the engineered Hamiltonian, stabilizing dynamical orders like discrete time crystals in the steady state, with the excess energy controlled by Fermi's Golden Rule rate theory.
AI.motivation: Floquet driving produces transient dynamical orders in well-isolated systems; the goal is to stabilize these orders in the steady state rather than having them decay.
AI.method: The authors use statically coupled dissipative auxiliaries to cool the system toward low-energy states of the Floquet-engineered Hamiltonian. They develop a rate theory based on Fermi's Golden Rule to capture the excess energy density, and numerically test the approach in a Floquet-engineered transverse-field Ising chain and a long-range Ising chain.
AI.result: Robust cooling is confirmed numerically in both phases of the Floquet-engineered transverse-field Ising chain. Discrete time-crystalline order with period-doubled magnetization is demonstrated in the steady state of a long-range Ising chain.
AI.conclusion: The approach provides a rare analytical handle on the steady states of driven dissipative systems, enabling stabilization of Floquet-engineered orders that have no equilibrium counterpart.

title: Entanglement Entropy in Quantum Networks with Tunable Geometry
summary: Quantum many-body Hamiltonians with two-body interactions can be represented by graphs, with sites as nodes and two-site couplings as edges. We investigate how the geometry of these graphs affects transport and entanglement growth. To do so, we study dynamics for quantum hopping on a random graph model with an effective range parameter. Tuning it, we interpolate between nearest-neighbor and all-to-all graphs, identifying a new localization regime that is robust in both single-particle and finite-density cases. This provides a model of Anderson localization induced by structural disorder, with implications for amorphous materials and tunable-range analog quantum simulators.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how graph geometry affects transport and entanglement in quantum many-body Hamiltonians, identifying a robust localization regime from structural disorder in random graphs with tunable interaction range.
AI.motivation: To understand how the geometry of graphs (representing quantum many-body Hamiltonians with two-body interactions) influences transport and entanglement growth, particularly in the context of structural disorder.
AI.method: Investigates quantum hopping dynamics on a random graph model with an effective range parameter, interpolating between nearest-neighbor and all-to-all graphs by tuning this parameter.
AI.result: Identifies a new localization regime that is robust in both single-particle and finite-density cases, demonstrating Anderson localization induced by structural disorder.
AI.conclusion: The findings have implications for understanding amorphous materials and for tunable-range analog quantum simulators.

title: Uncountably many inequivalent maximally entangled measurements for two qutrits
summary: Every two-qubit measurement basis composed of maximally entangled eigenstates can be transformed into the Bell basis via local unitary operations. For higher dimensions, in contrast, there exist inequivalent bases composed of maximally entangled eigenstates. Here, we provide a single-parameter family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases, and demonstrate that none of the bases are equivalent to each other under local unitaries. These bases are constructed from the continuous family of symmetric informationally complete sets of states in dimension three. By studying the local unitary bases that generate the family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases, we construct the first examples of wild error bases in the smallest dimension where these can exist. Finally, we discuss how distinct measurements in the family lead to differences in performance in several scenarios relevant in quantum information.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a single-parameter family of two-qutrit maximally entangled measurement bases that are all inequivalent under local unitaries, derived from SIC sets in dimension three, and provides the first examples of wild error bases in the smallest possible dimension.
AI.motivation: While all two-qubit maximally entangled measurement bases (e.g., Bell basis) are equivalent under local unitaries, for higher dimensions there exist inequivalent such bases. The authors aim to construct and study such inequivalent bases for two qutrits.
AI.method: The family is constructed from the continuous family of symmetric informationally complete (SIC) sets of states in dimension three. The authors study the local unitary bases generating these measurement bases to identify wild error bases.
AI.result: None of the bases in the single-parameter family are equivalent under local unitaries. The authors construct the first examples of wild error bases in dimension three, the smallest dimension where such bases can exist.
AI.conclusion: Distinct measurements in the family lead to different performance in quantum information scenarios, highlighting the practical relevance of inequivalent maximally entangled measurement bases beyond qubits.

title: Quantum-Centric Geometry Optimization with Wave-Function-Based Embedding
summary: The EWF-(FCI,SQD) method, a wave-function-based embedding approach combining full configuration interaction (FCI) and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), is a promising new tool for the simulation of molecular systems. However, applications of EWF-(FCI,SQD) have so far been limited to single-point calculations, whereas the study of complex chemical processes requires the ability to explore potential energy surfaces. In this work, we demonstrate geometry optimization with EWF-(FCI,SQD), scaling our simulations to molecules as large as menthone and benzidine within the STO-3G basis set. Without fragmentation, these systems comprise 73 and 82 molecular orbitals respectively, presenting an intractable Hilbert space for conventional exact or high-level subspace solvers and establishing a clear necessity for fragmentation-based methodologies. The underlying fragment SQD simulations in the EWF-(FCI,SQD) geometry optimizations use up to 70 qubits. The resulting geometries show exceptional accuracy relative to the classical reference, with deviations below 4 picometers.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates geometry optimization using the EWF-(FCI,SQD) embedding method on molecules up to 82 orbitals (70 qubits), achieving sub-4 pm accuracy compared to classical references, establishing this fragment-based quantum approach for potential energy surface exploration.
AI.motivation: Previous applications of EWF-(FCI,SQD) were limited to single-point calculations, but studying complex chemical processes requires exploring potential energy surfaces via geometry optimization.
AI.method: Applied EWF-(FCI,SQD) embedding, combining full configuration interaction (FCI) with sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), to geometry optimization of menthone and benzidine in STO-3G basis, using fragment SQD simulations on up to 70 qubits without fragmentation of the molecular system.
AI.result: Geometry optimizations succeeded for systems with 73–82 molecular orbitals (up to 70 qubits), yielding geometries with deviations below 4 picometers relative to classical reference calculations.
AI.conclusion: EWF-(FCI,SQD) is a viable fragmentation-based methodology for accurate geometry optimization on classically intractable Hilbert spaces, extending its utility beyond single-point calculations to potential energy surface exploration.

title: Remote Infrared Absorption Spectroscopy with Undetected Photons
summary: We demonstrate a novel method for remote open-path Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons. Similar to previous quantum spectroscopy works, a mid-infrared spectrum is reconstructed by detecting a near-infrared radiation only, thus bypassing important limitations of infrared detectors. Our study however relies on the co-propagation of the photon-pair and the pump-laser over the same optical path, which allows the probing of the open atmosphere over long distances. By sending the photons over unprecedented distances of up-to 43.4m in the outdoor atmosphere, we were able to detect butane released in the open-path, as well as natural atmospheric methane, thus demonstrating the first use of infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons for atmospheric measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates the first use of infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons for open-path atmospheric measurements, achieving remote detection of butane and methane over up to 43.4m outdoors using co-propagating photon-pair and pump-laser.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations of infrared detectors in remote sensing by using undetected photon quantum spectroscopy, enabling open-path atmospheric measurements over long distances.
AI.method: Mid-infrared spectrum is reconstructed by detecting only near-infrared radiation via co-propagation of photon-pair and pump-laser over the same optical path, with photons sent over up to 43.4m in outdoor atmosphere.
AI.result: Successfully detected butane released in the open-path and natural atmospheric methane over unprecedented outdoor distances up to 43.4m.
AI.conclusion: First demonstration of infrared spectroscopy with undetected photons for atmospheric measurements, showing feasibility for remote sensing applications.

title: Feynman Meets Turing: The Curse of Quantum Universality
summary: We consider a formal model of quantum circuit description languages (QCDLs) in which semantically meaningful programs correspond to computable unitary matrices. We show that any semantically universal QCDL -- that is, any QCDL able to describe all computable unitary matrices, which in turn form the set of matrices we can meaningfully represent on digital hardware -- cannot have a semi-decidable set of semantically meaningful descriptions. In particular, no such language admits a compiler that reliably recognizes all valid program descriptions. This result stands in contrast to classical programming languages. While compilation in languages such as C or C++ may itself involve non-terminating computations, the set of semantically meaningful programs remains recursively enumerable, since successful compilation provides a witness of validity. The essential difference lies in the nature of the semantic domains: classical languages describe partial recursive functions, whereas QCDLs describe total unitary operators. Our analysis establishes a fundamental limitation of quantum circuit description languages and highlights a structural distinction between classical and quantum models of computation at the level of formal language theory.

AI.tldr: Quantum circuit description languages (QCDLs) that are semantically universal (can describe all computable unitary matrices) cannot have a semi-decidable set of semantically meaningful programs, meaning no compiler can reliably recognize all valid programs—a fundamental limitation contrasting with classical programming languages where valid programs are recursively enumerable.
AI.motivation: To establish fundamental limitations of quantum circuit description languages and highlight structural distinctions between classical and quantum computation models at the level of formal language theory, particularly regarding compiler verifiability.
AI.method: Formal modeling of QCDLs where semantically meaningful programs correspond to computable unitary matrices; analysis using computability theory and formal language theory comparing semi-decidability properties of classical (partial recursive functions) vs. quantum (total unitary operators) semantic domains.
AI.result: Any semantically universal QCDL cannot have a semi-decidable set of semantically meaningful descriptions; no such language admits a compiler that reliably recognizes all valid program descriptions. This contrasts with classical languages where the set of semantically meaningful programs remains recursively enumerable.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental limitation of QCDLs rooted in the nature of their semantic domain (total unitary operators), establishing a structural distinction between classical and quantum models of computation.

title: Host-guest Crystal Engineering Tailors the Room Temperature Spin Dynamics in Molecular Quantum Devices
summary: Molecular materials that enable coherent control over an electron's spin state at room temperature are promising candidates for quantum technologies, including quantum sensors and ultra-low noise microwave amplifiers, known as masers. Host-guest molecular crystals enable independent control of spin-active guests and their local environments to enhance molecular spin properties and so improve device performance. Using electron paramagnetic resonance and optically-detected magnetic resonance, we demonstrate the ability to tune triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation by modulating host-dependent lattice rigidity and vibrational coupling to significantly reduce the operating requirements for building useful masers. Importantly, the most rigid host, picene, reveals the ability to slow spin-lattice relaxation without lengthening triplet lifetime, though at the cost of strain-induced line width broadening and reduced triplet spin polarisation. We also find that deuteration reduces the triplet resonance line width and vibrationally-mediated triplet depopulation. Consequently, we find that perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl is the most viable candidate for building a continuous wave maser. This work demonstrates host-guest engineering as an important and practical method for tuning the spin-dependent performance of room-temperature molecular quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: Host-guest molecular crystals enable tuning of spin properties (triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation) by modulating host rigidity and vibrational coupling, with perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl identified as the best candidate for room-temperature masers.
AI.motivation: To develop molecular materials that enable coherent control of electron spin states at room temperature for quantum technologies (sensors, masers), and to demonstrate host-guest engineering as a practical method for tuning spin-dependent performance.
AI.method: Host-guest molecular crystals with varying host rigidity; electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and optically-detected magnetic resonance (ODMR) to characterize triplet population, depopulation, and spin-lattice relaxation; deuteration studies.
AI.result: The most rigid host (picene) slows spin-lattice relaxation without lengthening triplet lifetime but causes strain-induced line width broadening and reduced triplet spin polarisation. Deuteration reduces triplet resonance line width and vibrationally-mediated triplet depopulation. Perdeuterated pentacene in perdeuterated p-terphenyl is the most viable continuous wave maser candidate.
AI.conclusion: Host-guest engineering is an important and practical method for tuning spin-dependent performance of room-temperature molecular quantum technologies.

title: Holographic quantum codes with trapped ions
summary: Holography is a central concept at the intersection of gravity, condensed matter theory, and quantum information, linking the interior bulk of a system to its boundary. A model realizing key features of holographic systems is the holographic pentagon code by Pastawski et al. Here we experimentally implement instances of the holographic pentagon and heptagon codes with trapped ions and test their properties: For the pentagon code, we recover logical bulk qubits from their nearby boundary and test the Ryu-Takayanagi entanglement area law. For the heptagon code, we show that the transversal Hadamard gate native to the constituent Steane codes induces a single-qubit, correctable error in the holographic code. Our implementation paves the way towards the use of holographic quantum codes for quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: This paper experimentally implements holographic pentagon and heptagon quantum error-correcting codes using trapped ions, demonstrating bulk-to-boundary qubit recovery, the Ryu-Takayanagi entanglement area law, and the effect of transversal Hadamard gates on the heptagon code.
AI.motivation: To experimentally realize holographic quantum error-correcting codes (the pentagon and heptagon codes) on a trapped-ion platform, bridging theoretical models of holography with physical quantum information processing.
AI.method: Trapped-ion experimental implementation of holographic pentagon code (recovering logical bulk qubits from boundary, testing Ryu-Takayanagi area law) and holographic heptagon code (testing transversal Hadamard gate from constituent Steane codes).
AI.result: Successful recovery of logical bulk qubits from nearby boundary in the pentagon code; verification of the Ryu-Takayanagi entanglement area law; demonstration that the transversal Hadamard gate in the heptagon code induces a single-qubit correctable error.
AI.conclusion: The experimental implementation is a step toward using holographic quantum codes for practical quantum information processing.

title: Split-quaternionic structure and canonical quantization of the Bateman dual oscillator
summary: Bateman's dual oscillator embeds a damped harmonic oscillator and an independent anti-damped adjoint coordinate in a conservative doubled system. We develop a split-quaternionic formulation that remains consistent from the classical equations through ordinary complex canonical quantization. The doubled dynamics is written as a two-sided hypercomplex evolution whose conserved indefinite quadratic form is the split norm, while the sign of the generator square unifies the underdamped, overdamped, and critical regimes. The Bateman Lagrangian is recovered as a real scalar action on the split-complex configuration subalgebra. After quantization, operator-valued split quaternions belong to the complexified algebra $\mathbb C\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb H_s\simeq M_2(\mathbb C)$. Noncommuting mechanical components require a symmetrized quantum split norm, which exactly reproduces the symmetrically ordered canonical Hamiltonian. Null idempotents resolve the crossed canonical structure of the doubled phase space. In particular, damping yields $[m\dot{\widehat y},m\dot{\widehat x}]=\mathrm{i}\hbar mγ$ and a Robertson--Schrödinger uncertainty relation. The limit $γ\to0$ retains the doubled positive/negative geometry; the ordinary single-oscillator Heisenberg relation is recovered only after selecting the positive normal mode, or by undoubling before quantization. The scalar split action gives the exact quadratic propagator and Gaussian evolution. A formal trace over the auxiliary coordinate is finally compared with high-temperature Caldeira--Leggett dynamics, clarifying that the doubled model is a coherent zero-noise embedding rather than a microscopic reservoir theory.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a split-quaternionic formulation of Bateman's dual oscillator, showing it remains consistent from classical equations through complex canonical quantization. It recovers the Bateman Lagrangian, derives symmetrized quantum split norms, and clarifies the doubled model as a coherent zero-noise embedding rather than a microscopic reservoir theory.
AI.motivation: To provide a unified mathematical framework (split-quaternionic) that bridges classical doubled dynamics and quantum canonical quantization for damped harmonic oscillators, resolving inconsistencies in previous treatments.
AI.method: The authors formulate Bateman's dual oscillator using split quaternions, where conserved quantities are expressed via the split norm and the sign of the generator square unifies damping regimes. They perform complex canonical quantization on the split-quaternionic algebra, employing symmetrized quantum split norms and null idempotents to resolve the crossed canonical structure.
AI.result: The quantization yields commutation relations $[m\dot{\widehat y},m\dot{\widehat x}]=\mathrm{i}\hbar mγ$ and a Robertson–Schrödinger uncertainty relation. The scalar split action gives the exact quadratic propagator and Gaussian evolution. The classical undoubled Heisenberg relation is recovered only after selecting the positive normal mode or undoubling before quantization.
