AI.conclusion: The Bateman doubled model is a coherent zero-noise embedding, not a microscopic reservoir theory. A formal trace over the auxiliary coordinate is compared with high-temperature Caldeira–Leggett dynamics, confirming this interpretation.

title: Efficient Exact Quantum Sampling from the Sun-Wootters Distribution for Optimal Polynomial Intersection
summary: Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) is a structured optimization problem for which Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) attains a satisfaction guarantee governed by the semicircle law. Sun and Wootters recently showed that, for balanced OPI over prime fields, a Fourier-defined distribution $P_u$ gives a strict worst-case improvement from limiting rate $0.6225$ onward and asymptotically perfect solutions from rate $0.7496$ onward, and asked whether $P_u$ can be sampled efficiently. We answer this question for Reed--Solomon OPI parameters satisfying their exponent condition strictly below the dual Johnson radius. Under coherent membership-oracle access, we give a bounded-error polynomial-time quantum sampler for $P_u$. The ideal circuit samples $P_u$ exactly conditioned on success, while a finite-precision implementation achieves any prescribed inverse-polynomial total-variation error. Consequently, every fixed limiting rate $0.6225\le r<1$ admits a strict worst-case improvement over the DQI semicircle value, and every limiting rate $r\ge 3/4$ admits solutions of satisfaction $1-o(1)$ with high probability. The algorithm coherently sums the amplitudes of all low-weight errors in each syndrome class using deterministic complete list decoding. Complete Reed--Solomon list decoding and the Sun--Wootters denominator estimate make the list size and postselection overhead polynomial. In concurrent and independent work, Horinaga and Yamakawa obtain worst-case OPI algorithms over prime-power fields and exact satisfaction at every fixed rate strictly above $3/4$.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a polynomial-time quantum algorithm for sampling the Sun-Wootters distribution $P_u$ in the Reed-Solomon Optimal Polynomial Intersection (OPI) setting, achieving strict worst-case improvement over Decoded Quantum Interferometry (DQI) for rates $r \ge 0.6225$ and asymptotically perfect solutions for $r \ge 3/4$.
AI.motivation: Sun and Wootters showed that a Fourier-defined distribution $P_u$ provides strict worst-case improvement over DQI for balanced OPI over prime fields, but left open whether $P_u$ can be sampled efficiently. This paper answers that question affirmatively for the Reed-Solomon OPI case.
AI.method: The algorithm uses coherent membership-oracle access, bounded-error polynomial-time quantum sampling, deterministic complete list decoding of Reed-Solomon codes, and coherent summation of amplitudes of all low-weight errors in each syndrome class. It employs complete Reed-Solomon list decoding and the Sun-Wootters denominator estimate to keep list size and postselection overhead polynomial.
AI.result: For any fixed limiting rate $0.6225 \le r < 1$, strict worst-case improvement over DQI semicircle value is achieved. For every limiting rate $r \ge 3/4$, solutions of satisfaction $1-o(1)$ are obtained with high probability. The ideal circuit samples $P_u$ exactly conditioned on success; finite-precision implementation achieves prescribed inverse-polynomial total-variation error.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides an efficient quantum algorithm for sampling $P_u$ under Reed-Solomon OPI parameters satisfying the exponent condition strictly below the dual Johnson radius, resolving the open question posed by Sun and Wootters.

title: Quantum dynamics of a levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope
summary: We develop a quantum model for the rotational dynamics of a freely floating levitated ferromagnetic gyroscope (LFG), emphasizing the interplay between intrinsic spin $\boldsymbol{S}$, mechanical angular momentum $\boldsymbol{L}$, and magnetic torque. The conserved total angular momentum projection along the $z$-directed magnetic field $\boldsymbol{B}$, $J_z=S_z+L_z$, is quantized, leading in the small-libration-amplitude limit to discrete precessional states $|m\rangle$ (eigenstates of $J_z$ with eigenvalues $J_z = m\hbar$) and librational harmonic oscillator states $|n\rangle$ ($n=0,1,2,\ldots$). The discreteness of the energies and dynamical variables is governed by the quantum precession scale $Ω_Q=\hbar/I$, where $I$ is the moment of inertia of the LFG. We find that the phenomenon of LFG precession persists into high-field regimes where the magnitude of the rotational angular momentum associated with precession exceeds the total intrinsic spin. We analyze the complementary quantum limits of localized semiclassical LFG orientation wave packets and exact $J_z$-eigenstates $|m\rangle$, clarifying the relation between classical precession signals and the underlying quantized spin-rotor dynamics. We further show that radio-frequency fields can drive $Δm = \pm 1$ and $Δn = \pm 1$ transitions, enabling ladder spectroscopy, tilt-angle control, and sideband-like coupling between precession and libration. The coupled dynamics also exhibit branch-point magnetic resonances where precession and librational motion become strongly coupled. These results establish a framework for using LFGs not only as ultrasensitive torque and magnetic-field sensors, but also as controllable mesoscopic quantum systems. The techniques developed here may be applied to searches for exotic, beyond-the-standard model spin-dependent interactions, ultralight dark matter, and spin-gravity couplings.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a quantum model for levitated ferromagnetic gyroscopes (LFGs), showing quantized precessional and librational states, discrete energy scales set by ℏ/I, transitions driven by RF fields, and applications to quantum sensing and searches for beyond-standard-model physics.
AI.motivation: To establish a quantum framework for understanding the rotational dynamics of levitated ferromagnetic gyroscopes, bridging classical precession signals with underlying quantized spin-rotor dynamics, and enabling their use as ultrasensitive sensors and controllable mesoscopic quantum systems.
AI.method: A quantum model is developed for an LFG describing the interplay between intrinsic spin S, mechanical angular momentum L, and magnetic torque. The conserved total angular momentum J_z = S_z + L_z is quantized. In the small-libration-amplitude limit, states are described by discrete precessional eigenstates |m⟩ (eigenstates of J_z) and librational harmonic oscillator states |n⟩. The quantum precession scale Ω_Q = ℏ/I governs discreteness. RF fields drive Δm = ±1 and Δn = ±1 transitions.
AI.result: LFG precession persists into high-field regimes where rotational angular momentum exceeds total intrinsic spin. The complementary limits of localized semiclassical wave packets and exact J_z eigenstates clarify the relation between classical signals and quantized dynamics. RF drives enable ladder spectroscopy, tilt-angle control, and sideband coupling. Branch-point magnetic resonances emerge where precession and libration couple strongly.
AI.conclusion: The framework enables LFGs as ultrasensitive torque and magnetic-field sensors and as controllable mesoscopic quantum systems, applicable to searches for exotic spin-dependent interactions, ultralight dark matter, and spin-gravity couplings.

title: Geometric quantum discord in the black hole quantum atmosphere
summary: We investigate the geometric quantum discord of bipartite Werner states influenced by Hawking radiation in the quantum atmosphere of a Schwarzschild black hole. We find that the geometric quantum discord in the physically accessible region exhibits a nonmonotonic behavior: it first decreases and then increases as the normalized radial distance increases, while the discord in the physically inaccessible region shows the exact opposite trend. A pronounced extremum of geometric quantum discord occurs precisely at the position corresponding to the peak intensity of Hawking radiation. Furthermore, we find that the Hartle Hawking constant and the event horizon radius exert opposite effects on the strength of quantum correlation redistribution: a larger Hartle Hawking constant enhances the redistribution effect, whereas a larger event horizon radius suppresses it.

AI.tldr: This paper studies geometric quantum discord of bipartite Werner states under Hawking radiation in a Schwarzschild black hole's quantum atmosphere, finding nonmonotonic behavior of discord in accessible/inaccessible regions, with extremum at Hawking radiation peak, and opposite effects of Hartle-Hawking constant and event horizon radius on quantum correlation redistribution.
AI.motivation: To understand how Hawking radiation and black hole geometry affect quantum correlations (specifically geometric quantum discord) in bipartite systems within the quantum atmosphere of a Schwarzschild black hole.
AI.method: The authors investigate geometric quantum discord of bipartite Werner states under the influence of Hawking radiation, analyzing its behavior as a function of normalized radial distance, Hartle-Hawking constant, and event horizon radius.
AI.result: Geometric quantum discord in the accessible region decreases then increases with radial distance (opposite trend in inaccessible region); extremum at Hawking radiation peak; Hartle-Hawking constant enhances redistribution while event horizon radius suppresses it.
AI.conclusion: Hawking radiation and black hole parameters significantly modulate quantum correlations, with the Hartle-Hawking constant and event horizon radius playing opposing roles in quantum correlation redistribution between accessible and inaccessible regions.

title: $p$-Body $\simeq$ Range $p-1$: Exact Order-Range Mapping and Dual-Unitarity
summary: We introduce and study a periodically kicked version of a one-dimensional spin-$1/2$ Ising model with contiguous $p$-body interactions. At specific interaction strengths of the model, we establish an exact Floquet interaction $\textit{order-range}$ mapping: the Floquet evolution operator of the $p$-body Ising model is exactly mapped to a two body Ising model with interactions having maximum range $p-1$ and exactly determined couplings. Upon further tuning the kicking strength, the mapped model becomes dual-unitary, thus providing an explicit family of $p$-body dual unitary models. We then determine exact entanglement dynamics of the $p$-body model for a class of solvable initial states at all times. We further illustrate the nontrivial structures that can emerge from the $\textit{order-range}$ mapping using a minimal example of $p=3$ and generalize it for all odd $p$. These findings provide a systematic route to constructing and studying $p$-body dual-unitary Floquet models.

AI.tldr: The paper studies a periodically kicked spin-1/2 Ising model with p-body interactions, establishing an exact Floquet order-range mapping that connects the p-body Floquet evolution operator to a two-body Ising model with maximum range p-1. By tuning the kicking strength, the mapped model becomes dual-unitary, enabling exact entanglement dynamics for solvable initial states. A minimal example with p=3 is provided and generalized to all odd p.
AI.motivation: To systematically construct and study p-body dual-unitary Floquet models by establishing an exact mapping between the p-body Ising model and a two-body model with controlled interaction range.
AI.method: The authors introduce a periodically kicked 1D spin-1/2 Ising model with contiguous p-body interactions, derive an exact Floquet order-range mapping to a two-body Ising model with range p-1, and tune the kicking strength to achieve dual-unitarity. They analyze entanglement dynamics for solvable initial states and study the p=3 case as a minimal example.
AI.result: An exact Floquet order-range mapping is established, showing that the p-body Ising model maps to a two-body model with maximum range p-1 and exactly determined couplings. Upon tuning, the model becomes dual-unitary, yielding exact entanglement dynamics. The p=3 case illustrates nontrivial structures, generalized to all odd p.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a systematic route to constructing and studying p-body dual-unitary Floquet models via the order-range mapping, enabling exact solvability of entanglement dynamics.

title: Geometric Power Capacity of Coherent Ergotropy in Quantum Batteries
summary: We explore coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries from a resource-geometric point of view. For an initial state $ρ$, we quantify the coherent extraction process by the coherent ergotropy $\mathcal{E}_c(ρ)$ and the coherent extraction distance $D_c^{\rm ext}(ρ)$ between the active state $σ_ρ$ and the passive state $P_ρ$. This defines the geometric power capacity $Π_c(ρ)=\mathcal{E}_c(ρ)/D_c^{\rm ext}(ρ)$, which measures the coherent ergotropy released unit minimal unitary distance. We prove that, for any driving Hamiltonian satisfying $\|V_t\|\leqν$, the actual coherent discharging power is bounded by $P_c^{\rm ext}(ρ;V_t)\leq νΠ_c(ρ)$, showing that $Π_c(ρ)$ is a capacity under unit driving norm rather than the power of a particular protocol. General bounds on $Π_c(ρ)$ are derived by combining relative entropy bounds on coherent ergotropy with geometric bounds on the coherent extraction distance. We also formulate coherence measure induced bounds and protocol-corrected capacities involving the effective speed of a given Hamiltonian. Qubit and qutrit examples demonstrate that $Π_c(ρ)$ captures a resource-geometric feature of coherent discharging beyond coherent ergotropy or coherence measures alone.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a geometric capacity measure $\Pi_c(\rho)$ for coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries, defined as the ratio of coherent ergotropy to coherent extraction distance. It proves this capacity bounds the actual coherent discharging power under any driving Hamiltonian with bounded norm, and establishes general bounds via relative entropy and geometric constraints, with qubit and qutrit examples demonstrating its resource-geometric character beyond standard coherence measures.
AI.motivation: To develop a resource-geometric framework for quantifying coherent ergotropy extraction in quantum batteries, capturing the interplay between the amount of extractable coherent work and the minimal unitary distance required to achieve it, and to establish fundamental power-capacity limits independent of specific driving protocols.
AI.method: The authors define the geometric power capacity $\Pi_c(\rho) = \mathcal{E}_c(\rho) / D_c^{\rm ext}(\rho)$, combining coherent ergotropy $\mathcal{E}_c(\rho)$ with a minimal unitary distance measure $D_c^{\rm ext}(\rho)$ between active and passive states. They derive bounds using relative entropy and geometric inequalities, and introduce coherence-measure-induced bounds and protocol-corrected capacities with effective speed. Qubit and qutrit examples are used for illustration.
AI.result: For any driving Hamiltonian with $\|V_t\| \leq \nu$, the actual coherent discharging power satisfies $P_c^{\rm ext}(\rho;V_t) \leq \nu \Pi_c(\rho)$, establishing $\Pi_c(\rho)$ as a capacity under unit driving norm. General bounds on $\Pi_c(\rho)$ are derived via relative entropy and geometric constraints. The capacity reveals resource-geometric features beyond what coherent ergotropy or coherence measures alone capture.
AI.conclusion: The geometric power capacity $\Pi_c(\rho)$ provides a fundamental, protocol-independent bound on coherent discharging power in quantum batteries, unifying resource-theoretic and geometric perspectives on coherent work extraction.

title: Mean-State Entropy Hierarchies and Classical Communication through Quantum Convolutions
summary: Quantum convolution provides a discrete-variable analogue of classical convolution, with the mean state capturing the stabilizer structure preserved under repeated convolution. We establish a finite-step entropy hierarchy generated by compatible stabilizer dephasings. Along every compatible isotropic flag, the entropy increases toward the mean-state entropy ceiling, while the relative-entropy distance to the mean state decomposes exactly into successive coherence losses and a terminal classical nonuniformity. Optimizing over compatible subspaces yields an intrinsic entropy profile of the state. For quantum convolutional channels, Weyl covariance reduces the one-shot classical communication problem to minimal output entropy. A spectral-transfer argument shows that suitable stabilizer inputs reproduce stabilizer-measurement distributions of the environment as channel-output spectra. This gives a computable Holevo lower bound over all complete stabilizer measurements; its compatible restriction is characterized by the entropy hierarchy and refines the previous mean-state bound of Bu, Gu, and Jaffe. The bound is exact for stabilizer-diagonal environments, for which the Holevo capacity is strongly additive, and yields a single-letter formula for a nonstabilizer qutrit family. The same family also exhibits a coexistence region with simultaneously positive classical and quantum communication rates

AI.tldr: This paper develops an entropy hierarchy for quantum convolution via compatible stabilizer dephasings, shows that relative entropy decomposes along isotropic flags, and uses Weyl covariance to derive a computable Holevo lower bound that is exact for stabilizer-diagonal environments, yielding a single-letter capacity formula for a nonstabilizer qutrit family.
AI.motivation: To understand the entropy structure and classical communication limits of quantum convolutional channels, and to improve upon previous mean-state bounds.
AI.method: The paper uses compatible stabilizer dephasings, isotropic flags, Weyl covariance, spectral-transfer arguments, and entropy hierarchy analysis to characterize quantum convolution and channel capacity.
AI.result: A finite-step entropy hierarchy, exact relative-entropy decomposition along compatible isotropic flags, a computable Holevo lower bound refining earlier bounds, strong additivity for stabilizer-diagonal environments, and a single-letter formula for a nonstabilizer qutrit family with a coexistence region of positive classical and quantum communication rates.
AI.conclusion: The entropy hierarchy provides a refined tool for analyzing quantum convolutional channels; the Holevo bound is exact under stabilizer-diagonal conditions and reveals novel nonstabilizer behavior in qutrit channels.

title: Graph State Generation Based on Quantum Photonic Devices, Enabling Measurement-Based Quantum Computing
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Qualifying exam paper, originally presented March 2025
summary: Photonic cluster states are fundamental resource for measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC), which is a promising approach for scalable quantum computing. These highly entangled states enable computation with applying local measurements rather than gate operations, which makes them essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Generation of the photonic cluster states requires high-quality entanglement and stability, which can be done by making use of cavity quantum electrodynamics (cavity QED), which is embedding quantum dots (QDs) into photonic microcavities. This method enables controlled single-photon emission and the entanglement of them, helping with key challenges in generating photonic cluster states. Enhancing the generation of the photonic cluster state requires improvement in the quality factor (Q-factor) and therefore, cooperativity of cavity and QD systems. A high Q-factor helps with reduction in photon loss and decoherence, ensuring more stable and high-fidelity quantum states. It also enables better light-matter interactions, improving cluster state quality. Cooperativity, which is a measure for the light-matter coupling strength relative to dissipation, directly impacts photon emission efficiency. Optimization of these parameters improves entanglement generation, which is essential for producing high-quality photonic cluster states. Therefore, optimized cavities are essential for improving the generation of the photonic cluster states. Scalability is also an important parameter for the generation of the large-scale cluster states used in quantum computing. In this paper, after reviewing MBQC, cluster states, and the generation of the photonic cluster states, we investigate the deterministic generation of the photonic cluster state resource for the purpose of MBQC, and highlights the importance of the inverse design techniques for this goal.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews measurement-based quantum computing (MBQC) and photonic cluster states, focusing on their deterministic generation using cavity QED with quantum dots in microcavities. It emphasizes that optimizing cavity parameters—particularly Q-factor and cooperativity—is critical for high-quality entanglement and scalable cluster state generation, and highlights inverse design techniques as a promising approach for achieving this optimization.
AI.motivation: Photonic cluster states are essential for measurement-based quantum computing, but their generation faces challenges in achieving high-quality entanglement, stability, and scalability. The paper aims to address these challenges by reviewing and improving generation methods using cavity QED systems.
AI.method: The paper reviews MBQC and cluster state fundamentals, then investigates deterministic generation of photonic cluster states using cavity QED with quantum dots embedded in microcavities. It emphasizes optimizing Q-factor and cooperativity, and proposes inverse design techniques for cavity optimization.
AI.result: High Q-factor reduces photon loss and decoherence while improving light-matter interactions. High cooperativity enhances photon emission efficiency and entanglement generation quality. Optimized cavities are essential for producing high-quality, scalable photonic cluster states.
AI.conclusion: Inverse design techniques are highlighted as important for achieving the cavity optimization needed for deterministic, scalable generation of photonic cluster states for MBQC.

title: A projection-free approach toward mapping the structured polarization fields
summary: We present a projection-free method for mapping two-dimensional polarization distributions using Hong-Ou -Mandel (HOM) interference. Conventional polarization characterization techniques, such as Stokes polarimetry, rely on sequential intensity measurements under multiple polarization projections, making their accuracy and sensitivity susceptible to the extinction ratio, calibration errors, and stability of the polarization analysis optics. Our approach overcomes these limitations by exploiting the sensitivity of two-photon bunching to polarization indistinguishability at a balanced beam splitter. Using a HOM interferometer driven by a high-brightness spontaneous parametric down-conversion photon-pair source at 810 nm, we introduced a birefringent vortex waveplate with spatially varying polarization rotations in one interferometer arm and measured the resulting coincidence counts with a high signal-to-noise ratio, enabling projection-free characterization of the sample-induced polarization transformations. This configuration maps spatially dependent polarization variations directly onto coincidence counts, providing a projection-free reconstruction of the polarization distribution. We demonstrate high-fidelity ($\sim$95$\%$) reconstruction of the spatial polarization pattern with an angular resolution of approximately $\sim0.4^\circ$. The use an estimator that saturates the Cramer-Rao bound, computed from the Fisher information, can improve resolution further at the cost of longer acquisition. The proposed quantum-optical technique offers a simple, scalable, and high-precision framework for characterizing structured polarization fields in birefringent materials.

AI.tldr: A projection-free method using Hong-Ou-Mandel interference maps 2D polarization distributions by exploiting two-photon bunching sensitivity to polarization indistinguishability, achieving ~95% fidelity and ~0.4° angular resolution for birefringent sample characterization.
AI.motivation: Conventional Stokes polarimetry requires sequential intensity measurements under multiple polarization projections, making accuracy susceptible to extinction ratio, calibration errors, and stability of polarization optics. A projection-free method is needed to overcome these limitations.
AI.method: Uses a HOM interferometer driven by a high-brightness SPDC photon-pair source at 810 nm. A birefringent vortex waveplate with spatially varying polarization rotations is placed in one interferometer arm; coincidence counts are measured to map polarization transformations without projective measurements.
AI.result: Demonstrates high-fidelity (~95%) reconstruction of spatial polarization patterns with ~0.4° angular resolution. An estimator saturating the Cramer-Rao bound can further improve resolution at the cost of longer acquisition time.
AI.conclusion: The quantum-optical technique offers a simple, scalable, and high-precision framework for characterizing structured polarization fields in birefringent materials, avoiding limitations of conventional polarimetry.

title: Quantum Metrological Detection of the Unruh Effect with Optimized Accelerated Two-Level Atoms
summary: For a uniformly accelerated two-level probe atom, the acceleration-dependent factor is encoded in the atomic state during the atom-field evolution. If this factor can be estimated through a large number of measurements with an uncertainty smaller than its magnitude, the Unruh effect can be experimentally verified. In this work, we show that the minimal uncertainty is inversely proportional to the square root of the total probe time. For a fixed total probe time, we minimize the estimation uncertainty by optimizing the atom-field interaction time, the initial atomic state, and the measurement basis in each probe. Results show that the uncertainty decreases as the evolution time of each individual probe becomes shorter. The optimal measurement basis is determined by the initial atomic state, while the optimal initial state depends on both the acceleration factor and the evolution time of each probe. For a fixed evolution time, we analyze the estimation uncertainty versus the acceleration factor and identify the optimal factor and minimal uncertainty for each initial state. The initial excited state outperforms other configurations in the small-acceleration regime, whereas the ground state can become advantageous for sufficiently large acceleration and long evolution time of each probe. Finally, we estimate the minimal total probe time required for testing the Unruh effect and demonstrate that it can be significantly reduced by using probe atoms with larger transition dipole moments.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to optimally estimate the acceleration-dependent factor in the Unruh effect using a uniformly accelerated two-level atom, showing that minimal estimation uncertainty scales inversely with total probe time, and that optimal measurement strategies (interaction time, initial state, measurement basis) depend on acceleration and probe parameters; excited states work better for small accelerations, while ground states can be advantageous for large accelerations, and total probe time can be reduced using atoms with larger transition dipole moments.
AI.motivation: To enable experimental verification of the Unruh effect by determining how to optimally estimate the acceleration-dependent factor encoded in the atomic state through repeated measurements, minimizing uncertainty through strategic choices of experimental parameters.
AI.method: Quantum estimation theory applied to a uniformly accelerated two-level atom coupled to a quantum field; optimization of atom-field interaction time, initial atomic state, and measurement basis per probe for a fixed total probe time; analysis of minimal estimation uncertainty scaling.
AI.result: Minimal uncertainty is inversely proportional to the square root of total probe time; uncertainty decreases with shorter individual probe evolution times; optimal measurement basis depends on initial state; excited states outperform other configurations in the small-acceleration regime, while ground states become advantageous for large acceleration and long evolution times; total probe time can be significantly reduced using atoms with larger transition dipole moments.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a practical framework for optimizing experimental designs to test the Unruh effect, identifying parameter regimes where different atomic state preparations are advantageous, and suggesting that larger dipole moment atoms can drastically reduce required measurement time.

title: Reliability Is Not Free in Universal Quantum Work Extraction
summary: Universal work extraction shows that input-state knowledge is unnecessary to attain the asymptotic free-energy rate. We ask whether this first-order universality extends to reliability, the exponential decay rate of extraction failure. In the work-battery fidelity formulation, we prove that no phase-independent Gibbs-preserving protocol can retain the state-aware Gibbs-preserving exponent throughout a coherent qubit time-translation orbit: at every positive target rate, its worst pointwise exponent is bounded by the corresponding state-aware thermal-operation value. The proof first establishes an exact finite-blocklength identity between phase-robust Gibbs-preserving extraction and state-aware thermal extraction. A trigonometric Remez inequality then upgrades this minimax identity to a pointwise theorem by ruling out exponential localization of the worst phase. For an explicit coherent-qubit family, known-phase Gibbs-preserving extraction is error free, whereas every phase-independent protocol has a finite worst-pointwise exponent. Thus input-state knowledge can be irrelevant to the first-order work rate yet indispensable for optimal exponential reliability.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that while input-state knowledge is unnecessary for achieving the asymptotic free-energy rate (first-order universality), it is essential for optimal exponential reliability in work extraction, showing that no phase-independent Gibbs-preserving protocol can match the state-aware Gibbs-preserving exponent across a coherent qubit time-translation orbit.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the universality of input-state knowledge in asymptotic work extraction extends to reliability (exponential decay rate of extraction failure), as opposed to just the first-order work rate.
AI.method: The proof establishes a finite-blocklength identity between phase-robust Gibbs-preserving extraction and state-aware thermal extraction, then uses a trigonometric Remez inequality to upgrade this minimax identity to a pointwise theorem, ruling out exponential localization of the worst phase.
AI.result: For a coherent-qubit family, known-phase Gibbs-preserving extraction is error-free, while every phase-independent protocol has a finite worst-pointwise exponent, proving that input-state knowledge is crucial for optimal exponential reliability.
AI.conclusion: Input-state knowledge can be irrelevant for the first-order work rate yet indispensable for achieving optimal exponential reliability in work extraction.

title: Extending the Frontiers of QNLP Beyond English: Grammar-Sensitive Pipeline for Hindi Sentiment Classification Using Compositional Quantum Models
summary: Advancements in Natural Language Processing (NLP), whether on classical or quantum platforms, have predominantly focused on English due to its widespread use and abundant linguistic resources. Although English remains the most studied language in computational linguistics, Hindi, the third most spoken language worldwide after Mandarin, has received comparatively limited attention. Spoken primarily in India, Hindi differs significantly from English in its script, syntactic structure, and linguistic characteristics. Hindi uses the Devanagari script, exhibits rich morphological inflection, and follows a subject-object-verb (SOV) word order, unlike English's subject-verb-object (SVO) structure. Motivated by Hindi's linguistic complexity and its underrepresentation in Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP), we propose a grammar-aware QNLP pipeline for Hindi sentiment classification with a focus on sentential negation. We use a manually annotated Hindi sentiment dataset labeled as positive, negative, or neutral, and encode sentences using pregroup grammar types. Sentences are processed with Lambeq to generate quantum circuits using a novel negation-aware compositional grammar. Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks (HQNNs) are trained for both binary and ternary sentiment classification. Our results demonstrate effective sentiment classification and highlight the potential of compositional QNLP for morphologically rich languages.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a grammar-aware Quantum Natural Language Processing (QNLP) pipeline for Hindi sentiment classification, addressing the underrepresentation of Hindi in QNLP. Using pregroup grammar and Lambeq to encode Hindi sentences (which use Devanagari script and SOV word order) into quantum circuits, the authors train Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks for binary and ternary sentiment classification, demonstrating effective classification for morphologically rich languages.
AI.motivation: Hindi is the third most spoken language worldwide but has received limited attention in computational linguistics and Quantum NLP. Hindi differs significantly from English in script (Devanagari), syntax (SOV vs SVO), and has rich morphological inflection. The paper aims to address this underrepresentation in QNLP.
AI.method: A grammar-aware QNLP pipeline using manually annotated Hindi sentiment dataset (positive, negative, neutral), pregroup grammar types for sentence encoding, Lambeq for quantum circuit generation with a novel negation-aware compositional grammar, and Hybrid Quantum Neural Networks (HQNNs) for binary and ternary sentiment classification.
AI.result: Effective sentiment classification results are demonstrated for both binary and ternary settings, showing the potential of compositional QNLP for morphologically rich languages like Hindi.
AI.conclusion: The proposed negation-aware compositional QNLP pipeline successfully classifies Hindi sentiment, highlighting the viability of quantum NLP approaches for languages beyond English, particularly those with rich morphology and different syntactic structures.

title: Identity-Paired Progressive Depth Training: When Trainability Persists Beyond Expressibility
summary: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a leading paradigm for near-term quantum computing, yet their training suffers from sensitivity to circuit depth, initialization, and landscape pathologies such as barren plateaus. We study \emph{progressive depth training} (PDT) -- a layerwise curriculum that trains a shallow circuit before appending new layers -- and identify a fundamental obstacle: fixed entangling gates (CNOTs) in hardware-efficient ansätze cause \emph{initialization shock}, an energy spike when new layers are added. We propose \emph{identity-paired progressive depth training} (IP-PDT), which appends forward/inverse block pairs -- each consisting of a standard rotation$+$CNOT block followed by its reverse -- that compose to the identity at initialization. Because the adjacent CNOT rings cancel, the effective circuit retains only \textit{a single entangling layer} surrounded by \textit{overparameterized local rotations}. We prove a simple \textit{Reachable Set Saturation Theorem}: under this construction the variational manifold expands exactly once (when post-entangler rotations are first introduced) and then \emph{saturates}; all subsequent depth increases provide pure overparameterization of single-qubit unitaries. Despite this saturation, progressive addition of rotation parameters can continue to improve optimization outcomes -- a phenomenon we term \emph{trainability beyond expressibility}. We formalize IP-PDT as a continuation method on nested manifolds, prove monotone energy guarantees under an acceptance rule, and connect energy error to ground-state fidelity through spectral-gap inequalities. A detailed resource analysis shows that IP-PDT achieves lower total gate cost than both baselines by eliminating most CNOT gates.

AI.tldr: Progressive depth training (PDT) in variational quantum algorithms suffers from "initialization shock" due to fixed entangling gates. The authors propose Identity-Paired PDT (IP-PDT), which appends forward/inverse block pairs that cancel at initialization, leaving only one entangling layer. They prove a Reachable Set Saturation Theorem showing the variational manifold saturates after one expansion, yet further depth still improves trainability ("trainability beyond expressibility"). IP-PDT achieves lower gate cost than baselines.
AI.motivation: To overcome initialization shock and barren plateaus in training variational quantum algorithms with progressive depth, where adding new layers causes energy spikes due to fixed CNOT gates disrupting the current variational state.
AI.method: Identity-Paired Progressive Depth Training (IP-PDT): appends forward/inverse block pairs (rotation+CNOT followed by its reverse) that compose to identity at initialization. Adjacent CNOT rings cancel, leaving a single entangling layer with overparameterized single-qubit rotations. Formalized as a continuation method on nested manifolds.
AI.result: Proven Reachable Set Saturation Theorem: the variational manifold expands exactly once (when post-entangler rotations are first introduced) and then saturates; all further depth increases provide pure overparameterization of single-qubit unitaries. This yields "trainability beyond expressibility" — improved optimization despite no expressibility gain. Lower total gate cost than baselines.
AI.conclusion: IP-PDT eliminates initialization shock, enables monotone energy guarantees under an acceptance rule, and achieves better resource efficiency. The concept of trainability beyond expressibility suggests that adding parameters can aid optimization independently of expanding the reachable state space.

title: Shortcuts to adiabaticity in five-level systems using counter-diabatic driving and time-rescaling optimization
summary: Shortcuts to adiabaticity (STA) is a common protocol to realize high-fidelity and robust quantum control in various quantum systems. To date, STA has been widely applied in two- and three-level systems, whereas designing feasible strategies to achieve perfect quantum state engineering in multi-level systems still remains a challenging task. Here, we propose to use counterdiabatic (CD) driving and time-rescaling (TR) methods to construct multi-state stimulated Raman shortcut-to-adiabatic passage protocols for realizing robust and fast population transfer in chainwise-connected five-state systems. The first protocol is implemented by initially reducing the original five-state system to an equivalent two-state counterpart, and then designing the corresponding driving field by combining CD driving and unitary transformation. Further, we introduce the TR method to optimize the first protocol and thus offers an alternative solution. Numerical calculations show that both protocols can achieve complete population transfer and effectively suppress transient populations of all intermediate states. Compared with the first protocol, the optimized second exhibits better performance within a shorter evolution time.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes two protocols using counterdiabatic driving and time-rescaling methods to achieve robust and fast population transfer in chainwise-connected five-state systems, demonstrating complete population transfer with suppressed intermediate state populations.
AI.motivation: Designing feasible strategies to achieve perfect quantum state engineering in multi-level systems remains challenging despite widespread success of STA in two- and three-level systems.
AI.method: Two protocols are proposed: (1) reducing the five-state system to an equivalent two-state system, then applying CD driving with unitary transformation; (2) optimizing the first protocol using the time-rescaling (TR) method.
AI.result: Both protocols achieve complete population transfer and effectively suppress transient populations of all intermediate states. The optimized second protocol exhibits better performance within a shorter evolution time.
AI.conclusion: Multi-state stimulated Raman shortcut-to-adiabatic passage protocols using CD driving and TR methods are viable for robust and fast population transfer in five-state systems, with the TR-optimized protocol being more efficient.

title: Removing inhomogeneous broadening in cross-relaxation spectra via hole burning
summary: Quantum relaxometry based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond is an easy-to-use technique that detects magnetic noise by measuring the longitudinal relaxation of NV centers. It is favored in chemical and biological applications due to the robustness against imperfect spin control. By tuning the energy level, NV relaxometry can detect magnetic noise generated by other spins and obtain magnetic resonance spectra through cross relaxation. However, the inhomogeneous broadening of NV centers greatly limits the spectral resolution of cross-relaxation spectra. Here we demonstrate a hole-burning technique to remove the inhomogeneous broadening. We utilize a weak pump field to deplete specific NV centers during the relaxation measurement, which contribute a reverse signal in the cross-relaxation spectra with a much narrower linewidth. Our method retains the convenience and sensitivity of NV relaxometry, opening up new avenues for high-resolution magnetic resonance spectroscopy in complex scenarios.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a hole-burning technique that removes inhomogeneous broadening in NV-center-based quantum relaxometry, enabling high-resolution cross-relaxation spectra while maintaining the method's convenience and sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Inhomogeneous broadening of NV centers greatly limits the spectral resolution of cross-relaxation spectra in NV relaxometry, hindering high-resolution magnetic resonance spectroscopy in chemical and biological applications.
AI.method: A hole-burning technique using a weak pump field to deplete specific NV centers during relaxation measurement, producing a reverse signal in cross-relaxation spectra with significantly narrower linewidth.
AI.result: The hole-burning technique effectively removes inhomogeneous broadening, yielding cross-relaxation spectra with much narrower linewidth while retaining the convenience and sensitivity of standard NV relaxometry.
AI.conclusion: The method opens up new avenues for high-resolution magnetic resonance spectroscopy in complex scenarios by combining the robustness of NV relaxometry with improved spectral resolution.

title: Geometric Qubits in Programmable Atomic Trimers
summary: Motivated by programmable tweezer arrays, we develop an exactly solvable shape-space theory for near-equilateral atomic trimers. The Higgs oscillator on Kendall's shape sphere gives a nonresonant spectral lattice whose fixed-angular-momentum relative-stationary minimizers are supported on two adjacent admissible sites. These symmetry-selected doublets are separated from higher relative-stationary branches by a finite branch gap. With phase-coherent shape-mode driving and Rydberg-mediated conditional phases, they furnish a candidate route to geometric qubits and entangling operations.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a solvable shape-space theory for near-equilateral atomic trimers using the Higgs oscillator on Kendall's shape sphere, revealing doublet structures with finite branch gaps that can be used for geometric qubits and entangling operations via shape-mode driving and Rydberg-mediated phases.
AI.motivation: Programmable tweezer arrays motivate the need for a theoretical framework to understand and control near-equilateral atomic trimers for quantum information processing.
AI.method: An exactly solvable shape-space theory is developed using the Higgs oscillator on Kendall's shape sphere, yielding a nonresonant spectral lattice structure.
AI.result: Fixed-angular-momentum relative-stationary minimizers are supported on two adjacent admissible sites, forming symmetry-selected doublets separated from higher branches by a finite branch gap.
AI.conclusion: Phase-coherent shape-mode driving combined with Rydberg-mediated conditional phases provides a candidate route to geometric qubits and entangling operations.

title: Attosecond delay metrology beyond the photon coherence time with spectrally resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry
summary: Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interferometry enables delay estimation at the quantum precision limit but is traditionally constrained to path differences within the coherence time of the interfering photons. Here, we demonstrate single-measurement path-delay sensing at the measurement Cramer-Rao bound using spectrally resolved HOM interference, thereby removing the conventional dynamic-range limitation imposed by the photon coherence window, with no scanning required for calibration. By extracting delay information from the spectral interference fringes of spectrally entangled photon pairs, we retain near-optimal sensitivity over an operational range exceeding the photon coherence time by over two orders of magnitude. Using one million detected photon pairs, we achieve a time-delay precision of 20 attosecond (6 nm), while real-time operation (at 1 Hz) yields 330 attosecond (100 nm) precision. Because the estimator relies on fringe periodicity rather than absolute coincidence rates, the method is intrinsically robust to photon losses and variations in interference visibility, eliminating the need for recalibration. As a practical demonstration, we measure the thickness of a 300 um transmissive target with nanometer-scale precision. These results mark a significant step towards deploying quantum-limited measurements in real-world sensing applications using HOM interferometry.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates spectrally resolved Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometry that removes the conventional coherence-time limitation on dynamic range, achieving attosecond-level time-delay precision and nanometer-scale thickness sensing over a range exceeding the photon coherence time by over two orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Traditional HOM interferometry is constrained to path differences within the photon coherence time, limiting its dynamic range for delay estimation. The authors aim to overcome this fundamental limitation while retaining quantum-limited precision.
AI.method: The authors use spectrally resolved HOM interference with spectrally entangled photon pairs. Delay information is extracted from spectral interference fringes rather than absolute coincidence rates, enabling single-measurement path-delay sensing at the Cramér-Rao bound without scanning or recalibration.
AI.result: With one million detected photon pairs, they achieve 20 attosecond (6 nm) time-delay precision. Real-time operation at 1 Hz yields 330 attosecond (100 nm) precision. The operational range exceeds the photon coherence time by over two orders of magnitude. They demonstrate thickness measurement of a 300 μm transmissive target with nanometer-scale precision.
AI.conclusion: Spectrally resolved HOM interferometry removes the conventional dynamic-range limitation and is robust to losses and visibility variations, marking a significant step toward practical quantum-limited sensing in real-world applications.

title: Universal Parent Hamiltonians for Adiabatic Warm Starts
summary: Computing the ground state properties of quantum systems is an important potential application of quantum computing. The success probability of quantum phase estimation approaches to ground state problems is proportional to the overlap of the input state with the ground state. Local ansatz state approaches suffer from the orthogonality catastrophe, whereas adiabatic state preparation (ASP) can prepare good approximations with a cost growing with the inverse square of the minimum spectral gap along the adiabatic path. When the initial and target Hamiltonians lie in quantum phases separated by a first order phase transition, the minimum spectral gap along the adiabatic path becomes exponentially small as a function of system size. We pursue a solution to this problem based on choosing an initial Hamiltonian for adiabatic state preparation whose ground state lies in the same quantum phase as the target ground state. We develop a protocol for universal adiabatic warm starts with universal parent Hamiltonians (UPHAWS) that can initialize ASP in any state whose preparation circuit is known. We use the Feynman--Kitaev clock Hamiltonian as a universal parent Hamiltonian, for preparation circuits with and without mid circuit measurement. We benchmark the framework on a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric matrix product state (MPS) family interpolating to a target GHZ Hamiltonian, and on the linear $H_6$ chain under symmetric bond stretching. For the $H_6$ system a bond-dimension-$4$ matrix product state warm-start increases the minimum gap on the adiabatic path by a factor of two relative to the Hartree-Fock initialization. To perform these classical benchmark simulations we develop a momentum-space truncation of the adiabatic Hamiltonian that may be of independent interest.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces UPHAWS, a protocol for adiabatic state preparation that uses universal parent Hamiltonians to initialize in any known state, overcoming exponentially small spectral gaps caused by first-order phase transitions. Benchmarks on $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric MPS and $H_6$ chain show improved minimum gaps compared to conventional Hartree-Fock initialization.
AI.motivation: Adiabatic state preparation suffers from exponentially small spectral gaps when the initial and target Hamiltonians belong to different quantum phases separated by a first-order phase transition, causing the cost to grow exponentially with system size. The authors aim to solve this by initializing ASP in a state already in the same quantum phase as the target.
AI.method: The paper proposes UPHAWS (Universal Adiabatic Warm Starts with Universal Parent Hamiltonians), using the Feynman-Kitaev clock Hamiltonian as a universal parent Hamiltonian. This allows ASP to start from any state whose preparation circuit is known, including states prepared with mid-circuit measurements. A momentum-space truncation of the adiabatic Hamiltonian is also developed for classical benchmarks.
AI.result: For the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric MPS family interpolating to a target GHZ Hamiltonian, and the linear $H_6$ chain under symmetric bond stretching, the warm-start approach increases the minimum gap. For $H_6$, a bond-dimension-4 MPS warm-start doubles the minimum gap on the adiabatic path compared to Hartree-Fock initialization.
AI.conclusion: Choosing an initial state in the same quantum phase as the target ground state via universal parent Hamiltonians can significantly improve the minimum spectral gap in adiabatic state preparation, mitigating the orthogonality catastrophe and enabling more efficient quantum phase estimation for ground state problems.

title: Experimental Nanoscale Thermodynamics
summary: Modern fabrication techniques have allowed artificial systems to be constructed on a nanometre length scale. The ideas underlying thermodynamics, a field invented to describe large macroscopic systems, need to be modified to describe much smaller systems. There are implications for our understanding of entropy, cooling, the arrow of time, heat flow, engines, erasure, and mutual information. The theoretical concepts have been implemented and tested in a wide range of experiments, many of which are at low temperatures. Nanoscale thermodynamics is not only a descriptive tool of nanoscale systems, but a design principle that helps us to build new architectures, processors and learning machines.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews how thermodynamics must be modified for nanoscale systems, covering entropy, cooling, the arrow of time, heat flow, engines, erasure, and mutual information, with experimental implementations at low temperatures.
AI.motivation: Modern nanofabrication techniques have enabled artificial systems at the nanometre scale, where classical thermodynamic principles derived for macroscopic systems break down, necessitating a modified framework.
AI.method: The paper presents a theoretical review of nanoscale thermodynamics concepts — entropy, arrow of time, heat flow, engines, erasure, mutual information — and discusses their experimental implementations, many performed at low temperatures.
AI.result: The theoretical concepts have been successfully implemented and tested in a wide range of low-temperature experiments, demonstrating that nanoscale thermodynamics works as both a descriptive tool and a design principle.
AI.conclusion: Nanoscale thermodynamics is not merely a descriptive framework for understanding small systems but also a design principle for building new architectures, processors, and learning machines.

title: Certified Optimal Measurement Reduction over Quantum Context Landscapes
comment: 20 pages; companion paper to "Beyond Orbital Rotations: Correlation-Rank Limits and Clifford-Accessible Measurement, from Algebra and Global Optimization"
summary: Quantum-measurement reduction contains two distinct global-optimization layers: a continuous problem of splitting an observable and allocating shots within a fixed measurement dictionary, and a nonconvex outer problem of designing the dictionary and calibrating its data-driven uncertainty model. We solve the inner layer globally and certifiably as a second-order cone program (SOCP), and use RANGE, a robust adaptive nature-inspired global optimizer, for the combinatorial and statistical outer layer. For any declared set of contexts, per-shot costs, score functions, and covariance model, the SOCP returns the minimum leading shot cost among unbiased linear stratified estimators. The conic dual supplies an independently checkable lower-bound witness; after feasibility repair, an external verifier recomputes $L \le Φ\le U$ from stored data without trusting the optimizer. Pilot measurements yield simultaneous finite-sample covariance brackets, and the dual becomes a pricing oracle for omitted contexts. Discrete RANGE searches covering sub-dictionaries, Pareto compression fronts, and candidate contexts; continuous RANGE performs an explicitly empirical, coverage-constrained calibration of covariance-radius models, while rigorous certificates retain the proved finite-sample radius. RANGE compresses molecular context dictionaries by 4.3-6.1x at 0.2-2.1% certified-frontier excess. Standard strategies are exactly optimal for H2 yet leave factors of 2.1-7.7 in shots within their own settings by H2O. Adding fully commuting contexts lowers the certified optimum by up to 56%; on 29-35-qubit production f-element Hamiltonians under a declared Hartree-Fock-proxy covariance model, the capped-dictionary enlargement saves 31-70% of the shots, and transformations reducing block-encoding cost need not reduce sampling cost.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a two-layer optimization framework for quantum-measurement reduction: an inner SOCP layer for globally optimal shot allocation within a fixed measurement dictionary, and an outer RANGE layer for designing the dictionary and calibrating uncertainty models. The approach provides certified bounds, compresses molecular context dictionaries by 4.3-6.1x, and reduces shot requirements by up to 56% on small molecules and 31-70% on production f-element Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: Quantum-measurement reduction involves two coupled optimization layers (continuous shot allocation and combinatorial dictionary design) that lack integrated, certifiably optimal solutions. Existing methods are heuristic or leave significant efficiency gaps.
AI.method: Inner layer: formulated as a second-order cone program (SOCP) solved globally and certifiably for unbiased linear stratified estimators. Outer layer: uses RANGE, a robust adaptive nature-inspired global optimizer, with discrete search over sub-dictionaries and contexts and continuous calibration of covariance-radius models under coverage constraints. Feasibility repair and dual certificates enable independent verification.
AI.result: Molecular context dictionaries compressed 4.3-6.1x with 0.2-2.1% certified-frontier excess. Standard strategies are optimal for H2 but leave 2.1-7.7x shot gaps for H2O. Fully commuting contexts lower certified optimum by up to 56%. On 29-35-qubit f-element Hamiltonians, capped-dictionary enlargement saves 31-70% of shots.
AI.conclusion: The proposed dual-layer optimization with certified guarantees significantly outperforms standard strategies for quantum measurement reduction, and transformations reducing block-encoding cost need not reduce sampling cost.

title: Beyond Orbital Rotations: Correlation-Rank Limits and Clifford-Accessible Measurement, from Algebra and Global Optimization
comment: 13 pages; companion paper to Certified Optimal Measurement Reduction over Quantum Context Landscapes
summary: Algebra and RANGE global optimization play complementary, explicitly separated roles in identifying measurement structure beyond orbital rotations. In the fixed (1,1)-particle sector of two spatial orbitals per spin, algebra proves that one particle-number-preserving orbital-rotation context contributes a rank-one two-body correlation block $T$: an observable needs at least $\mathrm{rank}\,T$ such contexts, and its best $K$-context correlation-block approximation is exactly the Eckart-Young singular-value tail, attained by the truncated SVD. A continuous RANGE search over the physical rotation angles independently corroborates this exact trade-off. A Bell-diagonal, Heisenberg-type witness has correlation rank three: it needs at least three orbital-rotation contexts, while one explicit physical Clifford circuit measures its commuting Pauli representatives. For spin-conserving Jordan-Wigner molecular Hamiltonians we also prove the parity ceiling $r_X \le 2(N-1)$ for any Pauli subset, tight even within commuting subsets; $X$-rank is a routing diagnostic, and the strict separation is carried by the correlation-rank theorem. The discrete mode of RANGE locates high-$X$-rank commuting families across molecular and production f-element Hamiltonians, finding ceiling-saturating witnesses for CH4 and NdO; values are best found unless a proved ceiling is attained. Applying the companion certificate framework, enlarging product settings by fully commuting, Clifford-accessible settings reduces the certified leading shot cost by 31-70% on four 29-35-qubit f-element Hamiltonians, a QWC-versus-QWC+FC result rather than a Gaussian-versus-Clifford pricing. Controlled-Pauli insertions in Hadamard tests are Clifford; these zero-$T$ statements concern measurement circuitry only, while shot counts and state preparation retain their full costs.

AI.tldr: The paper combines algebraic rank analysis with RANGE global optimization to characterize measurement structure in quantum systems. It shows that orbital-rotation contexts produce rank-one correlation blocks via SVD, identifies a Bell-diagonal witness with correlation rank three, proves a parity ceiling r_X ≤ 2(N-1) for Pauli subsets, and demonstrates that Clifford-accessible commuting settings reduce shot costs by 31-70% on f-element Hamiltonians.
AI.motivation: To understand measurement structure beyond orbital rotations by proving exact trade-offs between orbital-rotation contexts and correlation-block rank, and to develop practical diagnostic tools (X-rank, correlation-rank) for reducing measurement overhead in quantum chemistry.
AI.method: Algebraic rank analysis in the fixed (1,1)-particle sector with two spatial orbitals per spin; RANGE global optimization (continuous and discrete modes); Eckart-Young truncated SVD; parity ceiling proofs for spin-conserving Jordan-Wigner Hamiltonians; companion certificate framework for shot-cost reduction.
AI.result: Proved that each orbital-rotation context contributes a rank-one two-body correlation block T, with best K-context approximation given by truncated SVD. Correlation rank three for Bell-diagonal Heisenberg witness. Proved parity ceiling r_X ≤ 2(N-1) for Pauli subsets. Found ceiling-saturating witnesses for CH4 and NdO. Achieved 31-70% shot-cost reduction on 29-35-qubit f-element Hamiltonians using fully commuting Clifford-accessible settings.
AI.conclusion: Algebraic and RANGE methods reveal exact structure in orbital-rotation contexts and correlation ranks. The parity ceiling is tight and useful for routing diagnostics. Clifford-accessible commuting families significantly reduce shot costs, independent of state preparation costs.

title: Bargmann invariants and local unitary equivalence
summary: In this paper, we study the local unitary equivalence of quantum states on $\mathbb{C}^n\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$, which is an important notion in quantum information theory. For the case $n=2$, the local unitary orbits of two-qubit states are completely determined by their local unitary Bargmann invariants. We show that the local unitary Bargmann invariants do not form a complete set of invariants of local unitary orbits for $n\geqslant 3$, which negatively answers a problem proposed by L. Zhang and B. Xie.

AI.tldr: The paper studies local unitary equivalence of quantum states on $\mathbb{C}^n\otimes\mathbb{C}^n$. For $n=2$, local unitary orbits are determined by Bargmann invariants, but for $n\geqslant 3$, these invariants do not form a complete set, disproving a conjecture by Zhang and Xie.
AI.motivation: Local unitary equivalence is a fundamental notion in quantum information theory for classifying quantum states under local operations. The problem was whether local unitary Bargmann invariants completely characterize local unitary orbits for all $n$.
AI.method: The authors examine the completeness of local unitary Bargmann invariants for classifying local unitary orbits, building on prior results for $n=2$ and extending the analysis to $n\geqslant 3$.
AI.result: For $n=2$, the local unitary Bargmann invariants completely determine local unitary orbits. For $n\geqslant 3$, they do not form a complete set of invariants.
AI.conclusion: The paper negatively answers the problem posed by L. Zhang and B. Xie regarding the sufficiency of local unitary Bargmann invariants for $n\geqslant 3$.

title: Precision dynamics of resonantly enhanced optical parametric amplifiers
summary: Optical parametric amplification is a crucial technology for the production of continuous-wave squeezed vacuum, which is now applied to gravitational-wave interferometry and other highly sensitive measurements of optical phase. The amplifiers employed in gravitational-wave detection are resonantly enhanced with optical cavities, which introduces nontrivial dynamics to their operation and requires a frequency-domain model of the relations between optical fields. In this work, input-output relations between optical fields entering, circulating in, and exiting a model amplifier are solved directly to produce frequency-domain relations that fully incorporate the cavity dynamics. We also provide low-order zero-pole-gain expansions for these relations to facilitate their analysis from a feedback control perspective. In the limit of small cavity decay rates, our relations are shown to reduce to relations previously derived under a Hamiltonian formalism. Expressions for amplifier figures of merit and for squeezed quadrature variances are also analyzed. Along the way, we examine how information about the amplifier performance can be extracted from the frequency dependence of the input-output relations, providing characterization methods that are complementary to methods that examine the static amplifier behavior.

AI.tldr: This paper derives frequency-domain input-output relations for optical parametric amplifiers with cavity dynamics, provides low-order zero-pole-gain expansions for control analysis, and shows reduction to Hamiltonian-based results in the small cavity decay limit, along with analyses of figures of merit and squeezed quadrature variances.
AI.motivation: Continuous-wave squeezed vacuum production via optical parametric amplification is essential for gravitational-wave interferometry and precision optical phase measurements, but resonantly enhanced amplifiers with optical cavities introduce nontrivial dynamics requiring a proper frequency-domain model.
AI.method: Input-output relations between optical fields (entering, circulating, and exiting a model amplifier) are solved directly to produce frequency-domain relations incorporating cavity dynamics, with low-order zero-pole-gain expansions provided for feedback control analysis.
AI.result: The derived relations reduce to previously known Hamiltonian-based relations in the small cavity decay rate limit. Expressions for amplifier figures of merit and squeezed quadrature variances are analyzed. Methods for extracting amplifier performance from frequency-dependent input-output relations are demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: The frequency-domain characterization methods complement static behavior analysis and provide a more complete framework for understanding and controlling optical parametric amplifiers used in gravitational-wave detection and other sensitive phase measurements.

title: A Reponse to the Sheldon Goldstein Objection to a Series of Covariant Relativistic Bohmian Models
summary: In this work we try to answer a very important objection to the Covariant Bohmian Models type Nikolić and Hernández-Zapata that was formulated by the american physicist Sheldon Goldstein (private communication, 2010) about the imposibility to interpret the configuration space-time density found by the authors of these models like a probability density. The problem is that it is very dificult to show that the N space-time configuration density has a finite integral. That is very important in order to normalize the density to produce a PDF (probability density function). All the steps in the demonstrations seemed complete but this objection must be resolved imperatively before to continue using this kind of models with full confidence. Since the aim of Bohmian Mechanics (also known as the De Broglie-Bohm Mechanics) is to provide a precise and objective formulation of Quantum Mechanics free from vagueness and obscurity (Bell point of view at least), addressing this issue is crucial. In this article, we set out to tackle this by employing a specific type of function that we call an "Arrangement Function".

AI.tldr: This paper addresses Sheldon Goldstein's objection that the configuration space-time density in Covariant Bohmian Models cannot be normalized as a probability density due to its non-finite integral, resolving this by introducing an "Arrangement Function" to ensure finite normalization.
AI.motivation: To resolve a critical objection raised by Sheldon Goldstein regarding the impossibility of interpreting the configuration space-time density in Covariant Bohmian Models as a probability density, which is essential for maintaining the consistency and credibility of these models within the Bohmian Mechanics program.
AI.method: The authors employ a specific type of function called an "Arrangement Function" to address the non-finite integral problem of the N space-time configuration density, thereby enabling proper normalization to a probability density function.
AI.result: The introduction of the Arrangement Function successfully resolves the normalization issue, allowing the configuration space-time density to be interpreted as a valid probability density with a finite integral.
AI.conclusion: The objection raised by Goldstein is resolved, restoring full confidence in the Covariant Bohmian Models and reinforcing their viability as a precise, objective formulation of Quantum Mechanics.

title: Bound, Scattering, and Resonance States of the Symmetric Woods--Saxon Potential in Dunkl Quantum Mechanic
summary: We present the first unified analytical description of the bound, scattering, and Gamow (metastable) resonance states of the one-dimensional symmetric Woods--Saxon potential within the framework of Dunkl quantum mechanics, establishing a single analytical framework that consistently describes all physically relevant spectral regimes. The Dunkl deformation introduces a reflection-sector-dependent inverse-square interaction that precludes a direct analytical treatment of the corresponding Schrödinger equation. By employing a Pekeris-type approximation, the problem is transformed into a hypergeometric differential equation, enabling the derivation of analytical wave functions, bound-state quantization conditions, scattering amplitudes, and Gamow resonance solutions within a unified formalism. The results reveal that the Dunkl deformation fundamentally modifies the system's spectral properties by generating a reflection-sector-dependent splitting of the bound-state spectrum, along with quantitative changes in the reflection and transmission probabilities. The narrow transmission peaks are shown to originate from long-lived Gamow resonance states, whose complex energies, decay widths, and lifetimes are determined through analytic continuation into the complex-energy plane. In the limit of vanishing Dunkl deformation, the conventional Woods--Saxon results are fully recovered, confirming the consistency of the proposed formalism. The proposed analytical framework provides a versatile approach for investigating finite-range potentials in Dunkl quantum mechanics and opens the way to systematic studies of reflection-deformed quantum systems beyond the Woods--Saxon interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first unified analytical description of bound, scattering, and Gamow resonance states for the one-dimensional symmetric Woods–Saxon potential within Dunkl quantum mechanics, using a Pekeris-type approximation to derive analytical wave functions, quantization conditions, scattering amplitudes, and resonance solutions, revealing Dunkl-induced spectral splitting and reflection-sector-dependent modifications.
AI.motivation: To establish a single analytical framework that consistently describes all physically relevant spectral regimes (bound, scattering, and Gamow resonance states) of the Woods–Saxon potential under Dunkl deformation, which introduces a reflection-sector-dependent inverse-square interaction that precludes direct analytical treatment of the Schrödinger equation.
AI.method: A Pekeris-type approximation is employed to transform the Dunkl-deformed Schrödinger equation into a hypergeometric differential equation, enabling analytical derivations of wave functions, bound-state quantization conditions, scattering amplitudes, and Gamow resonance solutions. Gamow resonances are analyzed via analytic continuation into the complex-energy plane.
AI.result: The Dunkl deformation generates a reflection-sector-dependent splitting of the bound-state spectrum and quantitatively alters reflection and transmission probabilities. Narrow transmission peaks originate from long-lived Gamow resonance states with determined complex energies, decay widths, and lifetimes. The conventional Woods–Saxon results are fully recovered in the vanishing deformation limit.
AI.conclusion: The proposed analytical framework provides a versatile approach for investigating finite-range potentials in Dunkl quantum mechanics and enables systematic studies of reflection-deformed quantum systems beyond the Woods–Saxon interaction.

title: Operational Relation Between One-Time and Two-Time Work Protocols and Measurement-Resolution-Induced Transitions in Quantum Work Statistics
comment: 10 pages and 5 figures. Submitted to PRE
summary: We establish a direct operational connection between the one-time measurement (OTM) and two-time measurement (TTM) protocols for quantum work statistics, showing that OTM work values, including coherence signatures, can be reconstructed from standard TTM data through classical post-processing without any modification of the experimental setup. This reveals that coherence information commonly attributed to OTM schemes is already latent within TTM data and becomes explicit upon a natural post-processing step. For a driven two-level system subject to finite-resolution energy measurements, this reconstruction unveils a resolution-driven statistical transition in the work distribution: whereas projective and weak measurements yield smooth distributions, intermediate resolutions produce non-analytic structures whose character is determined by the dynamics and a critical meter resolution. We show that the non-analyticity of the OTM work distribution takes the form of square-root divergent peaks at specific work values, and that the separation between these singular points is an experimentally accessible quantity that vanishes at the critical resolution with a universal exponent. The same dynamical quantities that govern the transition also encode the relative entropy of coherence of the driven state, enabling coherence quantification from energy measurements alone. We demonstrate experimental accessibility in a nitrogen-vacancy center platform with parameters drawn from current experiments, where both sides of the transition and the coherence signatures are within reach of existing technology.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that one-time measurement (OTM) work statistics, including coherence signatures, can be reconstructed from two-time measurement (TTM) data via classical post-processing. For a driven two-level system, this reveals a resolution-driven statistical transition in work distributions, with non-analytic square-root divergent peaks appearing at intermediate resolutions and a universal critical exponent. The same dynamics encode coherence, quantifiable from energy measurements alone, with experimental feasibility demonstrated in NV-center platforms.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between OTM and TTM protocols for quantum work statistics, showing that coherence information attributed to OTM is already latent in TTM data, and to uncover a resolution-driven transition in work distributions that reveals non-analytic structures and enables coherence quantification from energy measurements alone.
AI.method: The authors theoretically establish a direct operational connection between OTM and TTM protocols, showing OTM work values can be reconstructed from TTM data via classical post-processing. They analyze a driven two-level system with finite-resolution energy measurements, examining the statistical transition in work distributions across projective, intermediate, and weak measurement regimes. They identify critical meter resolution, universal exponents, and link dynamical quantities to relative entropy of coherence, with experimental feasibility demonstrated in NV-center platforms.
AI.result: OTM work distributions can be reconstructed from TTM data without experimental modification. A resolution-driven statistical transition emerges: projective and weak measurements yield smooth distributions, but intermediate resolutions produce non-analytic structures with square-root divergent peaks at specific work values. The separation between singular points vanishes at the critical resolution with a universal exponent. The same dynamical quantities encode the relative entropy of coherence, measurable from energy measurements alone. Both sides of the transition and coherence signatures are experimentally accessible in NV-center platforms.
AI.conclusion: OTM and TTM protocols are operationally connected through classical post-processing, with coherence information latent in standard TTM data. The discovered resolution-driven transition and universal scaling behavior provide experimentally accessible signatures of quantum coherence and work statistics in driven quantum systems.

title: Entanglement Quantification via Symmetric Extensions: A Resource Theory Hierarchy
summary: We introduce a hierarchy of entanglement measures Ek based on k-symmetric PPT extensions. Each Ek, defined via a minimal eigenvalue shift and computed by semidefinite programming, is faithful, convex, and monotone under free operations. The hierarchy strictly refines PPT-robustness at k = 1, detects bound entanglement at k = 2, and converges exactly to the separability measure as k -> infinity. Numerical experiments on Horodecki, Werner, UPB, and random states demonstrate practical scalability. Our framework unifies computational efficiency with operational fidelity in a single tunable family -- a combination previously believed to be fundamentally incompatible in entanglement quantification. It supplies, for the first time, a systematically improvable resource-theoretic yardstick that accounts for all entangled states, including the bound entangled ones that have long resisted quantitative treatment.

AI.tldr: Introduces a hierarchy of entanglement measures \(E_k\) based on \(k\)-symmetric PPT extensions, computed via semidefinite programming, that is faithful, convex, and monotone. Refines PPT-robustness at \(k=1\), detects bound entanglement at \(k=2\), and converges to the separability measure as \(k\to\infty\). Numerical experiments on various states show scalability, unifying computational efficiency and operational fidelity.
AI.motivation: To develop a systematically improvable entanglement measure that is both computationally tractable (via SDP) and operationally faithful, capable of quantifying all entangled states including bound entangled states, overcoming the previously assumed incompatibility between efficiency and fidelity.
AI.method: Hierarchy of entanglement measures \(E_k\) defined via minimal eigenvalue shift under \(k\)-symmetric PPT extensions, computed by semidefinite programming (SDP).
AI.result: The hierarchy strictly refines PPT-robustness at \(k=1\), detects bound entanglement at \(k=2\), converges exactly to the separability measure as \(k\to\infty\), and is demonstrated on Horodecki, Werner, UPB, and random states with practical scalability.
AI.conclusion: Provides the first systematically improvable resource-theoretic entanglement yardstick that unifies computational efficiency and operational fidelity, accounting for all entangled states including bound entangled ones.

title: How many degrees of freedom describe a quantum N-particle state?
comment: 30 pages of main text, 25 pages of appendices, and 8 pages of references. No tables, no figures
summary: In Newtonian spacetime, the canonical description of a classical $N$-particle system requires $3N$ degrees of freedom. Not all of these are physical, however, since the conservation of the net momentum implies that only $3(N-1)$ accelerations are independent. Hence, three constraints can be used to eliminate the unphysical centre-of-mass variables, at the level of the Lagrangian, leaving only the subset of observable displacements and momenta, which are relational.
