Imposing the constraints does not change the dynamics of these variables, at the classical level, and is analogous to a gauge-fixing procedure, which removes redundancy in the description of the system. In classical physics, therefore, the number of physical degrees of freedom equals the number of independent relational degrees of freedom. Here, we show that this is not the case in quantum mechanics. While an operator-analogue of the classical net momentum exists, it cannot be used to impose constraints that restrict the degrees of freedom in the theory, without a loss of physical information. This means that all $3N$ canonical degrees of freedom are physical, even though only $3(N-1)$ of them are relational. We explore the physical consequences of the non-relational variables and show that they give rise to generalised uncertainty relations (GURs), for the relational quantities that define the quantum reference frame (QRF). Hence, it is shown that the non-relational degrees of freedom refer to the frame itself and that the non-Heisenberg terms in the GURs define its Galilean-invariant spreads, in both real space and momentum space. The implications of this result for recent work on relational models, including the ``perspective neutral'' framework for QRFs, are discussed. Its implications for the wider relational program, and, in particular, the relevance of the latter to quantum gravity research, are also critically assessed

AI.tldr: In Newtonian spacetime, classical N-particle systems have 3(N-1) physical degrees of freedom due to momentum conservation constraints. However, in quantum mechanics, all 3N degrees of freedom are physical; the extra non-relational variables give rise to generalized uncertainty relations (GURs) for quantum reference frames (QRFs), defining Galilean-invariant spreads in position and momentum. This challenges the relational program and its relevance to quantum gravity.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the classical reduction of degrees of freedom via momentum conservation constraints carries over to quantum mechanics, and to understand the physical role of non-relational variables in quantum reference frames.
AI.method: The authors compare the classical canonical description of an N-particle system (where constraints eliminate centre-of-mass variables) with an operator-analogue in quantum mechanics. They show that imposing constraints analogous to the classical net momentum conservation leads to loss of physical information. They then analyze the consequences of retaining all 3N degrees of freedom, deriving generalized uncertainty relations for relational quantities that define the quantum reference frame.
AI.result: Unlike in classical physics, all 3N canonical degrees of freedom are physically meaningful in quantum mechanics; only 3(N-1) are relational. The additional non-relational degrees of freedom are associated with the quantum reference frame itself and produce generalized uncertainty relations (GURs) with non-Heisenberg terms representing Galilean-invariant spreads in position and momentum.
AI.conclusion: The quantum description of an N-particle system inherently contains more physical degrees of freedom than its classical counterpart due to the non-commuting nature of observables. This implies that the relational program, including the "perspective neutral" framework for QRFs, must account for these extra degrees of freedom. The results also have implications for quantum gravity research by challenging the straightforward quantization of relational constraints.

title: Encoding Choices and Fault-Tolerant Resource Estimates for Digital Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
summary: Quantum Hamiltonian descent (QHD) formulates continuous optimization as time-dependent quantum dynamics, where a kinetic term drives exploration and a potential term encodes the objective function. Digital implementations of QHD require encoding the search space into qubits, and this choice can shift the dominant cost among logical qubits, circuit depth, non-Clifford rotations, and potential synthesis. In this work, we present an encoding-aware resource analysis comparing one-hot and binary amplitude encodings for QHD. We derive gate-count scalings, construct and validate circuits against classical \Sch-equation solvers, and estimate Clifford+$R_z$ and fault-tolerant Clifford+$T$ resources on benchmark optimization problems. Binary encoding reduces the data register from $O(dN)$ to $O(d\log N)$ qubits and gives comparable asymptotic scaling for both kinetic and potential evolutions. Across all benchmark problems studied, binary encoding also uses fewer $R_z$ rotations than one-hot encoding, making it the preferred option for fault-tolerant implementations where arbitrary rotations dominate the cost. Kinetic approximations based on low-momentum spectra and approximate QFTs can further reduce the binary kinetic cost to polylogarithmic scaling. However, for targets such as Ackley, potential synthesis can dominate the total cost and reduce the benefit of kinetic approximations. These results suggest that exploiting the analytic structure of the target function to compile the potential evolution in QHD more efficiently is needed for further resource reductions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an encoding-aware resource analysis comparing one-hot and binary amplitude encodings for Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD), showing binary encoding reduces qubit count from O(dN) to O(dlog N), uses fewer non-Clifford rotations, and is preferable for fault-tolerant implementations, though potential synthesis can dominate costs.
AI.motivation: To analyze and compare resource costs (qubits, circuit depth, non-Clifford gates) of one-hot vs. binary amplitude encodings for digital implementations of Quantum Hamiltonian Descent (QHD) in continuous optimization.
AI.method: Derived gate-count scalings for both encodings, constructed circuits validated against classical Schrödinger equation solvers, and estimated Clifford+R_z and fault-tolerant Clifford+T resources on benchmark optimization problems.
AI.result: Binary encoding reduces data register from O(dN) to O(dlog N) qubits, uses fewer R_z rotations across all benchmarks, and kinetic approximations can achieve polylogarithmic scaling, though potential synthesis can dominate and reduce the benefit of kinetic approximations.
AI.conclusion: Binary encoding is the preferred option for fault-tolerant QHD implementations, but further resource reductions require exploiting the analytic structure of the target function to compile the potential evolution more efficiently.

title: Rigorous characterization of continuous-variable quantum states via optical parametric amplifiers
summary: Characterizing non-Gaussian quantum states is of paramount importance for continuous-variable quantum information processing, yet conventional homodyne-measurement-based state tomography remains limited by optical loss, detector efficiency, and measurement bandwidth. Here, we introduce an integrated framework for loss-tolerant characterization and certification using high-gain phase-sensitive optical parametric amplification and power measurements. Our computationally efficient semidefinite programming approach enables faithful reconstruction of parity-symmetric quantum states from amplified quadrature measurements while substantially relaxing detector-efficiency requirements and increasing the measurement bandwidth. We further develop a certification framework that directly quantifies non-Gaussianity via stellar-rank witnesses and Wigner negativity, using the same quadrature-power measurements. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed framework through both simulated and experimental data for representative quantum states, including single-photon, Schrodinger cat, and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) states. By unifying loss-tolerant measurements, state tomography, and nonclassical-state certification within a single experimentally accessible framework, our approach provides a practical pathway toward verifying increasingly complex states and can be readily implemented with current quantum photonic technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an integrated framework for loss-tolerant characterization and certification of non-Gaussian quantum states using phase-sensitive optical parametric amplification and power measurements, employing semidefinite programming for state tomography and stellar-rank/Wigner-negativity-based certification, demonstrated on single-photon, Schrödinger cat, and GKP states.
AI.motivation: Conventional homodyne-measurement-based state tomography for non-Gaussian quantum states is limited by optical loss, detector efficiency, and measurement bandwidth, hindering practical continuous-variable quantum information processing.
AI.method: The framework uses high-gain phase-sensitive optical parametric amplification and power measurements, combined with semidefinite programming for loss-tolerant reconstruction of parity-symmetric quantum states, and a certification approach quantifying non-Gaussianity via stellar-rank witnesses and Wigner negativity.
AI.result: The approach substantially relaxes detector-efficiency requirements, increases measurement bandwidth, and is validated on simulated and experimental data for single-photon, Schrödinger cat, and GKP states.
AI.conclusion: The unified framework provides a practical, experimentally accessible pathway for verifying increasingly complex quantum states with current photonic technologies.

title: quchip: A Differentiable Toolkit for Modeling Quantum Devices
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Source code: https://github.com/quchip/quchip
summary: Predictive modeling of a superconducting quantum chip requires more than a Hamiltonian: the model must connect device physics, control-line transformations, chosen frames and approximations, dissipation, and measured observables. We present quchip, an open-source Python toolkit that represents these parts explicitly and assembles backend-independent simulations for QuTiP or dynamiqs; with dynamiqs, device and control parameters remain differentiable through the solve. We demonstrate the resulting experimental loop on a five-device model fitted to dressed observables. Simulated phase sweeps identify the complex crosstalk between two control lines, and inversion of the inferred response suppresses the effective leakage by more than two orders of magnitude. Over sixteen simultaneous $π$ pulses, the corrected pulse-end populations remain within $0.3$ percentage points of the crosstalk-free response. Adiabatically eliminating the bus and readout resonators reduces the Hilbert-space dimension from 576 to 16, after which gradients through simulated tomography recover the four injected crosstalk parameters with a maximum complex error of $1.5\times10^{-5}$. A single explicit model can therefore support prediction, correction, and inverse parameter recovery.

AI.tldr: quchip is an open-source Python toolkit for predictive modeling of superconducting quantum chips that assembles backend-independent simulations (QuTiP/dynamiqs) with differentiable device and control parameters. It demonstrates a closed experimental loop: identifying and correcting crosstalk (>2 orders of magnitude leakage suppression), maintaining pulse-end populations within 0.3% of target, and recovering injected crosstalk parameters via differentiable tomography with 1.5×10⁻⁵ error after adiabatic elimination from 576 to 16 dimensions.
AI.motivation: Predictive modeling of superconducting quantum chips requires more than just a Hamiltonian; it must integrate device physics, control-line transformations, frames, approximations, dissipation, and observables—a complexity not adequately addressed by existing tools.
AI.method: The paper introduces quchip, an open-source Python toolkit that explicitly represents all components of a quantum chip model and assembles backend-independent simulations for QuTiP or dynamiqs. With dynamiqs, device and control parameters remain differentiable through the solve. Adiabatic elimination reduces Hilbert-space dimension from 576 to 16.
AI.result: Simulated phase sweeps identify complex crosstalk between two control lines; inversion suppresses effective leakage by >2 orders of magnitude. Over 16 simultaneous π pulses, corrected pulse-end populations stay within 0.3 percentage points of the crosstalk-free response. Differentiable tomography recovers four injected crosstalk parameters with max complex error of 1.5×10⁻⁵.
AI.conclusion: A single explicit model can support prediction, correction, and inverse parameter recovery, forming a closed experimental loop for superconducting quantum chip modeling.

title: Against Many Worlds
comment: 22 pages, no figures; to appear in The Blackwell Companion to Philosophy and the Multiverse
summary: Any viable interpretation of quantum theory needs to account for the Born rule, from which the theory gets its probabilistic empirical predictions. In this paper, we give an overview of possible approaches to this problem in the context of the Many Worlds interpretation. We argue that, for structural reasons, none of them can possibly succeed. More precisely, we argue that the Many Worlds interpretation must obtain the Born rule by proceeding either axiomatically, deductively, or inductively, and that all three of these approaches run into general, fundamental obstructions.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that the Many Worlds interpretation of quantum theory cannot successfully derive the Born rule through axiomatic, deductive, or inductive approaches, as all three face fundamental structural obstructions.
AI.motivation: The Born rule is essential for quantum theory's probabilistic predictions, and the Many Worlds interpretation must account for it, but existing approaches face structural problems.
AI.method: The paper categorizes possible approaches to deriving the Born rule in the Many Worlds interpretation into three types—axiomatic, deductive, and inductive—and systematically argues that each faces fundamental obstructions.
AI.result: None of the three approaches (axiomatic, deductive, or inductive) can successfully derive the Born rule within the Many Worlds interpretation due to general, fundamental structural issues.
AI.conclusion: The Many Worlds interpretation cannot account for the Born rule, which poses a significant challenge to its viability as a complete interpretation of quantum theory.

title: GHZ-Equivalent State Distribution in Quantum Networks: Reducing Decoherence and Quantum Resource Consumption
summary: This study proposes a novel scheme for distributing GHZ-equivalent states across repeater-based quantum networks, with particular focus on the analysis and mitigation of decoherence effects during transmission. The proposed scheme enables remote users to share graph states, which can be leveraged to implement various quantum communication protocols, such as quantum key distribution and quantum secret sharing. Compared with existing approaches, the proposed distributed scheme requires only O(N) qubits without introducing redundant entanglement structures. Together with the linear-scaling merging procedure in both controlled gate count and qubit usage, the proposed framework supports more efficient large-scale graph state distribution. To evaluate its feasibility and correctness, this study utilizes the quantum network simulation tool, NetSquid, to implement the proposed scheme. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach is both effective and practical for executing quantum communication protocols within quantum networks.

AI.tldr: Proposes an O(N)-qubit scheme for distributing GHZ-equivalent states across repeater-based quantum networks, achieving efficient large-scale graph state distribution with linear-scaling merging, validated via NetSquid simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing graph state distribution approaches introduce redundant entanglement structures and scale poorly; this work aims to reduce qubit overhead to O(N) while mitigating decoherence effects in repeater-based quantum networks.
AI.method: Designs a distributed scheme for sharing GHZ-equivalent states across quantum repeaters with a linear-scaling merging procedure (both in controlled gate count and qubit usage); implements and validates using the NetSquid quantum network simulator.
AI.result: The proposed scheme requires only O(N) qubits without redundant entanglement; simulation results confirm the approach is effective and practical for executing quantum communication protocols (QKD, quantum secret sharing) within quantum networks.
AI.conclusion: The proposed O(N) distributed scheme with linear-scaling merging enables efficient large-scale graph state distribution and is validated as feasible for quantum network communication protocols.

title: Blind Transpiler: An open-source library for universally blind and homomorphic quantum computations
summary: Blind quantum computation is a cryptographic primitive that allows a limited-capability client to delegate its complex computation to a remote server without revealing its data and/or computation. This branch of quantum cryptography has been bifurcated into two distinct primitives, quantum homomorphic encryption (concerning the security of only data) and universal blind quantum computation (concerning the security of data and the computing algorithm). These primitives have immense applicability in problems like secure cloud computing, secure quantum variational algorithms, quantum federated learning, and secure multiparty computation. However, no software tools exist for the rapid prototyping of such protocols, hindering the academic interrogation for potential applications. In this paper, we describe the development of the first such library for transpiling circuits written in Qiskit to its blind counterpart, which can then be delegated in a client-server architecture without revealing the client's data and/or computation. The proposed library is designed in modular and reusable component layers, enabling easier scalability to newer BQC primitives and robustness against changes in underlying primitives. We show the implementation of these primitives to a blind variational quantum classifier for the IRIS dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first software library for transpiling Qiskit circuits into blind quantum computation (BQC) counterparts, enabling secure client-server delegation without revealing data or computation. It implements both quantum homomorphic encryption and universal blind quantum computation primitives in a modular, reusable architecture, demonstrated on a blind variational quantum classifier for the IRIS dataset.
AI.motivation: No existing software tools allow rapid prototyping of BQC protocols, hindering research into practical applications like secure cloud quantum computing, quantum federated learning, and secure multiparty computation.
AI.method: The authors developed a modular, multi-layered software library that transpiles Qiskit circuits into blind counterparts, supporting both data-only security (quantum homomorphic encryption) and full data-and-algorithm security (universal blind quantum computation) in a client-server architecture.
AI.result: Implementation of these BQC primitives was demonstrated on a blind variational quantum classifier for the IRIS dataset, showing practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: The first BQC prototyping library is now available, with modular design enabling scalability, robustness, and easier exploration of BQC applications.

title: QBism Logic
summary: QBism interprets quantum theory as a normative discipline for an agent's probability assignments and their revision across possible experience. This paper develops a logical formalization of that picture. A well-formed core datum consists of an admissible prior space, a finite family of actual measurements, Born kernels, and update kernels. For each such datum, we introduce a guarded dynamic language for histories and posterior states and prove a global reduction theorem. We next consider effectively semialgebraic data over an effectively presented real closed field. For data in this class, we translate the fragment without dynamic operators into first-order formulas in the corresponding language of ordered rings, thereby reducing validity to first-order reasoning over real closed fields. Together, the reduction and first-order translation yield a sound and complete recursive calculus and a decision procedure for validity. Finally, assuming a symmetric informationally complete (SIC) reference measurement, we show that quantum theory in finite dimensions realizes the framework through SIC coordinates, POVMs, and quantum instruments. We also prove that the corresponding SIC image satisfies the standard qplex geometry conditions, namely the consistency bounds and the lower polar condition, and that under explicit coefficient field hypotheses the resulting quantum datum is effectively semialgebraic.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a logical formalization of QBism, introducing a guarded dynamic language for quantum histories/posterior states, proving reduction and first-order translation theorems to obtain a sound and complete recursive calculus with a decision procedure, and showing that finite-dimensional quantum theory realizes this framework via SIC coordinates with the qplex geometry conditions.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous logical foundation for QBism's normative interpretation of quantum probability, enabling formal reasoning about agent beliefs, measurement updates, and validity checking.
AI.method: Introduces well-formed core data structures (admissible prior spaces, measurement families, Born/update kernels); defines a guarded dynamic language for histories and posterior states; proves a global reduction theorem; translates the dynamic-free fragment into first-order logic over real closed fields; validates the framework using SIC reference measurements, POVMs, and quantum instruments.
AI.result: A sound and complete recursive calculus and decision procedure for validity; demonstration that finite-dimensional quantum theory realizes the framework via SIC coordinates, satisfying qplex consistency bounds and lower polar condition; effective semialgebraicity under explicit coefficient field hypotheses.
AI.conclusion: QBism's probabilistic updating can be fully axiomatized in a logical calculus that is both decidable and realizable by standard quantum theory, bridging subjective Bayesian interpretation with formal logical reasoning.

title: Multi-level Random-Telegraph Noise Mitigation using a Single Spectator Qubit
summary: Preserving quantum coherence in the presence of environmental noise is one of the principal challenges for quantum technologies. Noise mitigation using spectator qubits (SQs) has recently emerged as a promising approach, enabling indirect probing of the noise without disturbing the data qubit (DQ). However, existing analyses that probe ultimate performance have been restricted to two-state random telegraph process noise, which does not capture more complex noise processes that may arise in the environment. Therefore, we here develop a SQ-based noise mitigation for DQs subject to general multi-level fluctuator noise. We first derive the coherence dynamics of the DQ under such noise, then develop a mitigation scheme in which information about the noise is inferred from sequential SQ measurements and used for phase correction. A memory-efficient heuristic adaptive protocol is proposed to dynamically select the SQ measurement time and angle based on the current noise estimate. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed strategy significantly suppresses decoherence under multi-level noise, achieving performance comparable to that in the two-level case despite the increased complexity of the noise process.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a spectator-qubit-based noise mitigation scheme for data qubits under general multi-level fluctuator noise, using an adaptive heuristic protocol that dynamically selects measurement parameters based on noise estimates, achieving decoherence suppression comparable to two-level noise cases.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum noise mitigation using spectator qubits has been limited to two-state random telegraph process noise, which fails to capture more complex environmental noise processes.
AI.method: Derives coherence dynamics of data qubits under multi-level fluctuator noise, then develops a mitigation scheme using sequential spectator qubit measurements for noise inference and phase correction, with a memory-efficient heuristic adaptive protocol that dynamically selects measurement time and angle based on current noise estimates.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show the proposed strategy significantly suppresses decoherence under multi-level noise, achieving performance comparable to the two-level noise case despite increased noise complexity.
AI.conclusion: Spectator-qubit-based noise mitigation can be effectively extended to general multi-level fluctuator noise, maintaining high performance with an adaptive heuristic protocol.

title: Heralded Leakage Detection with Preserved Computational-State Coherence in a Fixed-Frequency Transmon
summary: Leakage out of the computational subspace is a major error mechanism in superconducting quantum processors. Detecting leakage without disturbing the encoded quantum information can provide a heralded error signal that error-correction decoders exploit. However, standard dispersive readout collapses all qubit eigenstates indiscriminately. Here, we demonstrate heralded leakage detection on a fixed-frequency transmon by applying a Rabi drive on the computational transition during dispersive readout. The drive makes the computational states indistinguishable to the probe on the resonator while leaving the second and higher excited states distinguishable from the computational states. We achieve a leakage-detection fidelity of 97.1(3)% within the 80-ns detection window, with a false-flag rate of 2.3(3)% from the computational subspace. Conditioned on the no-leakage outcome, the post-detection state retains an average fidelity of 92.9(5)% across the six cardinal states for an equal mixture of computational and leakage population. The scheme requires no circuit elements beyond those used for standard dispersive readout, making it applicable to various types of superconducting qubits without hardware modification.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates a heralded leakage detection scheme for fixed-frequency transmon qubits that uses a Rabi drive during dispersive readout to distinguish leakage states from computational states without collapsing quantum information, achieving 97.1% detection fidelity with 2.3% false-flag rate and 92.9% post-detection state fidelity.
AI.motivation: Leakage out of the computational subspace is a major error mechanism in superconducting quantum processors, and detecting it without disturbing encoded quantum information is essential for error-correction decoders to exploit heralded error signals.
AI.method: Apply a Rabi drive on the computational transition during dispersive readout, making computational states indistinguishable to the probe on the resonator while leaving higher excited states distinguishable from computational states.
AI.result: Leakage-detection fidelity of 97.1(3)% within 80-ns detection window, false-flag rate of 2.3(3)% from computational subspace, and post-detection state fidelity of 92.9(5)% across six cardinal states.
AI.conclusion: The scheme requires no additional circuit elements beyond standard dispersive readout, making it applicable to various superconducting qubit types without hardware modification.

title: Relativistic quantum teleportation protected by the anti-Unruh effect
summary: We investigate standard quantum teleportation in a relativistic setting where one participant, Rob, undergoes uniform acceleration while Alice remains inertial. Rob interacts locally with a massive scalar field modeled by an Unruh-DeWitt detector. We show that for small detector energy gaps, the entanglement shared between Alice and Rob increases monotonically with acceleration. For larger gaps, entanglement initially decreases at low accelerations due to the Unruh effect, but is subsequently restored and enhanced at higher accelerations as a consequence of the anti-Unruh effect. This behavior is associated with a reduction of the effective detector temperature, leading to a recovery of quantum coherence previously lost to the field. As a result, the teleportation fidelity increases with acceleration and approaches unity in the high-acceleration regime. Our results demonstrate that the anti-Unruh effect can protect and recover quantum information, providing a potential mechanism to mitigate relativistic degradation of quantum correlations.

AI.tldr: In a relativistic quantum teleportation scenario where Rob accelerates uniformly, entanglement and teleportation fidelity can be restored at high accelerations due to the anti-Unruh effect, which reduces effective detector temperature and recovers quantum coherence, even overcoming initial degradation from the Unruh effect.
AI.motivation: To understand how relativistic acceleration affects quantum teleportation and whether quantum information can be protected or recovered from relativistic degradation using the anti-Unruh effect.
AI.method: A relativistic quantum information setting where Rob accelerates uniformly and interacts with a massive scalar field via an Unruh-DeWitt detector, while Alice remains inertial. The study analyzes entanglement and teleportation fidelity as functions of detector energy gap and acceleration.
AI.result: For small detector energy gaps, entanglement increases monotonically with acceleration. For larger gaps, entanglement initially decreases due to the Unruh effect but is subsequently restored and enhanced at higher accelerations due to the anti-Unruh effect, which reduces effective detector temperature and recovers quantum coherence. Teleportation fidelity approaches unity in the high-acceleration regime.
AI.conclusion: The anti-Unruh effect can protect and recover quantum information in relativistic quantum teleportation, offering a mechanism to mitigate relativistic degradation of quantum correlations.

title: Continuous Time Quantum Walk Propagation for Irregular Temporal Graph Forecasting
summary: Continuous time quantum walks built on graph Laplacians produce non monotonic graph propagation features through quantum interference during evolution, which classical diffusion cannot achieve. Such walks deliver a physically motivated propagation scheme for temporal graph signal modeling. We propose Quantum Walk Temporal Architecture (QWTA), which replaces classical graph propagation with a CTQW-type parameterized spectral propagator. QWTA embeds effective observation intervals into the spectral phase modulation of the propagation kernel. QWTA-Base preserves exact CTQW spectral evolution and serves as a physically faithful propagation reference. QWTA-GR further introduces phase soft clipping and gated residual fusion to stabilize propagation. The results show that explicit phase encoding of irregular time intervals, when combined with suitable stabilization, provides a physically motivated and competitive graph propagation design for temporal graph forecasting with missing historical observations.

AI.tldr: QWTA replaces classical graph propagation with continuous-time quantum walk (CTQW) propagators for temporal graph modeling, using spectral phase modulation to handle irregular/missing observations, with two variants: QWTA-Base (exact CTQW) and QWTA-GR (stabilized via phase soft clipping and gated residual fusion).
AI.motivation: Classical diffusion-based graph propagation fails to capture non-monotonic, quantum interference effects that arise in continuous-time quantum walks on graph Laplacians. The authors aim to leverage these quantum-inspired dynamics for temporal graph signal modeling, particularly under irregular or missing historical observations.
AI.method: QWTA employs a parameterized spectral propagator derived from CTQW evolution on graph Laplacians, encoding observation intervals as spectral phase modulations. QWTA-Base implements exact CTQW spectral evolution; QWTA-GR adds phase soft clipping and gated residual fusion to improve stability. The architecture directly processes temporal graph signals with missing data by leveraging the phase-encoded time intervals.
AI.result: Explicit phase encoding of irregular time intervals yields competitive temporal graph forecasting performance. The stabilized QWTA-GR variant mitigates instability in the exact CTQW propagation, demonstrating that physically motivated quantum walk propagators can match or outperform classical approaches for temporal graph forecasting with missing historical observations.
AI.conclusion: Quantum walk-based spectral propagation is a viable and physically motivated alternative to classical graph diffusion for temporal graph modeling, particularly under irregular sampling or missing data conditions. The combination of phase encoding and stabilization techniques makes this approach practically effective.

title: Truncated Wigner approximation for spins in continuous phase space
summary: We review the truncated Wigner approximation (TWA) for spins as a computationally inexpensive numerical approximation method to describe interacting and / or dissipative many-body spin systems. Using the Wigner-Moyal mapping from Hilbert space to a suitable phase space, the many-body density matrix is represented by a c-number distribution, the Wigner function. The gauge freedom in continuous phase space can be exploited to find positive Wigner functions for a large class of spin states, including entangled ones. Employing different sets of correspondence rules, we derive equations of motion for the Wigner function, which, applying controlled approximations, can be mapped to stochastic differential equations. This allows a computationally inexpensive simulation of expectation values. Using a phase-space analog of the quantum regression theorem also multi-time correlations and spectra can be obtained. To illustrate the potential of the method, we benchmark the TWA for spins with some exactly solvable problems of interacting, dissipative spin systems, and then discuss its application to collective processes, such as the superradiant emission of light. Extending the TWA to imaginary time furthermore provides a tool to approximately calculate thermal and ground states of spin Hamiltonians. Finally, we show that the TWA stochastic equations can equivalently be derived within a path-integral approach, provided that the operator products in the dissipator are rigorously mapped onto the curved phase space.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the truncated Wigner approximation (TWA) for spins as a computationally efficient method to simulate interacting/dissipative many-body spin systems, covering its theoretical foundations (Wigner-Moyal mapping, gauge freedom, correspondence rules), extensions to multi-time correlations and imaginary-time evolution, and benchmarking against exactly solvable problems and collective phenomena like superradiance.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive review of the truncated Wigner approximation (TWA) for spins as a computationally inexpensive numerical method for simulating interacting and dissipative many-body spin systems, which are otherwise challenging to solve exactly.
AI.method: The paper employs the Wigner-Moyal mapping from Hilbert space to phase space, uses gauge freedom to find positive Wigner functions for entangled spin states, derives equations of motion via correspondence rules, and applies controlled approximations to map them to stochastic differential equations. It also uses a phase-space quantum regression theorem for multi-time correlations and extends TWA to imaginary time for thermal/ground states, with an alternative path-integral derivation.
AI.result: Benchmarking against exactly solvable interacting/dissipative spin systems demonstrates the method's accuracy and computational efficiency. The TWA successfully describes collective processes such as superradiant light emission and can approximately compute thermal and ground states via imaginary-time evolution.
AI.conclusion: The truncated Wigner approximation for spins is a powerful, computationally inexpensive tool for simulating many-body spin dynamics and static properties, with demonstrated validity across a range of benchmark problems and collective phenomena. The equivalence to a path-integral approach is also established.

title: Chiral Entangled-State Generation through Dissipative Quantum Dynamics
summary: Dissipation, though often detrimental to quantum entanglement, can be manipulated for the preparation of entangled states, wherein ingeniously designed quantum jump processes drive the system toward the desired steady state. Here we venture beyond this paradigm, and demonstrate a new type of entanglement generation in dissipative quantum dynamics. Combining driven-dissipative steady-state engineering and adiabatic passage, we propose a general protocol where the final entangled state depends on the chirality of the evolution path in the parameter space, a scheme that is further extendable to multipartite entanglement. By simulating the Liouvillian dynamics through the quantum Langevin equation for a pair of photons, we experimentally confirm the noise-resistant chiral preparation of various entangled states with high fidelity and concurrence. Our work establishes parametric chiral dynamics as a scalable and robust tool for controllable entanglement generation, paving the way for its applications in quantum information.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new protocol combining driven-dissipative steady-state engineering and adiabatic passage to generate entanglement chirally, where the final entangled state depends on the evolution path's chirality in parameter space. This is experimentally confirmed using photon pairs via quantum Langevin equation simulations, demonstrating noise-resistant, high-fidelity entanglement preparation extendable to multipartite systems.
AI.motivation: To go beyond conventional dissipative entanglement preparation (which relies on steady-state engineering alone) by introducing chirality-dependent entanglement generation that is robust against noise and scalable to multipartite systems.
AI.method: Combines driven-dissipative steady-state engineering with adiabatic passage, where the chiral evolution path in parameter space determines the final entangled state. The Liouvillian dynamics are simulated via the quantum Langevin equation for a pair of photons.
AI.result: Experimental confirmation of noise-resistant chiral preparation of various entangled states with high fidelity and concurrence using photon pairs.
AI.conclusion: Parametric chiral dynamics is established as a scalable and robust tool for controllable entanglement generation, with promising applications in quantum information.

title: Constraints on recovering quantum information after erasure
comment: 6 pages, 6 pages of supplemental material, 3 figures. See arXiv:2607.08591 for an independent proof of the erasure-simulation conjecture
summary: Suppose that we encode quantum information into $ n $ physical carriers. With what probabilities can we perfectly recover the quantum information after sets of carriers have been erased? This question arises in the study of quantum erasure channels, for which M.B. Hastings conjectured that if each carrier is independently erased with probability $ t \geq 1/2 $, then it is impossible to recover the quantum information with asymptotically vanishing error and probability $ > 1-t $. We prove this conjecture by establishing new no-cloning constraints on realizable recovery probabilities.

AI.tldr: The paper proves Hastings' conjecture about quantum erasure channels: when each of n physical carriers is independently erased with probability t ≥ 1/2, it is impossible to recover quantum information with asymptotically vanishing error and probability exceeding 1-t. The proof uses new no-cloning constraints on recovery probabilities.
AI.motivation: To determine the fundamental limits of quantum information recovery in erasure channels, specifically resolving Hastings' conjecture about the threshold t ≥ 1/2 where recovery with probability > 1-t becomes impossible.
AI.method: The authors establish new no-cloning constraints on realizable recovery probabilities and use these to prove the conjecture.
AI.result: Proved Hastings' conjecture: if each carrier is independently erased with probability t ≥ 1/2, perfect recovery with asymptotically vanishing error and probability > 1-t is impossible.
AI.conclusion: New no-cloning constraints provide fundamental bounds on quantum error correction in erasure channels, confirming the threshold at t = 1/2.

title: Scaling law for optimal excitation storage and superradiant release in waveguide QED systems
summary: Driven-dissipative quantum emitters provide a powerful platform for controllable excitation storage and release, with promising applications in quantum batteries and quantum storage. Yet, transient excitation transfer in collective many-body systems is often obscured by the intricate interplay among coherent driving, dissipation, and correlation dynamics. Here, we uncover a scalable excitation-storage mechanism in two emitter ensembles coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide. A coherently driven ensemble acts as an effective excitation reservoir, while a second ensemble positioned near a dissipative node serves as a subradiant storage medium. Surprisingly, when the driven ensemble largely exceeds the storage ensemble in size, the transfer dynamics enters a nearly correlation-free regime, allowing the driven ensemble to behave effectively as a classical excitation source. This reveals a simple scaling law for optimal excitation transfer, under which the storage ensemble approaches near-complete population inversion as the driven ensemble size increases. Building on this mechanism, we propose a three-stage storage-and-release protocol enabling fast excitation storage and controllable photon emission. Our results demonstrate how coherent and dissipative collective interactions can be jointly harnessed for quantum energy storage and programmable nonequilibrium dynamics in waveguide QED platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper reveals a scalable excitation-storage mechanism in two emitter ensembles coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide, where a large driven ensemble acts as a classical excitation source for a subradiant storage ensemble near a dissipative node, enabling near-complete population inversion and a three-stage storage-and-release protocol.
AI.motivation: To uncover a scalable excitation-transfer mechanism in driven-dissipative many-body quantum systems, which is often obscured by the interplay of coherent driving, dissipation, and correlations, and to enable controllable quantum energy storage and release.
AI.method: Two emitter ensembles coupled to a semi-infinite waveguide: one coherently driven ensemble acts as an excitation reservoir, while a second ensemble positioned near a dissipative node serves as a subradiant storage medium. The size disparity between ensembles leads to a correlation-free regime where the driven ensemble behaves as a classical source.
AI.result: When the driven ensemble is much larger than the storage ensemble, transfer dynamics enters a nearly correlation-free regime, yielding a simple scaling law for optimal excitation transfer with near-complete population inversion in the storage ensemble as the driven ensemble size increases.
AI.conclusion: Coherent and dissipative collective interactions can be jointly harnessed for quantum energy storage and programmable nonequilibrium dynamics in waveguide QED platforms, demonstrated via a proposed three-stage storage-and-release protocol.

title: Locally Scrambled Quantum Memories for Loss-Tolerant Entanglement-Assisted Optical Interferometry
summary: We formulate a loss-tolerant extension of entanglement-assisted long-baseline optical interferometry in which the astronomical optical coherence is first mapped coherently to distributed quantum memories and is subsequently protected by local scrambling encoders. The proposal must be distinguished from existing memory-assisted Gottesman--Jennewein--Croke (GJC) interferometers, in which quantum memories store an ancillary single-photon-entangled reference rather than the astronomical state itself. We derive the weak-thermal-light model, its two-parameter quantum Fisher information (QFI) matrix, the GJC measurement probabilities, and the associated classical Fisher information (CFI). We then prove that exact local correction of flagged erasures restores the complete complex visibility, its QFI matrix, and the operational GJC CFI. The relevant protection criterion is reference--environment decoupling, not volume-law entanglement alone. We state, as conjectures, quantitative decoupling bounds for local random encoders and finite-depth scramblers, and derive the expected threshold of fewer than one half of the physical memories erased per node. Finally, we formulate the phase-covariance and superselection-rule constraints required for a physically meaningful distributed protocol.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a loss-tolerant entanglement-assisted long-baseline optical interferometry protocol that maps astronomical coherence to distributed quantum memories and protects it via local scrambling encoders, deriving Fisher information matrices and proving that local correction of flagged erasures restores complete complex visibility under reference-environment decoupling.
AI.motivation: To overcome losses in long-baseline optical interferometry by extending memory-assisted GJC interferometers—where quantum memories only store ancillary entangled references—to a framework where the astronomical state itself is coherently mapped to distributed quantum memories and protected by local scrambling encoders.
AI.method: Development of a weak-thermal-light model; derivation of two-parameter quantum Fisher information (QFI) matrix, GJC measurement probabilities, and classical Fisher information (CFI); proof that exact local correction of flagged erasures restores the complete complex visibility; quantitative decoupling bounds conjectured for local random encoders and finite-depth scramblers; formulation of phase-covariance and superselection-rule constraints.
AI.result: Exact local correction of flagged erasures restores the complete complex visibility, its QFI matrix, and the operational GJC CFI. The threshold for protection is fewer than one half of physical memories erased per node. The relevant protection criterion is reference-environment decoupling, not volume-law entanglement alone.
AI.conclusion: Loss-tolerant entanglement-assisted long-baseline optical interferometry is feasible by coherently mapping astronomical coherence to distributed quantum memories with local scrambling encoders, provided reference-environment decoupling is achieved and erasure rates remain below half per node.

title: Interpreting Quantum Learning Models via Stochastic Processes
summary: Quantum machine learning models define probabilistic input--output maps through coherent quantum evolution and measurement. While such models can exhibit computational advantages, their internal functioning and decision making generally resists interpretation in terms of stochastic trajectories through intermediate configurations. In contrast to classical (Markovian) stochastic processes, quantum dynamics generically violates the Chapman--Kolmogorov divisibility condition, preventing a decomposition into probabilistically meaningful intermediate transitions. We develop a probabilistic framework for representing quantum learning models as stochastic processes over configuration spaces where the dynamics are modeled as linear maps on probability distributions. Starting from a fixed POVM, arbitrary quantum channels induce transition kernels on the associated probability representation. For informationally complete POVMs, and in particular SIC-POVMs, these kernels are Markovian but generally quasi-stochastic, with non-classicality appearing as negativity. By contrast, projective spaces admit positive stochastic kernels but generally require non-Markovian dynamics due to the failure of Chapman--Kolmogorov divisibility. This yields a trade-off between negativity and dependence on past configurations, i.e. quantum dynamics can be represented either by Markovian quasi-stochastic maps or by positive stochastic processes with higher Markov order. We discuss how such representations of quantum dynamics can be interpreted as stochastic walks through a memory space in the spirit of Projective Simulation, a model of learning and agency in which decisions arise from random walks over an episodic memory network. We further outline how finite-order stochastic kernels can approximate such quantum deliberation processes and show in what regimes the classical machine learning model is recovered.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a probabilistic framework to represent quantum machine learning models as stochastic processes, revealing a trade-off between negativity (non-classicality) and non-Markovianity: quantum dynamics can be represented either by Markovian quasi-stochastic maps (using informationally complete POVMs) or by positive stochastic processes with higher Markov order (using projective spaces). The framework connects to Projective Simulation models of learning and agency.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning models lack interpretability in terms of stochastic trajectories through intermediate configurations, as quantum dynamics violate the Chapman-Kolmogorov divisibility condition that underlies classical stochastic processes. The authors aim to develop a probabilistic framework that bridges quantum and classical learning models.
AI.method: The authors start from a fixed POVM and show that arbitrary quantum channels induce transition kernels on the associated probability representation. They analyze two cases: (1) informationally complete POVMs (especially SIC-POVMs), which yield Markovian but quasi-stochastic kernels with negativity, and (2) projective spaces, which yield positive stochastic kernels but require non-Markovian dynamics due to failure of Chapman-Kolmogorov divisibility.
AI.result: A fundamental trade-off is identified between negativity and dependence on past configurations: quantum dynamics can be represented either as Markovian quasi-stochastic maps (with negativity) or as positive stochastic processes with higher Markov order. The framework is linked to Projective Simulation, where decisions arise from random walks over episodic memory networks.
AI.conclusion: Finite-order stochastic kernels can approximate quantum deliberation processes, and the paper outlines regimes where the classical machine learning model is recovered, providing a pathway to interpret quantum learning models through stochastic walks in memory space.

title: Broadband Polarization Compensation with Link Segment Reconstruction for Quantum Optical Links
summary: Polarization-encoded quantum communication requires compensation of polarization transformations induced by the optical links. If the compensator is embedded between two channel segments, the transformations before and after the compensator must be treated separately. Moreover, standard three-wave-plate polarization controllers can become non-universal when their retardances deviate from their ideal values. To address these two challenges, we introduce a four-wave plate compensator that synthesizes arbitrary SO(3) polarization transformations over a broad wavelength range, and an eight-Stokes vector protocol that reconstructs the two link-segment Mueller matrices on either side of the compensator. Our experiment reveals that the four-plate sequence suppresses polarization-induced excess quantum bit error rate (QBER) to the sub-percent level at an operating wavelength more than 100 nm from the design wavelength without further optimization. Combined with two auxiliary wavelengths, our scheme tracks the temperature-driven drift of a strongly wavelength-sensitive fiber spool while keeping the excess QBER below 1%. These results support flexible compensator placement and wavelength channel selection, as well as non-interruptive polarization control in wavelength-division-multiplexed quantum optical links.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a four-wave plate compensator and an eight-Stokes vector protocol to handle polarization transformations in segmented quantum optical links, achieving sub-percent excess QBER even 100 nm from design wavelength and enabling non-interruptive polarization control in WDM systems.
AI.motivation: Polarization-encoded quantum communication requires compensation of polarization transformations from optical links, but standard three-wave-plate controllers become non-universal when retardances deviate from ideal values, and compensators embedded between two channel segments require separate treatment of transformations before and after the compensator.
AI.method: A four-wave plate compensator that synthesizes arbitrary SO(3) polarization transformations over a broad wavelength range, combined with an eight-Stokes vector protocol that reconstructs the two link-segment Mueller matrices on either side of the compensator.
AI.result: The four-plate sequence suppresses polarization-induced excess QBER to sub-percent level at operating wavelengths >100 nm from design wavelength without optimization; with two auxiliary wavelengths, temperature-driven drift of a strongly wavelength-sensitive fiber spool is tracked while keeping excess QBER below 1%.
AI.conclusion: The scheme supports flexible compensator placement, flexible wavelength channel selection, and non-interruptive polarization control in wavelength-division-multiplexed quantum optical links.

title: Operator-centric Clifford algebra for variational eigensolvers and finite-shot adaptive selection
comment: 8 pages plus 3 pages Supplemental Material; 6 figures
summary: We develop a sparse operator-centric realization of $n$-qubit variational quantum algorithms in the complex Clifford algebra $\mathrm{Cl}(2n,\mathbb{C}) \cong M(2^n,\mathbb{C})$. Density operators, gates, observables, channels, fermionic modes, and adaptive-selection observables are represented in one Pauli-word algebra, with the Jordan--Wigner map providing the exact bridge to anticommuting Clifford generators. We distinguish general Pauli-word rotations from Spin-group rotors and derive an exact transpose-parity rule: for real Hamiltonians and real states, every candidate Pauli word containing an even number of $Y$ factors has zero ADAPT gradient, while odd-$Y$ rotations preserve the real sector. For the critical open transverse-field Ising chain, a depth-three Hamiltonian variational ansatz gives relative energy errors $4.84\times10^{-5}$, $2.19\times10^{-3}$, and $3.67\times10^{-3}$ for $n=4,5,6$. A compact local ADAPT pool is exact at $n=4$ but leaves residual errors at larger sizes; a systematic contiguous three-local odd-$Y$ pool reaches relative errors below $1.3\times10^{-12}$ for $n\leq6$. In 100-seed finite-shot tests at $n=4$, fixed-shot selection succeeds in $0/100$ runs, whereas uniform escalation and confidence-bound racing each succeed in $84/100$ runs; racing lowers median shots by $34\%$. We claim no asymptotic speedup over matrix methods. The contribution is a corrected algebraic formulation, an exact pool-pruning rule, and a reproducible study of measurement-limited adaptive selection.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a sparse operator-centric realization of n-qubit variational quantum algorithms in the complex Clifford algebra Cl(2n,C), representing density operators, gates, observables, channels, and fermionic modes in a unified Pauli-word algebra. Key contributions include an exact transpose-parity rule for ADAPT gradient selection, demonstrations on the open transverse-field Ising chain (relative energy errors as low as 1.3×10^{-12}), and a comparative study of measurement-limited adaptive selection strategies (confidence-bound racing achieves 84/100 success with 34% fewer shots).
AI.motivation: To provide a corrected algebraic formulation for variational quantum algorithms by unifying all quantum computing components (density operators, gates, observables, etc.) in a single Clifford algebra framework, and to derive exact pruning rules for ADAPT-VQE that improve efficiency and correctness.
AI.method: The paper uses the complex Clifford algebra Cl(2n,C) ≅ M(2^n,C) as the algebraic foundation, with the Jordan-Wigner map bridging to anticommuting Clifford generators. It distinguishes Pauli-word rotations from Spin-group rotors, derives a transpose-parity rule for ADAPT gradients, and tests on the open transverse-field Ising chain using Hamiltonian variational ansätze and local ADAPT pools. Finite-shot tests compare fixed-shot selection, uniform escalation, and confidence-bound racing.
AI.result: For the open transverse-field Ising chain, a depth-three Hamiltonian variational ansatz achieves relative energy errors of 4.84×10^{-5}, 2.19×10^{-3}, and 3.67×10^{-3} for n=4,5,6. A compact local ADAPT pool is exact at n=4 but leaves residuals for larger n; a contiguous three-local odd-Y pool reaches errors below 1.3×10^{-12} for n≤6. In finite-shot tests, fixed-shot selection succeeds 0/100 runs, while uniform escalation and confidence-bound racing each succeed 84/100; racing reduces median shots by 34%.
AI.conclusion: The paper claims no asymptotic speedup over matrix methods, but contributes a corrected algebraic formulation, an exact pool-pruning rule (transpose-parity rule), and a reproducible study of measurement-limited adaptive selection strategies for variational quantum algorithms.

title: The finite key effect of side-channel-secure quantum key distribution beyond post-selection technique
summary: By applying the framework of entropic uncertainty relation (EUR) and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma (QLHL), we introduce a security-proof method for variable-length side-channel-secure (SCS) quantum key distribution (QKD) against coherent attacks. This method reframes composable security as a statistical fluctuation problem of phase errors, enabling direct proofs against coherent attacks through observables and virtual observables. It yields tight key rates for the SCS protocol and reduces pulse requirements by over two orders of magnitude compared to prior works that employ the post-selection technique. We prove that the secure key length for the SCS protocol can be determined after error correction by exploiting the fact that untagged bits are free from bit-flip errors, using the actual information leakage during error correction and the post-error-correction statistics of each state to calculate the final key rate. We further identify sufficient conditions under which the final key length may be determined after error correction in a broader class of QKD protocols. Under the framework of EUR and QLHL, we clarify the applicability of several commonly used concentration bounds to variable-length QKD and the appropriate manner of their implementation. This work enhances the practical value of the SCS protocol and clarifies the security justification of key-rate formulas used in practical variable-length QKD implementations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a security-proof method for variable-length side-channel-secure QKD against coherent attacks using entropic uncertainty relations and the Quantum Leftover Hash Lemma, achieving tighter key rates and over two orders of magnitude reduction in pulse requirements.
AI.motivation: To develop a more efficient security-proof method for variable-length side-channel-secure QKD that yields tighter key rates and significantly reduces pulse requirements compared to prior post-selection techniques.
AI.method: The method reframes composable security as a statistical fluctuation problem of phase errors using EUR and QLHL, enabling direct proofs against coherent attacks through observables and virtual observables. The secure key length is determined after error correction by exploiting untagged bits' freedom from bit-flip errors, using actual information leakage and post-error-correction statistics.
AI.result: The method yields tight key rates for the SCS protocol and reduces pulse requirements by over two orders of magnitude compared to prior works using post-selection technique. Sufficient conditions for determining final key length after error correction in broader QKD protocols are identified.
AI.conclusion: This work enhances the practical value of the SCS protocol and clarifies the security justification of key-rate formulas used in practical variable-length QKD implementations, along with clarifying appropriate implementation of concentration bounds under the EUR and QLHL framework.

title: LLM-Driven Cross-Paradigm Design for Quantum Optimal Control
summary: Quantum optimal control (QOC) underpins adiabatic quantum computation, quantum annealing, and quantum state engineering, yet practical deployment is fundamentally bottlenecked by strict hardware constraints and substantial expert effort required to design protocols for each problem instance. To overcome this, we introduce QOC-Workbench, an auditable, large language model (LLM)-driven workflow that acts as an automated quantum co-scientist for cross-paradigm protocol design. Going beyond traditional numerical optimizers that merely tune parameters within a fixed formula, the LLM autonomously parses physics literature, proposes structural hypotheses, and writes code to validate them by direct simulation. This workflow supports cross-paradigm design by accumulating control motifs across tasks. We demonstrate this approach across three distinct settings: Case 1, Rydberg-atom maximum-independent-set arrays; Case 2, interacting XXZ spin chains; and Case 3, random transverse-field Ising models. In Cases 1 and 2, the workflow autonomously discovers hardware-compliant auxiliary controls, target catalysts, and schedule deformations that outperform literature baselines. In Case 3, it addresses the computational bottleneck of variational counterdiabatic driving by escalating from per-instance optimization to an amortized graph-neural-network generator, successfully transferring learned coefficient paths to larger unseen systems. By actively bridging the gap between theoretical algorithms and experimental restrictions across distinct control paradigms and Hamiltonian families, QOC-Workbench establishes a continuously evolving, cross-paradigm methodology for autonomous quantum control.

AI.tldr: QOC-Workbench is an LLM-driven automated workflow for quantum optimal control that autonomously parses physics literature, proposes structural hypotheses, writes simulation code, and discovers cross-paradigm control protocols across Rydberg-atom arrays, XXZ spin chains, and random transverse-field Ising models, outperforming literature baselines and enabling amortized learning for larger systems.
AI.motivation: Practical quantum optimal control deployment is bottlenecked by strict hardware constraints and substantial expert effort needed to design protocols per problem instance, motivating the need for an automated, scalable co-scientist that reduces human labor and generalizes across paradigms.
AI.method: An LLM-driven workflow that autonomously parses physics literature, proposes structural hypotheses, writes and executes simulation code for validation, accumulates control motifs across tasks, and escalates from per-instance optimization to amortized graph-neural-network generators.
AI.result: In Rydberg-atom MIS arrays and XXZ spin chains, the workflow autonomously discovers hardware-compliant auxiliary controls, target catalysts, and schedule deformations exceeding literature baselines. In random transverse-field Ising models, it learns amortized coefficient paths via GNNs that transfer to larger unseen systems.
AI.conclusion: QOC-Workbench establishes a continuously evolving, cross-paradigm methodology for autonomous quantum control that bridges theoretical algorithms and experimental restrictions, moving beyond fixed-formula parameter tuning to structural hypothesis generation and validation.

title: Neural Gauge-P Representation for Open Quantum Dynamics of Interacting Bosons
summary: Simulating the nonequilibrium dynamics of interacting open quantum systems remains challenging beyond small system sizes. Quantum phase-space representations provide a scalable approach, but their useful simulation time can be limited by broad distribution tails and the associated boundary terms. We introduce the neural gauge-$P$ representation for open bosonic systems, in which stochastic gauges are parameterized by neural networks and optimized using exact moment equation residuals. For the driven-dissipative Bose--Hubbard model in both single-site and square-lattice settings, the neural gauge-$P$ representation remains accurate during long-time evolution toward the steady state, whereas the corresponding ungauged representation becomes unreliable at substantially earlier times. These results demonstrate the potential of the neural gauge-$P$ representation for accurate simulations of nonequilibrium open quantum many-body dynamics.

AI.tldr: The neural gauge-P representation uses neural-network-parameterized stochastic gauges to extend the reliable simulation time of quantum phase-space methods for open bosonic systems, demonstrated on the driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard model.
AI.motivation: Simulating nonequilibrium dynamics of interacting open quantum systems remains challenging beyond small system sizes; quantum phase-space representations have limited useful simulation time due to broad distribution tails and boundary terms.
AI.method: Stochastic gauges are parameterized by neural networks and optimized using exact moment equation residuals.
AI.result: For the driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard model in single-site and square-lattice settings, the neural gauge-P representation remains accurate during long-time evolution toward steady state, while the ungauged representation fails at substantially earlier times.
AI.conclusion: The neural gauge-P representation shows potential for accurate simulations of nonequilibrium open quantum many-body dynamics.

title: Lie-Group Mode Connectivity in Quantum Machine Learning from a Dynamical Lie Algebra Perspective
summary: Mode connectivity has been widely studied in classical machine learning as a geometric property of low-loss regions in parameter space. In quantum machine learning (QML), however, the physically relevant object is not the parameter vector itself but the unitary transformation implemented by a parameterized quantum circuit. In this study, we formulate mode connectivity on the reachable unitary Lie group generated by the dynamical Lie algebra of the generators. We show that, under a near-minimum connectedness assumption and the absence of critical values in a low-loss band, the corresponding low-loss sublevel set on the reachable Lie group is path-connected. This provides a geometric interpretation of mode connectivity in QML that is independent of a particular parameterization. We further discuss how overparameterization can enable the lifting of Lie-group paths to parameter space, thereby making Lie-group connectivity observable in parameter-space experiments. Finally, we present toy numerical experiments in which geodesic interpolations between trained unitaries exhibit nearly zero loss barriers, consistent with the proposed interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates mode connectivity in QML by studying low-loss regions on the reachable unitary Lie group (generated by the dynamical Lie algebra), proving path-connectedness under certain conditions, and linking overparameterization to observable connectivity in parameter space.
AI.motivation: In classical ML, mode connectivity studies geometric properties of low-loss regions in parameter space, but QML's physically relevant object is the unitary transformation, not the parameter vector. A parameterization-independent geometric characterization is needed.
AI.method: Formulates mode connectivity on the reachable unitary Lie group generated by the dynamical Lie algebra; proves path-connectedness of low-loss sublevel sets under near-minimum connectedness and absence of critical values; discusses lifting Lie-group paths to parameter space via overparameterization.
AI.result: Under the stated assumptions, the low-loss sublevel set on the reachable Lie group is path-connected. Overparameterization enables lifting of Lie-group paths to parameter space. Toy experiments with geodesic interpolations show near-zero loss barriers.
AI.conclusion: Mode connectivity in QML is naturally understood on the unitary Lie group rather than parameter space, offering a geometric interpretation independent of parameterization. Overparameterization bridges the gap between Lie-group and parameter-space connectivity.

title: Temporal Diffraction Grating for Engineered Superconducting Qubit Dissipation
summary: Parametric frequency modulation is a standard tool in superconducting circuits for activating tunable interactions and implementing quantum gates. Here, we engineer dissipation in a flux-tunable transmon qubit by using sideband modulation to bring it into resonance with a lossy resonator, opening an on-demand Purcell decay channel. We find that pulsing this channel on and off does not simply lower the time-averaged decay rate; instead, it reorganizes the dissipation spectrum into a structured interference pattern. A Chebyshev-propagator model for the repeated on/off block reproduces the measured spectra and reveals a close structural correspondence to N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, with each on-window acting as a temporal aperture. By varying the pulse duration and duty cycle, we demonstrate control over the spacing, contrast, and envelope of the dissipation spectrum. These results establish pulsed parametric modulation as a direct method for shaping engineered dissipation in superconducting circuits and provide a new control knob for open quantum system dynamics.

AI.tldr: Using pulsed sideband modulation, a flux-tunable transmon qubit is brought into resonance with a lossy resonator to create an on-demand Purcell decay channel. The pulsed operation reorganizes dissipation into a structured interference pattern, analogous to N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction, with control over the dissipation spectrum via pulse duration and duty cycle.
AI.motivation: To engineer on-demand dissipation in superconducting circuits by using parametric frequency modulation to activate a Purcell decay channel, and to understand the spectral effects of pulsing this dissipation channel on and off.
AI.method: Sideband modulation brings a flux-tunable transmon into resonance with a lossy resonator, creating a pulsed on-demand Purcell decay channel. A Chebyshev-propagator model for repeated on/off blocks is used to simulate the dissipation spectrum, revealing a diffraction-like interference pattern.
AI.result: Pulsing the dissipation channel does not merely time-average the decay rate but produces a structured interference pattern in the dissipation spectrum, closely analogous to N-slit Fraunhofer diffraction. The spacing, contrast, and envelope of the spectrum are controlled by pulse duration and duty cycle.
AI.conclusion: Pulsed parametric modulation provides a direct method for shaping engineered dissipation in superconducting circuits, offering a new control knob for open quantum system dynamics.

title: Single-atom sensor for low-frequency electric field
summary: Precision measurement of low-frequency electric field (LFEF) signals with frequency from 30 kHz to 300 kHz is crucial for advancing both fundamental science and practical applications, owing to their unique frequency regime. For conventional electromagnetic antennas, the long wavelength (i.e., several kilometers) of the LFEF leads to a severe size constraint that efficient radiation becomes challenging to achieve when the antenna size is much smaller than the long wavelength of the LFEF signals, which in turn results in a reduction of measurement sensitivity and compromises antenna's performance. By exploiting the high intrinsic sensitivity of cold trapped ions to weak alternating electric signals via Coulomb interaction, we demonstrate a single-ion phonon laser sensor acted by an injection-locked 40Ca+ ion confined in a surface-electrode trap. Combining the beat frequency technique with the injection-locked phonon laser oscillation, we demonstrate a practical and efficient approach for simultaneous extraction of the frequency, phase, and amplitude from a single measurement, without the need for sideband cooling. This approach achieves precision detection for LFEF signals with the sensitivity of 404 uV/(m * Hz1/2) and the detection limit of 61.5 uV/m. Besides, this approach also shows remarkable robustness against noise. Our study helps realizing practical single-atom sensors in the low-frequency regime, opening avenues for applications in subsurface communication, precision metrology, mass spectrometry, and biomedical monitoring.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates a single-ion phonon laser sensor using a trapped 40Ca+ ion for precise measurement of low-frequency electric fields (30-300 kHz), achieving 404 μV/(m·Hz^(1/2)) sensitivity and 61.5 μV/m detection limit via injection-locked phonon laser oscillation and beat frequency technique.
AI.motivation: Conventional electromagnetic antennas face severe size constraints due to the long wavelength (kilometers) of LFEF signals, making efficient radiation difficult when antenna size is much smaller than the wavelength, which reduces measurement sensitivity and compromises performance.
AI.method: A single-ion phonon laser sensor utilizing an injection-locked 40Ca+ ion confined in a surface-electrode trap. Combines beat frequency technique with injection-locked phonon laser oscillation for simultaneous extraction of frequency, phase, and amplitude from a single measurement without requiring sideband cooling.
AI.result: Achieves sensitivity of 404 μV/(m·Hz^(1/2)) and detection limit of 61.5 μV/m for LFEF signals, with remarkable robustness against noise.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a practical single-atom sensor for the low-frequency regime, enabling applications in subsurface communication, precision metrology, mass spectrometry, and biomedical monitoring.

title: Spatial nonlocality imaging via metasurface
comment: 18 pages, 5 figures, with 21 pages of Supplementary Materials. Comments are welcome; please contact the corresponding authors for inquiries
summary: Bell nonlocality is both a defining signature of entanglement and a key quantum information resource. However, visualizing and certifying nonlocal correlations across a spatially multimode photonic field remains challenging due to the rapidly growing measurement cost of spatially resolved projective tests. To address this issue, we build a spatial nonlocality imaging scheme that directly reveals the spatial distribution of quantum nonlocality by integrating a metasurface that performs parallel polarization projections with a quantum-adaptive neural network. Spatially resolved Clauser--Horne--Shimony--Holt (CHSH) tests are realized over a 400-pixel biphoton field using an average of only 1.7 detected coincidence pairs per pixel per basis. This approach yields a nonlocality image that maps the two-dimensional spatial distribution of Bell violations across the optical field and reveals the target-state-dependent spatial evolution of Bell violations. It provides a highly resource-efficient route to large-scale Bell certification and opens new possibilities for exploiting spatially multimode entanglement in quantum imaging, quantum networking, and scalable photonic quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a spatial nonlocality imaging scheme that integrates a metasurface for parallel polarization projections with a quantum-adaptive neural network, enabling spatially resolved CHSH tests over a 400-pixel biphoton field using only ~1.7 coincidence pairs per pixel per basis, mapping the 2D distribution of Bell violations.
AI.motivation: Visualizing and certifying nonlocal correlations across spatially multimode photonic fields is challenging due to the rapidly growing measurement cost of spatially resolved projective tests.
AI.method: Integration of a metasurface performing parallel polarization projections with a quantum-adaptive neural network for spatial nonlocality imaging.
AI.result: Spatially resolved CHSH tests over a 400-pixel biphoton field using only ~1.7 detected coincidence pairs per pixel per basis, producing a nonlocality image mapping the 2D spatial distribution of Bell violations.
AI.conclusion: This provides a highly resource-efficient route to large-scale Bell certification and enables new possibilities in quantum imaging, quantum networking, and scalable photonic quantum technologies.

title: Fully-connected three-mode squeezed vacuum: Gaussian entanglement, steering, and collective photon subtraction
summary: We investigate a fully-connected three-mode squeezed vacuum (FC-C3MSV) state, where all three modes are pairwise coupled through nonlinear interactions in a triangle ($K_3$) topology. Using the integration-within-ordered-product technique, we derive the normal product form of the squeezing operator and obtain the covariance matrix directly from the Bogoliubov transformation. Under symmetric coupling, the physical state is genuinely tripartite entangled for any nonzero squeezing, while the three Armstrong-type witnesses provide a finite-window sufficient experimental test; in the chain-type C3MSV only one of these witnesses is violated. We find that, despite two-mode entanglement, the fully-connected topology admits \emph{no} two-mode Gaussian steering ($\mathcal{G}^{i\to j}=0$) between any pair of physical modes; the steering resource is instead collective one-mode-versus-two steering $\mathcal{G}^{i\to jk}$, which is $θ$-independent and grows with $r$. We analyze independent vacuum losses and obtain critical transmittances for steering survival: under full symmetric loss at $r=0.5$, one-to-two collective steering disappears at $η\approx0.58$, whereas reverse two-to-one collective steering survives down to $η\approx0.502$ and the underlying two-mode entanglement persists for all $η>0$. Finally, we revisit photon subtraction using a normalized phase-space derivation. A photon subtraction on a single physical mode does not generate Wigner negativity on another single mode, consistent with the absence of two-mode steering. Wigner negativity can instead be generated when Bob subtracts from the collective mode $(b+c)/\sqrt{2}$, with a loss threshold $η_c\approx0.667$ at $r=0.5$. These results distinguish pairwise and collective nonclassical resources in the FC-C3MSV and clarify the operational role of the complete-graph topology.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates a fully-connected three-mode squeezed vacuum (FC-C3MSV) state with triangle topology, deriving its covariance matrix and showing it exhibits genuine tripartite entanglement for any nonzero squeezing.
