Unlike chain-type states, FC-C3MSV has no two-mode Gaussian steering; steering is collective (one-mode vs two-modes). Under symmetric loss, one-to-two steering vanishes at η≈0.58, two-to-one at η≈0.502, while two-mode entanglement persists for all η>0. Photon subtraction on a single mode fails to generate Wigner negativity on another mode, but subtraction from a collective mode can, with a loss threshold η_c≈0.667.
AI.motivation: To understand the nonclassical resources—entanglement, steering, and Wigner negativity—in a fully-connected (K₃ topology) three-mode squeezed vacuum state, and to clarify how the complete-graph topology qualitatively changes the correlation structure compared to the chain-type configuration.
AI.method: The integration-within-ordered-product technique is used to derive the normal product form of the squeezing operator and the covariance matrix via Bogoliubov transformation. Linearization optics, Gaussian analysis of entanglement and steering, and a normalized phase-space derivation for photon subtraction are employed.
AI.result: Genuine tripartite entanglement exists for any nonzero squeezing. No two-mode Gaussian steering is present; steering is collective (one-mode vs two-modes). Under symmetric loss, one-to-two steering vanishes at η≈0.58, two-to-one at η≈0.502. Single-mode photon subtraction does not create Wigner negativity on another mode, but collective-mode subtraction does, with threshold η_c≈0.667.
AI.conclusion: The FC-C3MSV exhibits a distinct resource hierarchy from the chain-type C3MSV, with collective steering replacing pairwise steering and unique photon-subtraction behavior. The complete-graph topology is operationally significant for generating and detecting multipartite nonclassicality.

title: Active Optical Frequency Measurements with Superradiance Prolonged by a Modulated Magnetic Field
summary: Superradiant emission from long-lived excited states of an atomic ensemble confined in an optical cavity constitutes a practical source of light with narrow linewidth. In the pulsed regime, however, superradiance implies rapid emission and a broadening of the spectrum. Recent experiments have demonstrated constructive and destructive interference of superradiant emission by different strontium atomic transitions. In this article, we show that by modulating the atomic transition frequencies with a magnetic field, it is possible to control the release of the atomic excitation energy as a prolonged pulse or a train of superradiant pulses. By simulations, we show that heterodyne detection of the prolonged superradiance shows extremely sharp spectral features, which leads to significantly reduced frequency uncertainty and fluctuation.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that modulating atomic transition frequencies with a magnetic field can control superradiant emission from an atomic ensemble in an optical cavity, enabling prolonged pulse or pulse trains with extremely sharp spectral features via heterodyne detection.
AI.motivation: To overcome the spectral broadening and rapid emission inherent to pulsed superradiance from long-lived atomic excited states in an optical cavity, and to achieve controlled, narrow-linewidth light sources.
AI.method: The authors modulate atomic transition frequencies using a magnetic field to control the release of atomic excitation energy, producing either a prolonged single pulse or a train of superradiant pulses. Heterodyne detection is used to analyze the spectral features.
AI.result: Simulations show that prolonged superradiance under magnetic field modulation exhibits extremely sharp spectral features, leading to significantly reduced frequency uncertainty and fluctuation.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic field modulation provides a practical method to control superradiant emission dynamics, enabling narrow-linewidth pulsed light sources with improved frequency stability.

title: Variance-Reduced Trajectory Unravelings for GPU Noisy Quantum-Circuit Simulation: Characterization and a Qiskit-Aer Integration Gap
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables. Submitted for publication
summary: Monte-Carlo trajectory (quantum-jump) methods are the practical route to simulating noisy quantum circuits once the exact density-matrix method is precluded by its $4^n$ memory cost. Their bottleneck is estimator variance: resolving one expectation value can demand thousands of trajectories. Recent tensor-network work shows that \emph{variance-reduced unravelings} -- projector and analog sampling -- sharply cut this variance, but only on CPU matrix-product-state backends, with no path into production tooling. We implement both unravelings on a \emph{GPU dense-statevector} trajectory engine and validate them against the exact density matrix (ideal-circuit fidelity $1-2.2\times10^{-16}$; $1/\sqrt{N}$ convergence; all unravelings unbiased to trace distance $<0.01$). On a single consumer GPU, projector unraveling reaches a target standard error with $20.8\times$ fewer trajectories than Qiskit-Aer's \texttt{batched\_shots\_gpu} at $n=10$, a factor that holds at $19$--$26\times$ across $n=8$--$20$. A regime map places analog sampling optimal at weak noise and projector at strong noise, crossing near $γt\approx0.35$. We further report a systems finding: Qiskit-Aer applies noise at the \emph{channel} level and reconstructs a canonical Kraus decomposition at apply time, discarding any user-supplied unraveling, so variance-reduced unravelings cannot be delivered through its public API. Because Aer's Born-rule collapse machinery already exists, we specify a minimal change that would unlock the technique in production.

AI.tldr: This paper implements variance-reduced unravelings (projector and analog sampling) on a GPU dense-statevector trajectory engine, achieving up to 26× fewer trajectories than Qiskit-Aer's batched_shots_gpu for projector unraveling, and reveals that Qiskit-Aer's architecture prevents user-supplied unravelings due to channel-level noise application.
AI.motivation: Monte-Carlo trajectory methods for noisy quantum circuits suffer from high estimator variance, requiring thousands of trajectories for one expectation value. Recent tensor-network work proposed variance-reduced unravelings but only on CPU matrix-product-state backends with no path to production tooling.
AI.method: Implemented projector and analog sampling unravelings on a GPU dense-statevector trajectory engine; validated against exact density matrix; compared trajectory count reductions against Qiskit-Aer's batched_shots_gpu across n=8–20 qubits; analyzed Qiskit-Aer's noise application architecture.
AI.result: Projector unraveling achieves 20.8× fewer trajectories at n=10, holding at 19–26× across n=8–20; all unravelings unbiased to trace distance <0.01; ideal-circuit fidelity 1−2.2×10⁻¹⁶; analog sampling optimal at weak noise, projector at strong noise, crossing near γt≈0.35; Aer applies noise at channel level, discarding user-supplied unravelings.
AI.conclusion: Variance-reduced unravelings are practical on GPU backends with significant trajectory savings. However, they cannot be delivered through Qiskit-Aer's public API due to its channel-level noise architecture; a minimal change to Aer's Born-rule collapse machinery would unlock this technique in production.

title: Quantum Key Distribution Beyond Stationary Channels
summary: Quantum key distribution (QKD) over non-stationary channels, such as satellite links, is characterized by short, high-loss, and strongly fluctuating transmission windows that produce sparse detection events. In many QKD protocols, these data must be analyzed using non-IID statistical inequalities, yet existing methods either become loose for small sample sizes or heavily rely on fine-tuning, yielding poor estimates when the optical channel is mis-modeled. Using mixture martingale techniques, we introduce tight concentration inequalities that retain sharpness when the channel model is accurate, while remaining robust to model mismatch. In realistic simulations of satellite QKD with fluctuating loss, the resulting bounds can reduce the minimum required number of transmitted signals by more than $70\%$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces tight concentration inequalities using mixture martingale techniques for QKD over non-stationary channels (e.g., satellite links), which reduce required transmitted signals by over 70% in realistic simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing statistical methods for QKD over non-stationary channels (e.g., satellite links) are either too loose for small sample sizes or overly reliant on fine-tuning, leading to poor estimates when the optical channel is mis-modeled.
AI.method: The authors use mixture martingale techniques to derive concentration inequalities that are sharp under accurate channel models and robust to model mismatch.
AI.result: In realistic simulations of satellite QKD with fluctuating loss, the proposed bounds reduce the minimum required number of transmitted signals by more than 70%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed mixture martingale-based concentration inequalities offer a significant improvement in efficiency and robustness for QKD over non-stationary channels, enabling more practical satellite QKD implementations.

title: Image Classification on IBM Quantum Computers
summary: Quantum machine learning on real noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware has remained largely confined to binary or few-class tasks, limited by the cost of on-hardware training and the underuse of large devices at inference. We present a unified framework that classifies ten-class MNIST end-to-end on a $127$-qubit IBM Eagle processor, with three central contributions. First, a two-phase protocol decouples a gradient-based classical optimization of the encoder and readout from a gradient-free optimization of the quantum parameters, removing the parameter-shift gradient cost that makes on-hardware training impractical. Second, we introduce Quantum Multi-Programming to a trained quantum classifier for the first time, packing multiple circuit copies onto one device to deliver parallel inference at no mean-accuracy cost while cutting quantum-processor job submissions proportionally. Third, a controlled comparison shows that on-hardware fine-tuning yields no measurable accuracy gain, motivating a practical NISQ workflow: train on a classical simulator and reserve the hardware for inference only. Benchmarked against a matched-capacity classical network, the quantum module shows no per-parameter accuracy advantage at this scale; we therefore frame the work as a feasibility-and-workflow demonstration for multi-class quantum image classification on current hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates end-to-end ten-class MNIST classification on a 127-qubit IBM Eagle processor, introducing three key contributions: (1) a two-phase training protocol that avoids costly parameter-shift gradients, (2) Quantum Multi-Programming for parallel inference, and (3) evidence that on-hardware fine-tuning provides no accuracy gain, suggesting a simulator-for-training, hardware-for-inference workflow.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning on NISQ hardware is largely limited to binary or few-class tasks due to the prohibitive cost of on-hardware training and underutilization of large devices at inference.
AI.method: The framework includes: (1) a two-phase protocol decoupling gradient-based classical optimization (encoder/readout) from gradient-free quantum parameter optimization; (2) Quantum Multi-Programming packing multiple circuit copies onto one device for parallel inference; (3) a controlled comparison of on-hardware fine-tuning vs. simulator training.
AI.result: Ten-class MNIST classification on a 127-qubit IBM Eagle processor. Quantum Multi-Programming cuts quantum job submissions proportionally with no mean-accuracy loss. On-hardware fine-tuning shows no measurable accuracy gain. The quantum module shows no per-parameter accuracy advantage over a matched-capacity classical network.
AI.conclusion: The work is a feasibility-and-workflow demonstration for multi-class quantum image classification on current NISQ hardware, with a practical recommendation: train on classical simulators, reserve hardware for inference only.

title: Formal Verification of Continuous-Variable Quantum Programs
summary: We provide a formal framework for Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing (CQC). While CQC is supported by photonic quantum hardware, we are not aware of a formal semantics for continuous-variable quantum programs nor of a unary Hoare logic for their verification. There are several technical obstacles to extending to CQC any of the formal frameworks available for Discrete-Variable Quantum Computing (DQC). Most importantly, continuous-variable quantum programs act on {\em infinite-dimensional} Hilbert spaces; their measurement outcomes are often {\em unbounded} and have expected values that are defined by an improper integral (or an infinite series), which may not converge. We overcome these challenges to give a formal semantics to a universal programming language for CQC and to provide the first Hoare logic for CQC. The assertions of our logic are built from polynomials over canonical observables. Besides proving relative completeness, we implement a symbolic weakest-precondition calculator for CQC based on our logic. Our tool has successfully verified CQC algorithms from textbooks and calculated their approximation errors for physically realizable implementations, proved the correctness (i.e., equivalence) of gate decompositions for CQC hardware, and computed the resource requirements (i.e., number of photon-number states) for achieving a desired accuracy in the classical simulation of continuous-variable quantum programs.

AI.tldr: The paper provides the first formal semantics and Hoare logic for Continuous-Variable Quantum Computing (CQC), addressing challenges of infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, unbounded measurements, and convergence issues. The authors implement a symbolic weakest-precondition calculator and demonstrate its use on textbook algorithms, gate decompositions, and resource estimation.
AI.motivation: No formal semantics or Hoare logic existed for continuous-variable quantum programs, despite CQC being supported by photonic quantum hardware. Extending DQC frameworks to CQC is technically challenging due to infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, unbounded measurement outcomes, and non-convergent expectations.
AI.method: The authors develop a formal semantics for a universal CQC programming language and construct the first Hoare logic for CQC using polynomial assertions over canonical observables. They prove relative completeness and implement a symbolic weakest-precondition calculator.
AI.result: The tool successfully verified CQC textbook algorithms, computed approximation errors for physical implementations, proved correctness of gate decompositions for CQC hardware, and calculated resource requirements (photon-number states) for achieving desired accuracy in classical simulation of CQC programs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed formal framework overcomes fundamental obstacles (infinite-dimensional spaces, unbounded measurements, convergence issues) and provides a practically useful verification tool for continuous-variable quantum computing.

title: Light-Cone Scaling of In-Circuit Noise in Randomized Measurements
summary: Randomized measurements provide an efficient way to extract physical properties of an unknown quantum state from limited data. On near-term hardware, gate and readout errors bias the reconstructed observables. Here we develop a microscopic description of this bias for locally scrambled shallow circuits. Independent local twirling reduces local implementation noise to stochastic Pauli damping, and a noise event contributes only when it overlaps the Heisenberg evolution of the measured Pauli operator. This gives an activated path-average formula for the noisy Pauli coefficient. In one-dimensional shallow circuits, the activated noise volume grows linearly with the size of a contiguous observable, leading to an exponential damping ratio. We verify this scaling for two-qubit random Clifford and locally scrambled iSWAP circuits with two-qubit Pauli noise, including spatial fluctuations and temporal drift. The scaling supports a small-string calibration protocol that predicts larger string observables without learning the full noisy measurement channel. Our result relates the noise bias of shallow-shadow protocols directly to operator-evolving dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a microscopic description of noise bias in randomized measurements (shallow shadows) with locally scrambled circuits, showing that noise acts as stochastic Pauli damping and only affects observables when it overlaps the Heisenberg evolution of the measured Pauli operator. This leads to an activated path-average formula and exponential damping in 1D shallow circuits, enabling a calibration protocol for large observables without learning the full noise channel.
AI.motivation: Gate and readout errors in near-term quantum hardware bias observables extracted from randomized measurements. The authors aim to provide a microscopic, theoretically grounded understanding of how this noise bias arises in locally scrambled shallow circuits, and to develop a practical calibration protocol that predicts large-string observables without full channel learning.
AI.method: The authors use independent local twirling to reduce local implementation noise to stochastic Pauli damping. They derive an activated path-average formula for noisy Pauli coefficients by analyzing when noise events overlap the Heisenberg evolution of the measured Pauli operator. They verify scaling with two-qubit random Clifford and locally scrambled iSWAP circuits with spatially fluctuating and temporally drifting two-qubit Pauli noise.
AI.result: In one-dimensional shallow circuits, the activated noise volume grows linearly with the size of a contiguous observable, producing exponential damping. The proposed small-string calibration protocol successfully predicts larger string observables without learning the full noisy measurement channel. The scaling predictions are verified numerically for Clifford and iSWAP circuits under realistic noise conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work directly relates the noise bias of shallow-shadow protocols to operator-evolving dynamics, providing both a fundamental understanding of noise effects in randomized measurements and a practical calibration scheme that avoids the exponential cost of full channel tomography.

title: Geometry-Resolved Projection of RF Imbalance to Ion Micromotion in a Same-Phase Dual-RF Blade Trap
comment: Main text: 4 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary material: 3 pages, 1 figure, and 4 tables
summary: Common-mode metrics of a high-$Q$ helical resonator do not determine the residual ion-side field in a dual-electrode drive. We combine a two-node differential RF model with single-electrode finite-element bases to obtain a computation-only, geometry-resolved projection for a same-phase blade trap. For a 3.5 pF external load per branch, the model gives a total effective branch capacitance of 7.640 pF and an HWHM-equivalent full branch-difference scale of 12.7 fF at $Q_{\mathrm{loaded}}=600$. The seven-segment geometry gives center and axial-RMS differential field coefficients of 640 V m$^{-1}$ and 635 V m$^{-1}$ per differential peak volt. A representative 10 fF mismatch with an effective 0.1 pF balance scale projects to 44.5/44.1 nm center/RMS $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}^{+}$ micromotion at 100 V common peak voltage. Supplementary thermal, bypass-admittance, and tested numerical cases characterize model sensitivity. All reported displacements are projections; no RF-bench or ion-side validation is claimed.

AI.tldr: A computational model using a two-node differential RF model with finite-element bases predicts micromotion in a dual-electrode blade trap, showing that common-mode metrics alone cannot determine residual ion-side fields. For a representative 10 fF mismatch, the model projects ~44.5 nm center/44.1 nm RMS micromotion for ¹⁷¹Yb⁺ at 100 V common peak voltage, without experimental validation.
AI.motivation: To show that common-mode metrics of a high-Q helical resonator are insufficient for determining the residual ion-side field in a dual-electrode drive, and to provide a computation-only, geometry-resolved projection method.
AI.method: Combines a two-node differential RF model with single-electrode finite-element bases to compute field projections for a same-phase blade trap, using a seven-segment geometry and analyzing effects of mismatch, thermal, bypass-admittance, and numerical sensitivity.
AI.result: Total effective branch capacitance of 7.640 pF, HWHM-equivalent full branch-difference scale of 12.7 fF at Q_loaded=600, differential field coefficients of 640 V/m (center) and 635 V/m (axial-RMS) per differential peak volt. A 10 fF mismatch with 0.1 pF balance scale projects 44.5/44.1 nm center/RMS micromotion for ¹⁷¹Yb⁺ at 100 V.
AI.conclusion: Common-mode metrics alone are insufficient; a geometry-resolved differential model is necessary to predict residual ion-side fields. All reported displacements are projections without experimental validation.

title: Stochastic Pauli-path simulator for large-scale quantum optimization
summary: Pauli-based simulators offer a promising route to large-scale classical simulation of quantum circuits in the low-magic regime. Yet their applicability remains largely limited to forward simulation, making them inadequate for optimization-driven quantum tasks such as variational state preparation and parameter initialization. Existing approaches either lack native support for gradient-based optimization or suffer from severe gradient bias. Here we propose the stochastic Pauli-path simulator (SPPS), a computational framework for large-scale quantum optimization that enables unbiased stochastic gradient estimation via Pauli-path sampling across optimization iterations. Our theoretical analysis shows that the proposed simulator yields unbiased gradient estimates and admits provable convergence guarantees. We systematically evaluate our proposal, including quantum eigensolver benchmarks with up to 100 qubits and quantum neural network benchmarks with up to 40 qubits. Across these tasks, SPPS faithfully tracks optimization dynamics, converges within minutes, and broadens the role of Pauli-based simulation from forward estimation to large-scale quantum optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the stochastic Pauli-path simulator (SPPS), a framework for large-scale quantum optimization that provides unbiased stochastic gradient estimation via Pauli-path sampling, enabling convergence guarantees and practical optimization for up to 100 qubits.
AI.motivation: Pauli-based simulators are limited to forward simulation and cannot support gradient-based optimization tasks like variational state preparation and parameter initialization, due to lack of native gradient support or severe gradient bias.
AI.method: SPPS enables unbiased stochastic gradient estimation by sampling Pauli paths across optimization iterations, with theoretical guarantees of unbiasedness and convergence.
AI.result: Demonstrated on quantum eigensolver benchmarks with up to 100 qubits and quantum neural network benchmarks with up to 40 qubits; SPPS tracks optimization dynamics, converges within minutes.
AI.conclusion: SPPS broadens Pauli-based simulation from forward estimation to large-scale quantum optimization, enabling practical optimization-driven quantum tasks.

title: High-frequency dual-channel lock-in detection via rapidly oscillating driving
summary: Here we propose a general protocol for dual-channel lock-in detection of high-frequency ac signals. We find that the effect of a high-frequency target signal can be modulated through the application of rapidly oscillating driving fields. Based on this mechanism, we develop a quantum dual-channel lock-in detection protocol for high-frequency signals, which not only extends the accessible frequency range of quantum sensing but also enables the simultaneous estimation of the signal amplitude and initial phase. Furthermore, we present a feasible implementation scheme of the protocol based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed protocol can effectively filter out background noise and significantly improve the signal-to-noise ratio. Our results provide a promising approach for realizing noise-resistant detection of weak signals in the high-frequency regime.

AI.tldr: A quantum dual-channel lock-in detection protocol using rapidly oscillating driving fields to modulate high-frequency ac signals, enabling extended frequency range, simultaneous amplitude and phase estimation, and noise-resistant detection, with implementation feasibility demonstrated via nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond.
AI.motivation: To extend the accessible frequency range of quantum sensing and enable simultaneous estimation of signal amplitude and initial phase for high-frequency ac signals, while improving noise resistance.
AI.method: A general dual-channel lock-in detection protocol that modulates high-frequency target signals using rapidly oscillating driving fields, implemented with nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show the protocol effectively filters background noise and significantly improves the signal-to-noise ratio.
AI.conclusion: The protocol offers a promising approach for noise-resistant detection of weak signals in the high-frequency regime.

title: Entanglement geometry separates circuit cutting, classical hardness, and trainability
summary: Circuit cutting promises to scale quantum computations beyond current hardware, but variational quantum advantage also requires low cutting overhead, classical hardness, and trainability. We show that these properties are strongly constrained by entanglement geometry. Matrix product state (MPS) and tree tensor network (TTN) circuits with constant seam bond dimension can be cut with \(O(1/\varepsilon^2)\) sampling overhead, but remain efficiently classically simulable, ruling out asymptotic quantum advantage within these families. By independently controlling seam and intra-block entanglement, we construct a two-block circuit family that remains cheaply cuttable while requiring a super-polynomial global MPS bond dimension, as supported numerically up to \(n=100\). However, MPS hardness and trainability require incompatible depth regimes, \(d=ω(\log n)\) and \(d=O(\log n)\), respectively. Using magic rather than entanglement as the hardness resource avoids this conflict: shallow Clifford+\(T\) circuits remain cuttable and trainable while their stabiliser-simulation cost grows exponentially with the \(T\)-count.

AI.tldr: Circuit cutting for variational quantum advantage is constrained by entanglement geometry: MPS/TTN circuits with constant seam bond dimension are cuttable but classically simulable; a two-block circuit can be cheaply cuttable yet require super-polynomial MPS bond dimension, but MPS hardness and trainability require incompatible depth regimes; using magic (T-count) instead of entanglement as the hardness resource avoids this conflict.
AI.motivation: To scale quantum computations beyond current hardware via circuit cutting while maintaining low overhead, classical hardness, and trainability, which are strongly constrained by entanglement geometry.
AI.method: Analyzes entanglement geometry constraints on circuit cutting for MPS and TTN circuits, constructs a two-block circuit family with independent seam and intra-block entanglement control, and proposes using magic (Clifford+T circuits) instead of entanglement as the hardness resource.
AI.result: MPS/TTN circuits with constant seam bond dimension have O(1/ε²) sampling overhead but remain classically simulable. A two-block circuit family is cheaply cuttable while requiring super-polynomial MPS bond dimension (numerically supported up to n=100). MPS hardness requires d=ω(log n) while trainability requires d=O(log n), creating incompatibility. Shallow Clifford+T circuits avoid this conflict, remaining cuttable and trainable while stabiliser-simulation cost grows exponentially with T-count.
AI.conclusion: Circuit cutting for variational quantum advantage faces fundamental trade-offs governed by entanglement geometry, but using magic as a hardness resource (rather than entanglement) can reconcile cutting efficiency, classical hardness, and trainability.

title: Unifying Charge-Learnability Transitions in U(1)-Symmetric Quantum Circuits through Informational Power of Local Measurement
summary: Charge-learnability transitions in monitored symmetric quantum circuits reveal how local measurement records acquire sufficient information to infer a conserved charge. Here we extend charge learnability to probabilistic weak measurements, for which the measurement probability and measurement strength are independently tunable. We find that the learnability phase boundary is organized by the informational power of local measurement. We further introduce cross entropy as a label-sensitive diagnostic that distinguishes unbiased, biased, and antibiased decoder variants. Finally, the exact record--label mutual information provides a decoder-independent benchmark for the information fundamentally available for charge inference. Our results establish informational power of local measurement as a unifying principle for charge learnability under general monitoring protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper studies charge-learnability transitions in monitored symmetric quantum circuits under probabilistic weak measurements, finding that the learnability phase boundary is organized by the informational power of local measurement. It introduces cross entropy as a label-sensitive diagnostic and uses exact record-label mutual information as a decoder-independent benchmark.
AI.motivation: To extend charge learnability from projective measurements to probabilistic weak measurements, where measurement probability and strength are independently tunable, and to establish a unifying principle for charge inference under general monitoring protocols.
AI.method: The study analyzes charge-learnability transitions in monitored symmetric quantum circuits with probabilistic weak measurements, using informational power of local measurement to organize the phase boundary, and introducing cross entropy as a diagnostic for different decoder variants.
AI.result: The learnability phase boundary is organized by the informational power of local measurement. Cross entropy serves as a label-sensitive diagnostic distinguishing unbiased, biased, and antibiased decoders. Exact record-label mutual information provides a decoder-independent benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Informational power of local measurement is established as a unifying principle for charge learnability under general monitoring protocols.

title: How the Quantum Sorites Phenomenon Strengthens the Bell Argument and How a Random-Matrix Collapse Dynamics Answers It
summary: Bell proved that no theory of pre-existing local values can reproduce the predictions of quantum mechanics, but his proof leaves the culprit ambiguous: one may reject either of two independence conditions, Outcome Independence or Parameter Independence, and most commentators have found Outcome Independence the safer sacrifice. The first part of this paper presents, in a form adapted to spin-1/2 particles in the singlet state, an argument (Forster 2014) that removes the ambiguity: using a chained family of experiments in which quantum mechanics predicts an extreme pattern of correlations -- the quantum Sorites phenomenon -- a contradiction is derived without ever assuming Outcome Independence. Under the resulting theorem, anyone who holds that hidden variables could improve on the quantum probabilities must give up Parameter Independence itself. That looks like a heavy price, because Parameter Independence appears to be protected twice over: rejecting it seems to put superluminal influences into spacetime, and its statistical shadow -- the No-Signaling condition -- is experimentally beyond reproach The second part of the paper shows that the price is payable. In the random-matrix collapse dynamics proposed by Kryukov, measurement is a random walk of the quantum state, and the hidden variable is not a stock of values fixed at the source but the random stream that drives the walk -- like the stored random numbers of a computer simulation, with the measurement settings playing the role of seeds. In that framework Parameter Independence is false while Outcome Independence and No-Signaling are both true, and one can say exactly how the Sorites argument is blocked, why the violation involves no process propagating in spacetime, and why the influence of one wing's setting on the other wing's outcome -- demonstrated here in a simulation -- can never be used to send a message.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves Bell's ambiguity by presenting a chained Bell experiment (quantum Sorites) that proves hidden variable theories must reject Parameter Independence, not just Outcome Independence. It then shows this cost is payable via Kryukov's random-matrix collapse dynamics, where hidden variables are random streams (like computer simulation seeds) that violate Parameter Independence while preserving No-Signaling.
AI.motivation: To resolve the longstanding ambiguity in Bell's theorem about whether hidden variable theories must sacrifice Outcome Independence or Parameter Independence, and to show that sacrificing Parameter Independence is actually viable.
AI.method: A chained family of experiments (quantum Sorites phenomenon) is used to derive a contradiction without assuming Outcome Independence, proving Parameter Independence must go. Then Kryukov's random-matrix collapse model is presented where the hidden variable is a random stream driving state evolution, not fixed values at the source.
AI.result: Hidden variable theories must reject Parameter Independence, not Outcome Independence. The random-matrix model demonstrates Parameter Independence can be false while Outcome Independence and No-Signaling both hold, with a simulation showing cross-wing setting influence without signaling capability.
AI.conclusion: The apparent heavy price of rejecting Parameter Independence is payable: Kryukov's framework shows how superluminal influence can exist without superluminal signaling, exactly blocking the Sorites argument while preserving No-Signaling.

title: Sensing relativistic quantum fields with minimally perturbing local measurements
summary: We develop a framework for minimally perturbing local measurements in relativistic quantum field theory, with the aim to sense local properties of the field in a non-destructive manner. The field properties are sensed by weakly coupled pointers and encapsulated in conditional expectation values dependent on a postselection of the field state. Our operational protocol uses causally admissible Kraus updates for the field, in line with recent relativistic measurement theories, keeping in mind restrictions related to ``impossible measurements''. We illustrate our approach with three applications: a spacelikeness detector for causal-structure sensing, counting particle-creation densities in a supercritical potential and non-destructive discrimination between entangled states of the field and mixtures.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a framework for minimally perturbing local measurements in relativistic quantum field theory, using weakly coupled pointers and conditional expectations to sense field properties non-destructively, with applications to causal-structure sensing, particle creation detection, and entangled state discrimination.
AI.motivation: To enable non-destructive sensing of local properties in relativistic quantum field theory while respecting causality and avoiding "impossible measurements."
AI.method: The framework uses weakly coupled pointers to sense field properties, with conditional expectation values dependent on postselection of the field state. It employs causally admissible Kraus updates for the field, consistent with relativistic measurement theories.
AI.result: Three applications are demonstrated: a spacelikeness detector for causal-structure sensing, counting particle-creation densities in a supercritical potential, and non-destructive discrimination between entangled field states and mixtures.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables minimally perturbing local measurements in relativistic QFT, providing practical tools for quantum sensing while respecting relativistic constraints.

title: Variational non-gaussian approach to interacting spin-boson models
summary: We apply a hybrid variational framework to interacting spin-boson Hamiltonians, targeting regimes where simulations are limited by the unbounded bosonic Hilbert space and strong many-body correlations. The bosonic sector and spin-boson correlations are captured within a compact non-Gaussian variational manifold, while the minimized spin sector is obtained as the solution to an effective spin Hamiltonian. Minimization is carried out inside a self-consistent energy-minimization loop, where variational parameters are minimized and the effective Hamiltonian is solved via DMRG. The results are obtained without eliminating or truncating the photonic field. We benchmark the method on the Dicke and Dicke-Ising models by comparison to converged spin-boson DMRG, finding accurate ground-state solutions with reduced bond dimension.

AI.tldr: A hybrid variational framework for spin-boson Hamiltonians is proposed, combining non-Gaussian bosonic manifolds with DMRG-solved effective spin Hamiltonians, achieving accurate ground states without photon truncation.
AI.motivation: To overcome limitations in simulating spin-boson systems caused by unbounded bosonic Hilbert spaces and strong many-body correlations.
AI.method: A hybrid variational approach where: (1) bosonic and spin-boson correlations are captured via a compact non-Gaussian variational manifold, (2) the spin sector is solved as an effective spin Hamiltonian using DMRG, (3) minimization runs in a self-consistent loop without truncating the photonic field.
AI.result: Benchmarked on Dicke and Dicke-Ising models against converged spin-boson DMRG, the method yields accurate ground-state solutions with reduced bond dimension.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid framework accurately handles strongly correlated spin-boson systems without photonic field truncation, achieving efficiency gains via reduced bond dimensions.

title: Noise structuring in fixed-depth Trotter simulation: stationary channels and observable-level depolarization
summary: We analyze fixed-depth Trotter simulation as a method for structuring hardware noise in digital many-body dynamics. The number of layers is chosen using the largest endpoint time and is then kept fixed throughout the time scan, making the total noise dose approximately independent of the endpoint time. For local stochastic faults, we show that, once propagated faults lose memory of their insertion layer, the noisy circuit factorizes into ideal evolution followed by a stationary finite-depth binomial channel. In the dilute-layer limit, this channel reduces to a Poissonian exponential. The memory time of a single fault is related to a Loschmidt echo. An important consequence is observable-level depolarization: for selected macroscopic observables at low to moderate noise levels, the stationary channel can act as an almost time-independent affine contrast correction, even though the full channel need not be depolarizing, which is crusial for error mitigation purposes. At short times, the same protocol produces a digital Zeno-like transient, in which a fixed number of noise opportunities competes with a vanishing coherent angle per layer. Our results also reveal limitations of naive zero-noise extrapolatin strategies based on oversimplified functions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes fixed-depth Trotter simulation as a method for structuring hardware noise in digital many-body dynamics. It shows that with a fixed number of layers, noise becomes approximately time-independent and factorizes into ideal evolution followed by a stationary binomial channel, which at low noise acts as an affine contrast correction. The work also reveals limitations of naive zero-noise extrapolation strategies.
AI.motivation: To understand and structure hardware noise in digital quantum simulations of many-body dynamics, particularly how fixed-depth Trotter circuits can make noise approximately stationary (time-independent), which is beneficial for error mitigation.
AI.method: The authors analyze fixed-depth Trotter simulation where the number of layers is chosen based on the largest endpoint time and kept fixed throughout the time scan. They study local stochastic faults, showing that once propagated faults lose memory of their insertion layer, the noisy circuit factorizes into ideal evolution followed by a stationary finite-depth binomial channel. In the dilute-layer limit, this reduces to a Poissonian exponential. The memory time of a single fault is related to a Loschmidt echo.

At short times, the protocol produces a digital Zeno-like transient. The results also reveal limitations of naive zero-noise extrapolation strategies based on oversimplified functions.
AI.conclusion: Fixed-depth Trotter simulation is a promising strategy for making noise approximately stationary in digital quantum simulations, enabling effective error mitigation via simple affine corrections. However, care must be taken with zero-noise extrapolation approaches, as oversimplified noise models can lead to inaccurate results.

title: Strong Quantum Mpemba Effect from Exact Slow-Mode Selection in Constrained Rydberg Chains
summary:
Can a many-body state relax faster because it is blind to the slowest decay channel? We show that this mechanism gives rise to a robust strong quantum Mpemba effect in locally dephased constrained Rydberg chains. The key observation is that, for constrained single-spin-flip Hamiltonians, local dephasing turns the Hamiltonian itself into an exact left Liouvillian slow mode,
  $\mathcal L^\dagger(H)=-γH$.
  A thermal state generically retains this slow channel, whereas translationally invariant states with vanishing energy expectation remove it and are forced to relax through faster visible modes. This exact selection rule produces a strong quantum Mpemba effect in the locally dephased PXP chain, including for a zero-energy scar eigenstate, the $|0\cdots0\rangle$ product state, and a translation-invariant $Z_2$ cat state. We further show that the same mechanism persists in the $(2,3)$ model and in the longer-range blockade family. Our results identify exact slow-mode selection, rather than special scar wave functions, as a general organizing principle for anomalously fast relaxation in constrained open quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that strong quantum Mpemba effect (faster relaxation from hotter initial states) arises in dephased constrained Rydberg chains because certain states are "blind" to a slow decay channel—the Hamiltonian itself becomes an exact left Liouvillian slow mode, and states with zero energy expectation remove this channel, forcing faster relaxation through visible modes.
AI.motivation: To understand whether a many-body state can relax faster because it is blind to the slowest decay channel, and to identify a general organizing principle for anomalously fast relaxation in constrained open quantum systems beyond special scar wave functions.
AI.method: The authors study locally dephased constrained Rydberg chains (PXP chain, (2,3) model, longer-range blockade models). They show analytically that for constrained single-spin-flip Hamiltonians, local dephasing turns the Hamiltonian into an exact left Liouvillian slow mode with $\mathcal L^\dagger(H)=-γH$. They identify that translationally invariant states with vanishing energy expectation remove this slow channel, forcing relaxation through faster visible modes.
AI.result: The exact selection rule produces a strong quantum Mpemba effect in the locally dephased PXP chain for zero-energy scar eigenstate, $|0\cdots0\rangle$ product state, and translation-invariant $Z_2$ cat state. The mechanism persists in the $(2,3)$ model and longer-range blockade families.
AI.conclusion: Exact slow-mode selection, rather than special scar wave functions, serves as a general organizing principle for anomalously fast relaxation in constrained open quantum systems.

title: New bound on $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting Bell locality of a nonseparable Werner state
summary: In many quantum applications it is important to know whether or not a Bell nonlocal two-qudit state exhibits its nonlocality under correlation scenarios with some given numbers $S_{1},S_{2}\geq1$ of generalized quantum measurements at two sites. In the present article, we find analytically a new general condition sufficient for a nonseparable Werner state with a dimension $d\leq\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\}$ to satisfy all Bell inequalities under every $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting correlation scenario with outcomes of an arbitrary spectral type, discrete or continuous $-$ that is, to be $S_{1}\times S_{2}$-setting Bell local, for short. For a variety of $S_{1},S_{2}\geq1$ values, this new general locality condition is beyond Werner's and Barrett's locality conditions for a nonseparable Werner state. We also prove explicitly in the operator terms the optimization result by Terhal et. el. [Phys. Rev. Lett. \textbf{90,} 157903 (2003)] via semi-programming that every nonseparable Werner state with a dimension $d>\min\{S_{1},S_{2}\}$ is $S_{1}\times S_{2}$ -setting Bell local. The new results of the present article are important both for Bell nonlocality theory and for quantum applications based on Bell nonlocality.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a new analytical condition for Werner states to be Bell local under S₁×S₂-setting correlation scenarios with arbitrary outcome types, generalizing Werner's and Barrett's conditions. It also proves Terhal et al.'s optimization result in operator terms, showing that Werner states with d > min{S₁, S₂} are S₁×S₂-setting Bell local.
AI.motivation: Determining whether a Bell nonlocal two-qudit state exhibits nonlocality under correlation scenarios with given numbers S₁, S₂ ≥ 1 of generalized quantum measurements at two sites is important for many quantum applications.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of a new general sufficient condition for nonseparable Werner states with dimension d ≤ min{S₁, S₂} to satisfy all Bell inequalities under S₁×S₂-setting correlation scenarios with arbitrary spectral type outcomes. Explicit operator-term proof of Terhal et al.'s optimization result via semi-programming.
AI.result: A new general locality condition beyond Werner's and Barrett's conditions for nonseparable Werner states is found for various S₁, S₂ ≥ 1 values. It is proven that every nonseparable Werner state with d > min{S₁, S₂} is S₁×S₂-setting Bell local.
AI.conclusion: The results are important for both Bell nonlocality theory and quantum applications relying on Bell nonlocality.

title: Topology of the Set of Entangled State
summary:
We investigate the topology of the set $\mathsf E$ of entangled bipartite density operators acting on $\mathbb{C}^{n_1}\otimes\mathbb{C}^{n_2}$. We start by showing that $\mathsf E$ is path-connected, and even simply connected except in the two-qubit case. In this exceptional case $\mathsf E$ turns out to be homotopy equivalent to the set of maximally entangled states, which itself is homeomorphic to $\mathbb{RP}^3$. Here we also compute the complete homology of the closure and interior of $\mathsf E$.
  In all larger dimensions, we show that the homology and homotopy groups of $\mathsf E$ vanish in degrees $1\leq k\leq 2(n_1-1)(n_2-1)-2$, and all homology groups of degree $k\geq (n_1n_2)^2-3$ also vanish. This range is controlled by the space $\mathsf W$ of entanglement witnesses, which we show is highly connected beyond two qubits and homotopy equivalent to $\mathsf E$. By computing the Euler characteristic, using a torus-action fixed point argument together with Alexander duality, we show that $\mathsf E$ nevertheless has non-trivial reduced homology over every field for all $n_1, n_2 \geq 2$.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the topology of the set E of entangled bipartite density operators on ℂⁿ¹⊗ℂⁿ², showing it is path-connected and simply connected except for the two-qubit case (where it's homotopy equivalent to ℝℙ³). For larger dimensions, homology and homotopy groups vanish in certain ranges, controlled by the highly connected space W of entanglement witnesses. Despite these vanishings, E has non-trivial reduced homology over every field for all n₁,n₂≥2.
AI.motivation: To understand the global topological structure of the set of entangled quantum states, which is fundamental for quantum information theory and entanglement theory.
AI.method: Topological analysis using homotopy theory, homology computation, torus-action fixed point arguments, Alexander duality, and the relationship between entanglement witnesses W and the entangled state space E.
AI.result: E is path-connected and simply connected except in two-qubit case (homotopy equivalent to ℝℙ³). For larger dimensions, homology and homotopy groups vanish for 1≤k≤2(n₁-1)(n₂-1)-2 and for k≥(n₁n₂)²-3. Reduced homology is non-trivial over every field for all n₁,n₂≥2.
AI.conclusion: The entangled state space has rich topological structure with both vanishing and non-vanishing homology groups, revealing its complex connectivity properties that depend on dimension.

title: Exponential Reduction of Mesh Dependence in Quantum Estimation of Parabolic PDE Observables
summary:
Can a quantum PDE algorithm avoid the polynomial cost of resolving a fine spatial mesh? For standard fixed-order discretizations, direct classical methods require work polynomial in $h^{-1}$, or equivalently in the number of spatial degrees of freedom $N_h=Θ(h^{-d})$. Direct quantum implementations of a parabolic semigroup still have coherent complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(\sqrt{T}/h)$, and gradient-dependent observables such as heat flux and dissipation introduce additional mesh dependence. Decay of the solution norm will further suppress the postselection probability for preparing a normalized final state.
  We develop a multilevel quantum algorithm that estimates linear and quadratic observables $directly$ and places the fine--coarse cancellation inside the circuit before measurement. A contour-based LCU reconstructs each target-time correction from a coherent family of shifted resolvent differences. Rather than block encoding the fine and coarse inverses separately, we encode their difference through a shifted Ritz--Schur factorization, exposing its $\mathcal O(h_\ell^2)$ two-grid normalization. For Fourier hierarchies, the corresponding SELECT oracle consists of a quantum Fourier or sine transform, a spectral-band selector, and reversible diagonal arithmetic. We also give a non-Fourier realization based on energy-orthogonal dyadic midpoint details in one dimension, together with structured tensor-product extensions under fixed-rank coefficient and access assumptions.
  For readouts with derivative order $0\leχ\le2$, optimized amplitude estimation removes $all$ polynomial dependence on the finest mesh size. Under the stated access assumptions, both linear and quadratic observables can be estimated with complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(1+(Tε)^{-1})$, with only polylogarithmic dependence on $h^{-1}$.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a multilevel quantum algorithm for PDEs that eliminates polynomial dependence on mesh size ($h^{-1}$) for estimating linear and quadratic observables. By incorporating fine-coarse cancellation inside the quantum circuit via a contour-based LCU and shifted Ritz-Schur factorization, the algorithm achieves complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(1+(T\varepsilon)^{-1})$ with only polylogarithmic dependence on $h^{-1}$, overcoming the polynomial mesh cost that plagues both classical and standard quantum PDE solvers.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum PDE algorithms still suffer polynomial cost in $h^{-1}$ (mesh resolution), and gradient-dependent observables introduce additional mesh dependence. Moreover, decay of the solution norm suppresses postselection probability. The goal is to eliminate all polynomial mesh dependence when estimating observables.
AI.method: A multilevel quantum algorithm that: (1) places fine-coarse cancellation inside the circuit before measurement; (2) uses a contour-based LCU to reconstruct target-time corrections from shifted resolvent differences; (3) encodes the difference of fine and coarse inverses via a shifted Ritz-Schur factorization, exposing $\mathcal O(h_\ell^2)$ two-grid normalization; (4) implements SELECT oracles via quantum Fourier/sine transform and spectral-band selectors for Fourier hierarchies, or energy-orthogonal dyadic midpoint details for non-Fourier cases; (5) applies optimized amplitude estimation for derivative orders $0\le\chi\le2$.
AI.result: The algorithm removes all polynomial dependence on the finest mesh size for readouts with derivative order $0\le\chi\le2$. Under stated access assumptions, both linear and quadratic observables can be estimated with complexity $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(1+(T\varepsilon)^{-1})$, achieving only polylogarithmic dependence on $h^{-1}$.
AI.conclusion: A multilevel quantum PDE algorithm can indeed avoid the polynomial cost of resolving a fine spatial mesh. By embedding multilevel cancellation into the quantum circuit itself, the approach eliminates mesh-dependent polynomial overhead for observable estimation, offering exponential improvement over both classical and naive quantum methods.

title: CutBackdoor: A Circuit Cut Triggered Backdoor Attack on Variational Quantum Algorithms
summary:
Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) are a leading paradigm for near-term quantum computing, combining parameterized quantum circuits with classical optimization across quantum chemistry, combinatorial optimization, and quantum machine learning. Since real-world VQA deployments routinely require circuits that exceed available hardware capacity, quantum circuit cutting has become an indispensable execution strategy, and pre-trained parameters are increasingly distributed through public repositories, introducing supply-chain security risks that have received little attention. Prior quantum backdoor attacks either introduce detectable circuit modifications or depend on device-specific noise, and none consider circuit cutting as an attack surface. We present CutBackdoor, the first parameter-supply-chain backdoor that uses cut circuit execution from CutQC as the deployment-time trigger against VQAs. Under noisy finite-shot circuit-cut execution, poisoned parameters preserve full-circuit validation performance while substantially increasing cut-path reconstruction error, without any circuit modification. The trigger activates when a resource-limited victim responds to a qubit-capacity mismatch by invoking the cutting workflow, requiring no attacker presence at deployment. We provide a theoretical analysis and empirically validate it across varying shot budgets. Evaluation across multiple VQA benchmarks on IBM quantum backends demonstrates cut-path energy amplification of $1.3\times$ to $2.9\times$ \revA{over clean baselines on the VQE and VQD benchmarks while maintaining small stealthiness error on the full-circuit path. The cut-path gap persists across the evaluated backends and cut placements under matched compilation; Zero-Noise Extrapolation provides only partial mitigation, and the diagonal-cost QAOA benchmark
  delineates the attack's structural boundary

AI.tldr: CutBackdoor is the first backdoor attack targeting the parameter supply chain of Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs), using circuit cutting (CutQC) as a deployment-time trigger. Poisoned parameters appear benign under full-circuit validation but substantially degrade cut-path reconstruction under noisy finite-shot execution, achieving 1.3× to 2.9× energy amplification on IBM quantum backends without detectable circuit modifications.
AI.motivation: Real-world VQA deployments often require circuits exceeding hardware capacity, making quantum circuit cutting essential. Pre-trained parameters distributed through public repositories introduce supply-chain security risks that have been largely overlooked. Existing quantum backdoor attacks either modify circuits detectably or rely on device-specific noise, and none consider circuit cutting as an attack surface.
AI.method: CutBackdoor embeds a backdoor into pre-trained VQA parameters such that the trigger activates when a resource-limited victim invokes circuit cutting (e.g., CutQC) due to qubit-capacity mismatch. Under noisy finite-shot cut-circuit execution, poisoned parameters preserve full-circuit validation fidelity while causing substantially increased cut-path reconstruction error. No circuit modification is required.
AI.result: Evaluated on multiple VQA benchmarks (VQE, VQD, QAOA) across IBM quantum backends. CutBackdoor achieves 1.3× to 2.9× cut-path energy amplification over clean baselines while maintaining small stealthiness error on the full-circuit path. The attack persists across backends and cut placements under matched compilation. Zero-Noise Extrapolation provides only partial mitigation. The diagonal-cost QAOA benchmark reveals the attack's structural boundary.
AI.conclusion: CutBackdoor introduces a new class of supply-chain backdoor attack against VQAs that leverages circuit cutting as a stealthy trigger. The attack is practical (no circuit modification, no attacker presence at deployment) and empirically robust across quantum backends, though bounded by certain problem structures (e.g., diagonal-cost QAOA).

title: Phase-Sensitive Benchmarking of Composite Quantum Gates with Chiral-Interference Circuits on Quantum Hardware
summary: We construct and experimentally implement compact gate-native circuits that simulate the state-transfer interference underlying three- and four-level chiral-resolution protocols. Both models are encoded in a two-qubit register, with the enantiomer-dependent sign of one of the couplings simulated by a conditional-phase operation in the four-level circuit and by the sign of a final rotation in the three-level circuit. On an IBM quantum processor, the two circuits produce the expected enantiomer-dependent output states with probabilities of nearly $98\%$. We then use these circuits as physically motivated, phase-sensitive benchmarks for composite quantum gates. We introduce rotation-angle error to the single-qubit operations and replace them by several composite gates, including B5, SK1, BB1, H5s, and X5. The comparison demonstrates that single-gate robustness does not translate to equivalent whole-circuit robustness. In particular, variable-rotation sequences do not preserve the required relative phases, making them unsuitable for error correction in circuits. By contrast, the H5s/X5 sequences maintain high target-state populations for relative errors as large as $50\%$, whereas elementary rotations reach the same threshold only for approximately $8\%$. The three-level circuit exhibits a similar enhancement and additionally reveals an error-cancellation symmetry whose protection under composite replacement is exact only when the relevant full propagators satisfy an inverse relation.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs and experimentally implements compact gate-native circuits simulating chiral-resolution protocols on a two-qubit quantum register. Using an IBM quantum processor, they achieve ~98% fidelity, then use these circuits as benchmarks to test composite quantum gates (B5, SK1, BB1, H5s, X5) under rotation-angle errors, finding that single-gate robustness doesn't translate to whole-circuit robustness and that H5s/X5 sequences outperform others, maintaining high fidelity up to 50% relative error compared to ~8% for elementary rotations.
AI.motivation: To construct physically motivated, phase-sensitive benchmark circuits derived from chiral-resolution protocols for testing composite quantum gates under realistic error conditions, and to investigate whether single-gate robustness properties persist at the circuit level.
AI.method: Compact gate-native circuits encoding three- and four-level chiral-resolution protocols on a two-qubit register were designed and experimentally implemented on an IBM quantum processor. The enantiomer-dependent coupling sign was simulated via conditional-phase operations (four-level) and sign of final rotation (three-level). These circuits were used as benchmarks for composite gates (B5, SK1, BB1, H5s, X5) by introducing rotation-angle errors to single-qubit operations.
AI.result: The circuits produced enantiomer-dependent output states with ~98% probability on IBM hardware. Single-gate robustness did not translate to whole-circuit robustness. Variable-rotation sequences failed to preserve required relative phases. H5s/X5 sequences maintained high target-state populations for relative errors up to 50%, while elementary rotations only reached the same threshold at ~8% error. The three-level circuit revealed an error-cancellation symmetry requiring inverse propagator relations for exact protection under composite replacement.
AI.conclusion: Composite gate robustness at the single-gate level is insufficient for circuit-level error correction; H5s/X5 sequences are significantly more robust than variable-rotation sequences and elementary rotations for phase-sensitive circuits; the discovered error-cancellation symmetry in the three-level circuit imposes constraints on composite gate design for preserving circuit-level fidelity.

title: Hardware Robustness of Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization
summary: Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) is a hybrid quantum-classical method that replaces variational optimization with a self-consistent recovery loop over QPU samples. Although SQD is considered robust to noisy samples and imperfect classical inputs, its robustness across practical deployment choices has not been systematically analyzed. As a result, shot budgets, qubit layouts, noise mitigation strategies, and the coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) amplitudes that initialize the ansatz are often chosen without clear empirical guidance. We analyze SQD robustness on IBM Heron hardware across these dimensions. Structured CCSD-amplitude perturbations, including complete zeroing, produce only modest energy shifts from the clean baseline. Differences across layouts and noise-mitigation settings are large in the first recovery iteration but narrow within a few iterations. Accuracy saturates at moderate shot budgets, while very large budgets slightly worsen recovered energies, likely because working-set selection limits the value of additional samples. These results identify where SQD provides genuine deployment robustness and where its limits remain.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically analyzes the robustness of Sample-based Quantum Diagonalization (SQD) across deployment choices (shot budgets, qubit layouts, noise mitigation, CCSD initialization) on IBM Heron hardware, finding that SQD is robust to structured amplitude perturbations, quickly converges across layouts and noise settings, and saturates at moderate shot budgets with slight degradation at very high budgets.
AI.motivation: Although SQD is considered robust to noisy samples and imperfect classical inputs, its robustness across practical deployment choices (shot budgets, qubit layouts, noise mitigation strategies, CCSD initialization) has not been systematically analyzed, leading to choices made without clear empirical guidance.
AI.method: Systematic robustness analysis of SQD on IBM Heron hardware across four deployment dimensions: structured CCSD-amplitude perturbations (including complete zeroing), qubit layouts, noise-mitigation settings, and shot budgets.
AI.result: (1) Structured CCSD-amplitude perturbations produce only modest energy shifts. (2) Layout and noise-mitigation differences are large in the first iteration but narrow within a few iterations. (3) Accuracy saturates at moderate shot budgets; very large budgets slightly worsen recovered energies due to working-set selection limits.
AI.conclusion: SQD provides genuine deployment robustness across several practical dimensions, but has identifiable limits, particularly regarding very large shot budgets where recovered energies slightly degrade.

title: QuantiSpect: A Structure-Aware Lightweight 3D CNN Pre-Decoder for Scalable Surface Code Quantum Error Correction
summary: Real-time decoding is a critical bottleneck for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. AI-based neural pre-decoders locally correct most physical errors before passing residual syndromes to a global decoder, enabling sub-microsecond latencies. However, existing architectures carry significant overhead from dense 3D convolutions. We present QuantiSpect, a lightweight 3D convolutional neural network (CNN) pre-decoder for the rotated surface code, built on the decoding pipeline of Chamberland et al. The key idea is to replace the dense 3D convolutions with three parallel branches in each residual block: a depthwise spatial branch, a depthwise temporal branch, and a grouped spatio-temporal branch, followed by a squeeze-and-excitation channel gate. This reflects the structure of surface code errors, where spatial and temporal syndrome correlations are partially separable. On a unified 4xA100 GPU benchmark, QuantiSpect matches the receptive field of the Accurate baseline at R=13 while using ~2.71x fewer parameters (0.663M vs 1.80M) and ~2.84x fewer per-voxel convolutional MACs. It matches Accurate's circuit-level threshold and accuracy at moderate and large code distances, reduces the logical error rate by up to ~1.85x relative to uncorrelated PyMatching at d=13, p=0.5%, and speeds up the PyMatching decode by up to 3.11x at d=23. We also explored enlarging the receptive field by adding blocks. Even at R=21, the model uses only 1.18M parameters, fewer than both the R=13 Accurate baseline (1.80M) and the R=17 dense model (4.22M), despite its larger receptive field. This expanded variant significantly outperforms the Accurate model, raising the circuit-level threshold to ~0.80% and further reducing the logical error rate. Together, both variants show that a structure-aware factorized design is an effective, parameter-efficient alternative to a dense one for decoding the surface code.

AI.tldr: QuantiSpect is a lightweight 3D CNN pre-decoder for surface code error correction that replaces dense 3D convolutions with factorized spatial, temporal, and grouped spatio-temporal branches plus squeeze-and-excitation gating. It achieves 2.71x fewer parameters and 2.84x fewer MACs than the Accurate baseline while matching threshold accuracy, reducing logical error rate up to 1.85x, and speeding up PyMatching decoding up to 3.11x.
AI.motivation: Real-time decoding is a critical bottleneck for large-scale fault-tolerant quantum computing. Existing AI-based neural pre-decoders suffer from significant computational overhead due to dense 3D convolutions, limiting their efficiency for sub-microsecond latency requirements.
AI.method: QuatiSpect replaces dense 3D convolutions with three parallel branches in each residual block: a depthwise spatial branch, a depthwise temporal branch, and a grouped spatio-temporal branch, followed by a squeeze-and-excitation channel gate. This factorized design exploits the partially separable spatial and temporal syndrome correlations in surface code errors.
AI.result: On a unified 4xA100 GPU benchmark: 2.71x fewer parameters (0.663M vs 1.80M), 2.84x fewer per-voxel convolutional MACs, matches circuit-level threshold and accuracy at moderate/large code distances, reduces logical error rate up to 1.85x (d=13, p=0.5%), speeds up PyMatching decode up to 3.11x (d=23). Expanded variant (R=21) uses only 1.18M parameters, raises threshold to ~0.80%.
AI.conclusion: A structure-aware factorized design is an effective, parameter-efficient alternative to dense 3D convolutions for decoding the surface code, enabling better performance with significantly lower computational cost.
